**First-run failure on any repository without a github.com origin.** Running `setup` in a local repo with no remote failed the semantic phase with:

```
semantic snapshot repo_key "local/repo" does not match current repo "local/repo-<hash>"
```

**Root cause: two independent derivations of repository identity that are not the same rule, by design.**

| | rule |
|---|---|
| brain storage key | the `origin` remote for **any** host; with no origin, `local/<base>-<sha256(abs dir)[:12]>`. The hash suffix is **load-bearing** — the key *is* the on-disk directory name under `<data>/repos/`, so two checkouts sharing a basename must not collide onto one brain. |
| provider label | the first **github.com** remote. No hash, no suffix. |

So demanding equality was wrong in principle, not just in this case: it fails for every repository whose origin is not github.com, including a brand-new local repo — the exact first-run path.

**Fix:** the brain mirrors the provider's rule to compute the key the provider *should* emit for this repository and accepts that, keeping its own hashed key for storage. A genuinely foreign snapshot is still rejected (pinned by `TestSemanticIndexRejectsForeignProviderRepoKey`).

**Diagnosability:** a mismatch that survives both checks now names both keys, the expected key, the repository, the provider binary, and two concrete remedies — instead of failing bare mid-phase.

**Tests (5):** accepts a repo with no remote; accepts a non-GitHub remote; rejects a foreign key; the mirror matches entire-graph's documented rule; and `TestProviderRepoKeyMatchesInstalledEntireGraph` checks the rule against the **actually installed** binary, so drift between the two implementations fails a test rather than a user's first run.

**Mutation-verified:** removing the provider-rule acceptance path fails both acceptance tests.","created_at":"2026-08-28T22:30:40Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/job1-repokey","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/150","number":150,"sha":"2e82a87c0e74146de3642734f525cfe51d0794a6","title":"fix(semantic): accept the provider's own repo-key rule instead of demanding the brain's","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:24:13Z"}

**Fixes a standing flake generator, with measurements rather than a guess.**

The windows `-race` lane runs against `-timeout 20m`. Measured on **green** runs, `internal/cli` alone takes **811-997s against that 1200s cap** — a healthy suite routinely consuming 68-83% of its budget. Runner draws vary widely: the `phase1-semantic (windows)` job, an identical test subset, ranges **4m46s to 13m10s across PRs (2.75x)**.

So a slow draw tips an otherwise passing PR into `panic: test timed out`. That is not hypothetical — two audit PRs (#104, #108) failed exactly this way during the audit campaign, and **both passed on an unchanged re-run**. Local timings under `-race` across main, #108 and #104 were within **1.6%** of each other, and #108 touches **zero** `internal/cli` lines, so the failures were runner variance, not code.

**Change:** 20m → 30m on that one lane.

**Why this is the right shape of fix:** a timeout is a guard against a *wedged* test, not a performance budget. 30m still surfaces a genuine hang promptly, while leaving a normal run real margin instead of a coin flip. The structural fix is splitting `internal/cli` (it is by far the largest package and dominates every lane); that is worth doing separately and is noted in the commit.

No test was weakened and no assertion was skipped to achieve this.","created_at":"2026-08-28T22:28:15Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/ci-windows-timeout","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/149","number":149,"sha":"93254e821b8e794c01fa3aff545aa7c4cb401a5f","title":"ci: give the windows race suite a timeout that is a hang guard, not a budget","updated_at":"2026-08-28T22:28:21Z"}

**Two things: permanent fuzz infrastructure, plus one new bug it found.**

### The targets
The campaign's crashers were each fixed on their own branch (#126, #127, #128, #129) but the *targets that found them* were not kept, so nothing stops the same classes returning. This adds them as the permanent regression surface, each with its minimized seed corpus: canonical encoding + signature verification (`FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper`, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, `FuzzSignatureEnvelope`, `FuzzCheckCompatibility`), the fact-set NDJSON round trip, git-meta tree paths and target sharding, the hosted client's response handling, the entity-index document, and agent transcript scanning (`FuzzScanConversationTranscript`, `FuzzDistillDocumentConversation`, …).

**This branch is stacked on #126–#129** — those fixes are merged in, so the targets run green here. On bare main two of them correctly fail, which is the point.

### The new finding
Running them turned up one more, fixed in this commit: **`encoding/json` does not fail on invalid UTF-8, it substitutes U+FFFD.** A record written with such a byte **read back changed, with no error on either side** — silent corruption. Fact paths come from real filenames and POSIX permits arbitrary bytes there, so an ordinary repository reaches this; on the shared cross-member head the mangled path would then merge into every other member.

`WriteNDJSON` now refuses such a record with `ErrInvalidUTF8`, naming the offending field, on exactly the rule already established by `ErrRecordTooLarge`: never persist what this package cannot faithfully return.

**Tests:** refusal across paths/text/locus/provenance, each asserting the field is named and nothing was written; plus `TestWriteNDJSONAcceptsValidUTF8` so the guard cannot start rejecting legitimate non-ASCII (`café/日本語.go`, `naïve — ünïcode ✓`).

**Mutation-verified:** disabling the guard reproduces the original fuzz failure — `Paths:[]string{"\x85"}` written, `Paths:[]string{"�"}` read back.","created_at":"2026-08-28T08:32:26Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fuzz-targets","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/140","number":140,"sha":"db6a7ef60f809bcfa601710e26f89d360902fa52","title":"test(fuzz): keep the fuzz targets, and refuse records JSON would mangle","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:44:41Z"}

**Fixes a real product failure and the load-sensitive test flake behind it.** Under load the local dial can fail with `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (ephemeral ports exhausted) or a reset **before the request is ever sent**. Every hosted call turned that into a hard sync failure.

This was observed for real during the audit campaign: `dial tcp: connect: cannot assign requested address` on a machine running many concurrent suites — the same signature as the unexplained `internal/cli` failures seen earlier.

**Fix:** route hosted calls through one `do()` that retries **only** failures which happened before the request reached the server, on a bounded budget.

**The two dangers, both guarded by tests:**
- `TestHTTPServerDoesNotRetryARealConnectivityFailure` — a genuine connectivity failure is returned immediately, never masked by retries.
- `TestHTTPServerRetriesTransientDialFailureOnPOSTWithoutDoublingTheMutation` — a POST is retried only when the *dial* failed, so a mutation cannot be applied twice.
- Plus `...GivesUpAfterTheRetryBudget` so the budget is real.

**Mutation-verified:** bypassing `do()` straight to `client().Do` fails with `Advance through transient dial failures = "", ... dial tcp: connect: cannot assign requested address`.

**Verification:** `go build ./...` clean; `./internal/factsync/` green.","created_at":"2026-08-28T08:25:57Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fix-flake-transient-dial-retry","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/137","number":137,"sha":"2fa108ed8d9380d831b2e5d61fff9220658d2e78","title":"fix(factsync): retry a transient dial failure instead of failing the sync","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:13:18Z"}

**Tests (2):** a 2005-entity commit is truncated *and marked*; a full pass repairs a truncated commit once the cap has risen.

**Mutation-verified:** dropping the marker from serialization fails with `delta.Truncated = false, want true for a 2005-entity commit capped at 2000`.

**Severity: MED (availability / self-DoS).** `brain_ingest_traces` accepted any path from the caller. A size ceiling does not bound a read: `open(2)` on a FIFO with no writer blocks *inside the syscall* before a single byte is read, and a character device yields bytes forever. Worse, the read happened **while holding the semantic index lock**, so one such call wedges the brain for every other caller — daemon, hook, and human alike.

**Fix, three independent layers:**
1. `os.Lstat` (never `os.Stat`) so a symlink pointing at a FIFO cannot slip through the type check a resolving stat would pass.
2. A post-open `SameFile` + `IsRegular` recheck, closing the regular-to-FIFO swap-during-open TOCTOU window.
3. A read deadline on descriptors that support one, so a pollable file that never yields EOF cannot park the caller. Regular files do not support deadlines and are unaffected.

Plus: the trace file is now read **before** the index lock is taken, so even a slow regular file cannot hold the lock.

**Tests (4):** FIFO rejected promptly; FIFO does not wedge the index lock; trace read happens before the lock is taken; regular-to-FIFO swap during open is rejected.

**Mutation-verified honestly:** disabling any *single* guard still fails safe — the other layers catch it, which is the point of defense in depth. Disabling **all three** fails `TestIngestTracesRejectsRegularToFIFOSwapDuringOpen` with `swap rejection error = <nil>, want it to name the regular-file requirement`. Reported this way rather than claiming a single-guard mutation proved the tests.

**Verification:** `go build ./...` clean; targeted FIFO/safe-read tests pass. https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/58
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

**Severity: HIGH (code execution).** A repository is data, not a trust boundary — but git resolves several configuration keys to *commands it executes*, honoured from the target repository's own `.git/config` and in-tree `.gitattributes`. Indexing or fingerprinting an untrusted repo ran code that repo carried.

**Three vectors, each confirmed against git 2.54.0 by arming a scratch repo and watching the payload run:**
- `diff.external` / `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` — runs for every `git diff` form. It also *replaces* the diff, so an armed repo makes `git diff --binary HEAD` return nothing: silent corruption of any fingerprint computed from that output.
- `diff.<driver>.textconv`, selected by an in-tree `.gitattributes` entry — runs for every command that renders patch text.
- `core.fsmonitor` — runs for `status`, all `diff` forms, `ls-files`, `diff-tree`.

**Why flags, not config:** neutralizing with `-c diff.external=` does NOT work — git still takes the external-diff path and aborts ("external diff died"), losing the output. `--no-ext-diff`/`--no-textconv` both stop execution and preserve correct output. `core.fsmonitor=false` is behaviour-preserving (pure perf cache) so it is applied globally.

**Why it is unbypassable:** the rewrite lives at the single point where this binary spawns git, so every call site in every package — including `internal/entityindex`, which receives `ExecRunner` straight through — is covered without each one having to remember. Flags are inserted after the subcommand (before any `--` pathspec separator) and skipped if the caller already passed them; the dedup check deliberately ignores pathspecs, since `.brainignore` feeds repo-controlled pathspecs and a repo shipping a literal `--no-ext-diff` pattern must not suppress its own neutralizer.

**Tests:** 9 added, 6 of them real exploit tests (arm the vector in a scratch repo, assert the payload never runs) across worktree fingerprinting, `gitDiffBinary`, changed-range/file detection, status, and seed collection.

**Mutation-verified:** removing the two rewrite hooks in `runner.go` fails the exploit tests with `SECURITY: repo-local core.fsmonitor executed an attacker-controlled program during indexing`.

**Verification:** `go build ./...` clean; targeted `internal/cli` hardening + exploit tests pass. Full-suite not re-run on a heavily loaded host — stated plainly rather than overclaimed.","created_at":"2026-08-28T08:14:35Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-git-no-ext-diff","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/130","number":130,"sha":"e3aff9e0a41810c1485af1ff4284f12913465200","title":"fix(git): stop repo-local git config turning a read into code execution","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:35:15Z"}
{"base":"audit/ndjson-line-cap","body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/57
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

Canonical form passes unknown members through on purpose (ADR 0001, additive-only: an older verifier must be able to canonicalize and verify a **newer** producer's artifact). "Unknown" was decided by **exact** match against the contract keys — but Go's `encoding/json` matches object members to struct fields **case-insensitively**.

So a member like `manIfest` is unknown to this canonicalizer and **is** the manifest to `encoding/json`. The same signed bytes then carry two different meanings depending on which decoder reads them:

```go
raw := `{"manIfest":{"repo_key":"EVIL","generated_at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05Z","brain_schema_version":"1.0"}}`

json.Unmarshal(raw, &BrainArtifact{})   // RepoKey == "EVIL"
CanonicalUnmarshal(raw, &artifact)      // RepoKey == ""      (zero-filled)
```

and `VerifyBytes` accepts the bytes either way, because canonicalization preserves the unknown key verbatim. One signature, two readings, decided by the consumer's parser rather than by the signer.

This is the same class of cross-parser differential `canonical.go` already rejects duplicate members for, and it is not hypothetical: the artifact is consumed across a repo boundary (`entire-api`) by a Go decoder this repo does not control.

## The fix

`normalizeObject` rejects an unknown member that case-folds to a contract field. Every contract key is lowercase ASCII, so no legitimate artifact carries one. Genuinely unknown newer-minor fields still pass through untouched, and canonical form is still a fixed point over them — `TestUnknownFieldsStillPassThrough` pins both. Unknown keys are visited in sorted order so input with several collisions produces a deterministic error.

`strings.EqualFold` is a superset of `encoding/json`'s own fold matching for ASCII contract keys, so nothing the decoder would fold slips past.

## How it was found

`FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, which states the ADR 0001 obligation as a testable property: for any two byte strings that verify under the same signature, the decoded `BrainArtifact` must be identical. It failed in ~3 s. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestCanonicalizeRejectsCaseFoldedContractKeys` and `TestSignedArtifactCannotBeReinterpretedByFolding` are the standalone regressions; the latter reproduces the full smuggling scenario end to end.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/brainwire/` (173 tests) — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle` ran 11.0M execs and `FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper` 19.8M execs with no crasher. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:35:02Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/canonical-case-fold","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/129","number":129,"sha":"918854e8aa17269bdff60d7423a300a835b04d64","title":"fix(brainwire): reject case-folded contract keys in canonical form","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:14Z"}

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`ParseNDJSON` scanned with a 64 KiB line bound. `WriteNDJSON` enforced nothing. A fact whose serialized record exceeded that bound wrote cleanly and then failed to load:

```
bufio.Scanner: token too long
```

So the store could persist a fact-set it could not read back — with no position and no bound in the error to act on.

On the shared cross-member head this is worse than local corruption. `factsync.Sync` parses the pulled blob with `ParseNDJSON`, so **one** member's oversized fact permanently fails **every other** member's sync, and the affected members cannot repair it, because the fact only exists on the head they cannot read.

## The fix

- `MaxLineBytes` is **16 MiB**, matching the ceiling the rest of the brain applies to untrusted inputs it reads whole (`safe_read.go`).
- `WriteNDJSON` refuses a record whose line would exceed it (`ErrRecordTooLarge`), so the two halves can never disagree again. Nothing is written when it refuses.
- An oversized line already on disk is reported as a `*ParseError` naming the line number and the bound, not as an opaque `bufio` error.

## How it was found

`FuzzNDJSONWriteReadRoundTrip`, which asserts the property directly: any record the store is willing to write, the reader must be able to read back. It failed on the first non-trivial size. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestWriteReadRoundTripAtRealisticSizes`, `TestWriteRefusesUnreadableRecord`, and `TestParseReportsOversizedLineWithPosition` are the standalone regressions.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factmerge/ ./internal/factsync/` — all green. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:44Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/ndjson-line-cap","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/128","number":128,"sha":"64f62e43548093efe2235ab84028ceb4379f3700","title":"fix(factmerge): stop the fact-set writer emitting lines its own reader rejects","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:12Z"}

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/55
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`ValidateTargetValue` returned early for path targets, so **no** rule applied to them. Path values legitimately contain `/` — they are stored as nested, escaped segments under the `__target__` sentinel — but that exemption also skipped every segment-level check the format needs.

A value with an empty segment (`"/"`, `"a//b"`, a leading or trailing slash) encodes to a tree path with an empty component:

```
path:"/"  key:"0"   ->   "path///__target__/0/__value"
```

`BuildTree` then refuses that path — and it refuses the **whole `Serialize` call**, not just the offending record. One such record therefore makes the entire store unwritable for every writer that materializes it, with no repair path from the reading side.

## The fix

`ValidatePathTargetValue` restores the segment rules: no empty segment, no `.` or `..` segment, no NUL. Values that legitimately contain slashes are unaffected (`src/main.rs`, `a/b/c`, `~weird`, `__reserved/x` all still serialize).

`parseLeafPath` validates the path target it reconstructs from a tree, for the same reason the other target types do: on a shared ref the tree is untrusted input, and a value the serializer could not have produced belongs to `ErrMalformedTree` at the read boundary.

The `entire-api` copy of this vendored engine already carries a check of this name; this copy had lost it — the divergence note at the top of the file already flagged exactly this.

## How it was found

`FuzzTreePath`, from the fuzzing campaign, after 7.4M execs: `encoded path "path///__target__/0/__value" has an empty component (type="path" value="/" key="0")`. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factgitmeta/...` — all green. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.

## Note

Touches the same two files as #126 (a separate defect: a commit target value too short to shard, which panics). Both are independently valid off `main`; whichever lands second will need a small conflict resolution in `ValidateTargetValue` and `parseLeafPath`.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:29Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fuzz-path-target-validation","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/127","number":127,"sha":"2334f0415d4f2cb657cdd2e00af7dc74e46540e4","title":"fix(gitmeta): validate path-target values instead of exempting them","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:10Z"}

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/54
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`TreeBasePath` shards a commit target on its own first two hex characters (`t.Value[:2]`). `ParseTarget` enforced a 3-character minimum — but nothing else did, and the `Target` `materialize.go` rebuilds from a tree leaf path never goes through `ParseTarget`.

A metadata tree carrying `commit/ab/a/k/__value` materialized into a `State` with a one-character commit value, and the very next write re-serialized it:

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:2] with length 1
    gitmeta.TreeBasePath      treepath.go:40
    gitmeta.buildKeyTreePath
    gitmeta.TreePath
    gitmeta.Serialize         <- MetaStore.updateLocked, every write
```

That is the whole read-materialize-CAS loop `MetaStore` runs, so one such record crashes the process on every subsequent pass. The store is local today; once git-meta records are exchanged over a shared ref (P1), the tree is bytes another member wrote.

## The fix

Three changes, at the three places that can stop it:

- **`ValidateTargetValue` enforces `MinTargetValueLen`**, the minimum `ParseTarget` has always documented. `Serialize` is the only gate between a materialized `State` and the tree, so the rule belongs where every write path passes through it. `ParseTarget` now delegates rather than keeping a second copy.
- **`parseLeafPath` validates the target it reconstructs**, so a hostile tree is classified as `ErrMalformedTree` at the READ boundary — the permanent failure a consumer is already documented to drop — instead of being carried into `State`.
- **`TreeBasePath` shards through `shardPrefix`.** It returns no error, so a caller that somehow reaches it unvalidated must get a wrong-but-total path rather than a panic.

## Blast radius

Nothing in this repo builds a branch or change-id target, and the only commit target is `entityindex.commitTarget(sha)` with a 40-hex SHA, so the minimum cannot regress real usage.

## How it was found

`FuzzTreePath`, from the fuzzing campaign. The minimized inputs ship as seed corpus entries for `FuzzTreePath` and `FuzzMaterializeRoundTrip` (inert until those harnesses land in the fuzz-targets PR). `TestShortTargetValueIsRejectedNotPanic` and `TestMaterializeRejectsShortTargetValue` are the standalone regressions; both fail on the pre-fix code.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factgitmeta/... ./internal/entityindex/...` — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzTreePath` ran 16.5M execs and `FuzzMaterializeRoundTrip` 7.5M execs with no crasher. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:14Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/gitmeta-shard-panic","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/126","number":126,"sha":"84173018bb1b67c02c33ffeb510fc9a9e52403dc","title":"fix(gitmeta): reject a target value too short to shard instead of panicking","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:48Z"}
{"base":"main","body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/53
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

`ENTIRE_API_URL` (and the `--api-url` flag that overrides it) had **no scheme floor and no host allowlist**. Any value it was given received brain content — and the member's bearer token — in the clear. This adds a single shared validator (`internal/apiurl`) that requires `https://`, carves out loopback for local dev, and fails closed on everything else.

## What actually egressed over `http://` today (measured, not asserted)

I stood up a plaintext HTTP server bound to a **non-loopback** address (this machine's LAN IP, `192.168.1.121`), pointed `ENTIRE_API_URL` at it, and drove the real `publish` and `facts sync` code paths on the pre-fix tree. Both succeeded. Captured:

**`entire brain publish` → `POST http://192.168.1.121:PORT/api/v1/repos/{repo_id}/brain/artifacts`**

```
Authorization: "Bearer SECRET-BEARER-TOKEN-abc123"     <-- token crosses plaintext: YES
body: 2437 bytes, 4 artifacts
  kind=manifest  ref=<HEAD sha>   -> repo_key "gh/example/repo", default_branch, generated_at,
                                     provider/provider_version, and the full content index:
                                     sha256 digests, sizes, media types and on-disk PATHS of every
                                     snapshot / overlay / facts blob
  kind=snapshot  ref=<commit>     -> semantic snapshot NDJSON: {"symbol":"Foo","kind":"func"}
  kind=overlay   ref=<base>..<head> -> {"base":...,"head":...,"branch":"feature/x"}
  kind=facts     ref=main         -> durable fact text: {"branch":"main","text":"the repo uses go"}
```

**`entire brain facts sync --facts-backend http` → three plaintext calls, all bearing the token**

```
GET  .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts?branch=main            Authorization: Bearer <token>
POST .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance                Authorization: Bearer <token>
     body.data (303 bytes) = the merged fact-set NDJSON, in the clear:
       {"id":"fact:60e95c57ed6370b3f79e74a5","paths":["ops.deploy.secret"],
        "text":"the prod deploy key lives in vault path kv/prod/deploy","branch":"main",
        "origin":"distilled","status":"active","provenance":[{"session_id":"session-EV"}],
        "created_at":...,"updated_at":...}
GET  .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/proposals?branch=main  Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

So: **the whole brain artifact bundle, the merged durable fact-set (fact text, paths, provenance session ids), and the bearer token all crossed plaintext to an arbitrary attacker-named host.** `internal/cli/publish_test.go` already did `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_API_URL", server.URL)` against an `httptest` (plain http) server — the plaintext path was live and exercised.

Two aggravating details found while verifying:

- The refusal for a malformed URL happened *after* the whole bundle was built. `publish.go`'s own doc comment promises a refusal "BEFORE any resolution, disk read, or HTTP request"; with `ENTIRE_API_URL=http://evil.example` the pre-fix run got as far as `no brain found for this repo`, i.e. it had already resolved storage and read local state for an unsafe target.
- Non-HTTP schemes were passed straight to `http.Client` — `ftp://`, `file:///etc/passwd`, `//api.entire.io` and bare `api.entire.io` all produced a built request and a confusing transport error rather than a config refusal.

## The fix

New `internal/apiurl` — one validator, no I/O of any kind (no DNS, no disk, no network), so callers run it as their first act after resolving the flag/env and every refusal is egress-free:

- `https://` — always allowed.
- `http://` — allowed **only** when the URL's literal host is loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, `localhost`). This is what local dev and every `httptest`-based test in the repo use, so they keep passing unchanged. The name carve-out is exactly `localhost`, matching the plugin's existing `isLoopbackHTTPURL` check for the local model server; `api.localhost` is RFC 6761 loopback in principle but resolver-dependent in practice, so it takes the opt-in.
- `http://` anywhere else — refused (`insecure_api_url:`) unless the new documented opt-in **`ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_INSECURE_API_URL`** is explicitly truthy.
- Anything else — empty, relative, schemeless, protocol-relative, `ftp`, `file`, garbage — refused (`invalid_api_url:`), and the opt-in does **not** rescue it.

Loopback is decided from the URL's literal host only. No DNS: resolving would be a TOCTOU check, would need the network to validate a URL, and would let a hostile DNS answer widen the carve-out.

**Fail-closed direction.** `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_INSECURE_API_URL` uses the *opt-in* spelling — only `1/true/yes/on/enable/enabled` unlocks plaintext; anything unrecognized (a typo'd `ture`) leaves the floor in place, with a deduped stderr warning so the operator learns their value was not understood. This is deliberately the mirror image of `securityToggleEnabled` / `toggleOn`, which fail an unrecognized value **ON**: those switch a protection *on*, so a typo must not disable it; this one switches a protection *off*, so the same fail-closed principle resolves the other way. It matches the existing `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED` publish opt-in.

Wired at every site that accepts a base URL:

| site | where |
|---|---|
| `internal/cli/publish.go` | right after the base URL is resolved — before `repoStoragePaths`, before the brain is read, before the bundle is built. Restores the doc-comment promise. |
| `internal/cli/facts_sync_cmd.go` | in the `http` fact backend resolution, before the backend is constructed. |
| `internal/cli/facts_proposals_cmd.go` | in `resolveHostedProposalTarget`, which is documented to make no network call. |
| `internal/factsync/httpserver.go` | in `newRequest`, the single request chokepoint for **both** `httpserver.go` (fact-set `Current`/`Advance`) and `httpproposals.go` (list/get/publish/resolve). Defense in depth: a caller that bypasses the CLI is still covered. |
| `internal/hostedbrain/client.go` | in `rpc`, the hosted MCP query chokepoint, next to the existing no-egress gate. |

`Validate` is idempotent, so the CLI-level check and the transport-level check compose without changing or re-rejecting the value.

## Tests (failing-first, then mutation-verified)

Written and shown failing against the pre-fix tree, then made to pass:

- `internal/cli/https_floor_test.go` — `ENTIRE_API_URL=http://evil.example` is refused for `publish`, `facts sync`, and `facts proposals`; each asserts the error is *not* a dial/DNS error, which would prove a request had already been attempted (pre-fix, `facts sync` and `facts proposals` failed exactly that way: `dial tcp: lookup evil.example: no such host`). Also: publish refuses **before** the disk read (it must not reach `no brain found`); the malformed-URL table; and the carve-out fence — loopback v4/v6/`localhost` stay allowed, the opt-in works, and a garbage opt-in value fails closed.
- `internal/factsync/https_floor_test.go` — `Current`, `Advance`, `ListProposals`, `PublishProposals` all refuse, with a counting `http.RoundTripper` proving **zero** requests reached the transport; loopback still round-trips.
- `internal/hostedbrain/https_floor_test.go` — same, for `CallTool`.
- `internal/apiurl/apiurl_test.go` — the validator table (schemes, loopback literals, `localhost` subdomains and lookalikes, opt-in truthiness incl. fail-closed garbage, malformed input), idempotence, and `IsLoopbackHost`.

Mutation check: with the floor neutered, the refusal tests fail; restored, they pass.

## Compatibility

- Every existing `httptest`-based test passes unchanged — they bind `127.0.0.1`, which is the loopback carve-out.
- Local dev against `http://localhost:8787` is unaffected.
- Breaking only for an operator pointing at a non-loopback plaintext endpoint, who now gets a clear error naming the opt-in.
- `--api-url` help text, the `publish` long help, and the README env table document the floor and the new variable.

## Green gate

## Impact

ADR 0001 (`docs/adr/0001-ga-schema-contract.md` in entire-graph) states the tolerant-reader duty this consumer owes:

> Consumers ignore unknown fields within a supported major, and **warn (not fail) when they see a newer supported-major minor**, since additive facts may have been skipped.
> `entire-brain` ingestion MUST follow the tolerant-reader rules above: accept any `1.x`, ignore unknown fields, warn on a newer minor.

`validateSemanticSchema` (`internal/cli/semantic.go`) implemented only half of that:

```go
major, _, ok := strings.Cut(version, ".")
if !ok { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema version %q", version) }
if major != semanticSupportedMajor { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema major version %q", major) }
return nil
```

Three defects:

1. **No newer-minor warning anywhere.** A `1.2` snapshot from a newer entire-graph is accepted in silence. The resulting index is quietly less complete than the snapshot it came from — additive facts this build cannot ingest are dropped with nothing recorded. That is precisely the case the ADR requires a warning for. (`brainwire.CheckCompatibility`, `internal/brainwire/version.go:36`, implements the same ADR policy correctly one layer over; this path did not reuse it.)
2. **Only the text before the first dot is examined,** so `"1.abc"` and `"1."` are accepted as ordinary 1.x minors and a malformed header rides straight into the store.
3. **The rejection message never says what this build supports** — only what it received — collapsing "upgrade the provider" and "upgrade the brain" into one unactionable string.

## Fix

- `parseSemanticSchemaVersion` requires a well-formed `major.minor` (a trailing patch component is tolerated and ignored, since refusing it would itself violate the tolerant-reader rule).
- `validateSemanticSchema` keeps the major as the compatibility boundary and now names the supported range in every rejection.
- `semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` emits `provider_schema_newer_minor` for a newer minor within the supported major, naming both versions and the remedy.

### Applied at every point a provider `schema_version` crosses into this build

Recording the warning at index time alone is not enough — each of these is an independent way for an under-ingested snapshot to be trusted as complete:

| site | sink |
|---|---|
| `runSemanticIndex` | live `entire graph snapshot` header → warning recorded on the persisted manifest |
| `semanticStaleReport` | the `provider` freshness axis read by `brain doctor`/`status` and every semantic query/context/impact/changes/boundary/tests command → **degraded**, not a clean `ok` |
| `validateImportedBundle` | imported bundle manifest → warning appended to the semantic source that is then persisted |

`semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` is the single implementation behind all three. `validateSemanticSchema` remains the sole authority on rejecting an unparseable or unsupported-major version, and runs first at each site.

> Supersedes #120, which wired the same three sinks behind a weaker parser (`validateSemanticSchema` left lenient, and a minor parse that silently gave up on `1.2.3`). This PR carries the union: #123's strict parser plus #120's full call-site coverage. #120 is closed.

## Verification

- `TestValidateSemanticSchemaFollowsTheTolerantReaderContract` — accept `1.0`/`1.1`/`1.2`/`1.17`/`1.2.3`; refuse `""`/`1`/`2.0`/`0.9`/`1.abc`/`1.`/`x.1`.
- `TestSemanticSchemaNewerMinorWarns`, `TestSemanticSchemaErrorsNameTheSupportedRange`.
- One positive and one negative test per sink: `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`; `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor` / `TestSemanticStaleReportSilentAtSupportedMinor`; `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning` / `TestBundleImportSilentAtSupportedMinor`.
- **Mutation-verified per site:** disabling the warning at each of the three sites in turn fails exactly one test — index → `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`, stale-report → `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor`, bundle-import → `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning`. Restoring the lenient major-only parse, computing the warning but dropping it, and stripping the supported range from the message each also fail a test.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/cli/`, `go test ./internal/cli/` (2413 tests, green).

### Known gap, deliberately out of scope

`readSemanticSnapshotSummary` also calls `validateSemanticSchema` on a snapshot header, but it is a pure read helper returning `(semanticHeader, semanticCounts, error)` with no warning sink, and it only re-reads a snapshot whose manifest was already warned on at one of the three sites above. Wiring it needs a signature change and is not required for ADR 0001 compliance here.

## Finding

Two production HTTP clients fell back to `http.DefaultClient`, which has **no timeout**:

- `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:55-60` — used by every hosted-brain RPC (`rpc`, and through it `Initialize`/`ListTools`/`CallTool`/`Search`/`Get`/`MultiGet`/`Status`).
- `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:39-44` — used by `Current`, `Advance`, and all four proposal calls in `httpproposals.go`.

The factsync one is **live today**, not only on the P1 hosted path: `internal/cli/facts_sync_cmd.go:573` constructs `&factsync.HTTPServer{BaseURL: baseURL, Token: token}` with no `Client`, so `entire brain facts sync --backend http` ran on an untimed client on both its read and its write path.

The realistic caller is the CLI or the workspace daemon passing `context.Background()`. With no caller deadline, the client's own bound is the only thing that can end the call.

## Proof

A test server that accepts the request and never responds, called with `context.Background()`:

```
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHang (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002033333s against a wedged endpoint (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHangFactsync (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002050125s (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
```

Both calls never return. The endpoint completes the TCP dial and only then stalls, so a dial-phase bound would not have helped either — the bound has to cover the wait for the response, which `http.Client.Timeout` does.

## Audit of every HTTP client construction (non-test)

| site | bound before | action |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:59` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 60s |
| `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:43` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 5m |
| `internal/cli/publish.go:543` | `Timeout: publishRequestTimeout` (5m) | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/embed_ollama.go:73` | `Timeout: 60s` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:1992` | `Timeout: timeout` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |

No `http.Get`/`http.Post`/`http.Head` call sites and no other `&http.Client{}` exist outside tests.

## Fix

Each package gets a documented default bound and keeps the caller-supplied-client override:

- `hostedbrain`: 60s. The hosted tools are bounded reads (search / get / status).
- `factsync`: 5m. `Advance` uploads the whole merged fact-set, so the bound matches the five minutes the hosted publish path already allows for a body-carrying request (`cli.publishRequestTimeout`) rather than a short read timeout.

Both are plain `http.Client.Timeout`, the same shape `publish.go` already uses, so `http.DefaultTransport` and its connection pool stay shared. Both are `var`, not `const`, so tests can shorten them.

An earlier draft also set `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout` on a cloned transport; that was dropped after it was measured to cause connection churn and ephemeral-port exhaustion in the existing suite. `Client.Timeout` already covers the response wait, which is the property under test.

## Tests

Per package: a direct assertion that the default client carries a non-zero `Timeout` (and that a caller-supplied client still wins), plus a behavioural test driving a wedged server with `context.Background()` and asserting the call returns.

Mutation-verified: restoring `return http.DefaultClient` in each package fails all four tests (the behavioural ones by hanging out their 15s budget); restoring the fix passes them.

## Verification

`gofmt -l .` clean, `go vet ./...` clean, `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/hostedbrain/ ./internal/factsync/` green over 4 consecutive runs, `go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'Publish|FactsSync'` green.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:09:56Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-http-timeout","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/121","number":121,"sha":"4e2984b9317cff92776fec7e71d81bdaf901090b","title":"fix(hostedbrain,factsync): bound the default HTTP client","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:10:48Z"}

## Finding

`internal/hostedbrain/client.go:116` built the brain MCP endpoint by raw string concatenation:

```go
url := strings.TrimRight(c.BaseURL, "/") + "/api/v1/repos/" + repoID + "/brain/mcp"
```

`repoID` was not escaped. Every sibling call in the repo already escapes it — `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:63,107`, `internal/factsync/httpproposals.go:46,105,252`, `internal/cli/publish.go:534` all use `url.PathEscape`. This was the one that did not, so it was an oversight rather than a convention.

## Proof

An `httptest` server recording the request target, driven through `Client.Initialize`, observes the request going somewhere other than the brain MCP route (unfixed code):

| repo id | observed path | observed query |
|---|---|---|
| `a/b` | `/api/v1/repos/a/b/brain/mcp` | — |
| `../../admin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `..%2f..%2fadmin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `x?admin=1` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | `admin=1/brain/mcp` |
| `x#frag` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | — |
| `x/brain/facts/advance` | `/api/v1/repos/x/brain/facts/advance/brain/mcp` | — |

The `?` and `#` cases are the sharpest: the POST — carrying the member's `Authorization: Bearer` token — lands on `/api/v1/repos/x`, a different endpoint entirely, and the rest of the intended path is smuggled into the query string. The dot-segment cases reach the wire un-normalized, so any server or proxy that normalizes resolves them above the `/api/v1` prefix.

## Fix

`url.PathEscape(repoID)`, matching the siblings. The local variable is renamed `endpoint` (as in `publish.go`) so it no longer shadows the `net/url` package.

## Test

`TestRPCEscapesRepoID` asserts, for each payload above plus a benign id, that the server sees the `/api/v1/repos/` prefix and `/brain/mcp` suffix intact with the repo id occupying exactly one path segment and no query string smuggled out of it. It asserts on `r.URL.EscapedPath()`, which is what an HTTP router matches on, so a percent-encoded separator is correctly seen as staying inside one segment.

Mutation-verified: reverting the one-line fix fails 6 of the 7 subtests; restoring it passes all 7.

## Verification

## Summary

Contract audit of the entire-brain MCP tool surface (all 36 tools registered in `internal/cli/mcp.go`), comparing each tool's declared name/description/JSON-schema against what its handler actually reads and does, and cross-referencing `README.md` and `docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md`. Three real drift items found and fixed (smallest complete fix on the side judged wrong — see notes):

- **`brain_search_graph`'s `offset` and `brain_get_code_snippet`'s `context_lines`** declared `minimum: 1` in their JSON schema, but both handlers (`mcpNonNegativeInt`) accept and default to `0`. A schema-validating MCP client would wrongly refuse to send the default value. Fixed the schema (added a `nonNegativeIntegerArg` helper, `minimum: 0`) since the handler behavior is correct and long-standing; the declared contract was stale.

- **`docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md`'s tool catalog** was missing `brain_entity_history` — registered in code and documented in `README.md`, but absent from the guide's "Available tools" list.

Added regression tests for each: schema-minimum lock for the two zero-accepting params, a description lock for `brain_get_architecture`, and a doc-contract test that every registered MCP tool name appears in the guide (would have caught the `brain_entity_history` gap).

## Impact

`mcpPositiveInt` and `mcpNonNegativeInt` (`internal/cli/mcp.go:1378`, `:1396`) enforced a floor and nothing else — `typed <= float64(math.MaxInt)` is not a bound, it is a type check.

An MCP client is not a trusted peer in this design: the agent driving it carries repository text in its context that an untrusted checkout can influence, and a `tools/call` is one line of JSON.

The argument is not merely a result count. It reaches allocation sizing:

- `internal/cli/history_fts.go:581` — `out := make([]scoredHistoryRecord, 0, limit)`
- `internal/cli/doc_fts.go:199,204` — `LIMIT ?` with `limit*4`, and `make([]scoredDocRecord, 0, limit*4)`
- `internal/cli/retrieve.go:209,322` — the history arm scales the same value by 2 then 3 (with overflow guards, but no ceiling)

So `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000000}}` decides how many elements the server asks the runtime for. Depending on element size that is either a panic the request recovery turns into an opaque `-32603 internal error` (what I observed end to end), or an allocation request under the `makeslice` cap that the process attempts and does not survive. Either way an unauthenticated argument, not the server, picks the number.

`context_lines` on `brain_get_code_snippet` has the same shape — `semantic_graph.go:894` adds it to `record.EndLine`, and `math.MaxInt64` there overflows the sum negative.

## Repro

`internal/cli/mcp_int_bounds_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestMCPIntegerArgumentsAreCapped
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1e+09; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpNonNegativeInt accepted limit=1e+09
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1.099511627776e+12; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=2147483647; it sizes a slice capacity
--- FAIL: TestMCPToolCallRejectsOversizedLimit
    error = {"code":-32603,"message":"internal error handling \"tools/call\""}
```

That last line is the whole point: on `main` an oversized `limit` does not produce a validation error, it produces a recovered internal failure. After the fix it is a clean `-32000 limit must be an integer between 1 and 10000`.

## Fix

`mcpIntegerArgMax = 10000`, enforced in both decoders. Far above any useful result count, depth, offset or context window; far below the point where the value becomes an allocation problem.

Enforced in the decoders rather than declared as `"maximum"` in each `inputSchema` **on purpose**: the tool definitions are sent on every `tools/list` and their size is budgeted in tokens — `TestMCPBrainBriefToolDefinitionGolden` asserts an exact 747-byte definition and documents the tokenizer accounting for the whole `tools/list` payload. Adding a `maximum` to ~25 integer properties would spend that budget restating a bound the server must check itself regardless. `brain_get_conversation` and `brain_concepts`, which already declare real semantic maxima, keep them.

Two existing assertions in `mcp_test.go` move from `"limit must be an integer greater than zero"` to `"limit must be an integer between 1 and"`. The rejection behaviour they cover is unchanged; only the message is more accurate.

## Mutation

Restoring `math.MaxInt` in either decoder reproduces the failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli/` clean.","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:46:27Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-mcp-int-bounds","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/117","number":117,"sha":"5d54f0d9083828e5ec2821aec996a04352c16609","title":"fix(mcp): integer tool arguments have no upper bound, so a tool call chooses an allocation size","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:40:37Z"}

## Impact

A proposal id is content-derived — `ProposalID` (`internal/factsync/proposals.go:82`) hashes action, candidate id, target id, branch and proposer. That is the entire basis for showing an id to a member and accepting it back: `facts proposals apply prop-abc123` is meant to name one decision and nothing else.

The open set, though, is served by the hosted brain, and a server-supplied non-empty id was taken verbatim. Only an **empty** id was recomputed:

```go
for i := range set.Proposals {
    if set.Proposals[i].ID == "" {
        set.Proposals[i].ID = ProposalID(set.Proposals[i].Proposal)
    }
}
```

(`httpproposals.go:93-97`, and the same at `:129-131` for `GetProposal`.)

Settling is not read-only:

- accept marks the **target** fact superseded, and a `merge` action calls `removeFactByID` on the candidate (`factmerge/admin.go:36-46`);
- the settled proposal is then mirrored into the member's **local** fact store — `facts_proposals_cmd.go:261` → `applySettlementLocally` at `:320` — and the same mirror runs unattended from `facts sync` via `reconcileLocalProposalQueue`;
- `FindProposal` (`proposals.go:109-118`) resolves the member's reference against that same server-supplied id.

So a hosted brain could display one decision under an id and execute a different one when the member confirmed it, against local facts of the server's choosing. The id a human sees is not bound to what applying it does — confirm-what-you-did-not-see.

## Repro

`internal/factsync/proposal_id_binding_test.go` drives the real `HTTPServer` adapter over the existing `hostedContractServer` fake. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestListProposalsRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    proposal id prop-c92b6250535b7a6c does not derive from the decision it names
    ({Action:supersede CandidateID:fact:attacker TargetID:fact:victim Branch:main})
--- FAIL: TestGetProposalRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    GetProposal returned {ID:prop-c92b6250535b7a6c Proposal:{Action:supersede ...}}
    under an id that does not derive from it
```

## Fix

`bindProposalID` derives an absent id exactly as before (older/looser servers omit it — pinned by `TestProposalsStillAcceptDerivedAndOmittedIDs/omitted`), and requires a present one to equal the derived value. A mismatch is refused with `ErrProposalIDMismatch` rather than silently corrected: correcting the id would leave it no longer resolving the reference the member was handed.

## Mutation

Dropping the mismatch branch reproduces both failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet` clean.

## Related

This is the proposal-side counterpart to #95, which binds *fact* ids to their content on the same transport. Neither is subsumed by the other: `VerifyIdentities` checks records, and a proposal carries no record — only ids.","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:43:15Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-proposal-id-binding","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/116","number":116,"sha":"83fa0675340573bd17cff8fc23cb7ab191427ce6","title":"fix(factsync): hosted proposal ids are not bound to the decision they name","updated_at":"2026-08-28T04:43:20Z"}

## What breaks

A graft truncates `git log --format=%P`, so in a shallow clone the boundary commit reports **no parents** and is indistinguishable from a real root to the walk:

```
$ git clone --depth=1 file://origin clone && cd clone
$ git log -1 --format=%P            # empty
$ git cat-file commit HEAD | head -2
tree   b7130d30b0ce47edf9a8f30a0a38d3c22f953d5e
parent ab142df864ba9d51317289381fc969732e35baa4   # the parent is right there
```

A root commit is diffed against the empty tree so its entities are recorded as `added`. The boundary therefore gets a forward delta document declaring that it **added every entity in the whole tree**, plus one reverse-index entry per entity pointing at it.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. Those records are durable git-meta, and from then on `entities history` answers "this symbol was introduced by `<boundary>`" — naming a commit that introduced none of them. The same join is what fact provenance anchors to, so the fabricated commit propagates into stored facts.

Any CI checkout (`actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`) or any `git clone --depth=N` hits this.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_shallow_test.go` makes a real 3-commit origin, `git clone --depth=2` off it, verifies the boundary really is grafted (`%P` empty), and indexes the clone.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_shallow_test.go:142: the shallow boundary 3a000de3 was indexed against the empty tree:
    base=4b825dc6 entities=[{Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_first ... Path:first.go ...}
    {Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_second ... Path:second.go ...}]
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit (4.08s)
```

`first.go` was added three commits before the boundary, in history this clone does not have.

## Fix

A shallow boundary is not a root: its parent exists, it is just not in this clone, so its delta genuinely cannot be computed. Treat it as the hole it is — exactly the way a commit the provider could not diff is already treated. Nothing is written for it, no cursor steps over it (so the window keeps its "every first-parent commit from floor to tip carries a document" claim honest), and the pass reports it in `Warnings`.

Telling a boundary from a root is one `cat-file commit`: the raw object still carries its parent lines even when the graft hides them from `%P`. The check only runs for commits the walk reported as parentless, and `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` is memoized per pass, so a full clone pays one extra `git rev-parse` at most and a repository with no parentless commits in range pays nothing at all.

The tradeoff, stated plainly: a `--depth=1` clone now indexes nothing rather than indexing one fabricated document. That is the correct direction for a store whose contents are durable and feed provenance — a deeper clone indexes everything except its boundary, which is exactly right.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, disabling the guard (`if false && commit.Parent == "" && b.isGraftedBoundary(...)`) makes the new test fail again with the identical "indexed against the empty tree" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass.

## What breaks

Workspace retrieval reports a member repo whose retrieval **failed** as:

```json
{"repo_key": "acme/broken", "results": [], "error": "load history index: parse history/index.json: unexpected end of JSON input"}
```

When the 128 KiB response budget binds, `trimWorkspaceExtrasOnce` resolved the overage by **clearing that error** — and it did so *before* dropping a single ranked row. The member then serializes as:

```json
{"repo_key": "acme/broken", "results": []}
```

which is byte-identical to a healthy member that simply had no matches. The only signal left is the envelope-level `response_truncated: true`, which says *rows were dropped*, not *a member's failure was suppressed*. So a caller searching a workspace reads a broken repo as "searched successfully, nothing found" — a wrong answer with no error, and the wrongness is worst exactly when the workspace is large enough for the budget to bind.

The same trimmer backs the text surface, which renders `"<repo> error <detail>"` per member; the line disappears there too.

The priority was also inverted: a member's failure is small and load-bearing, a marginal ranked row is neither, yet the error was sacrificed first.

## Repro

```
go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1 -run 'TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrieval'
```

On `origin/main` @ `a812069d`:

```
--- FAIL: TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrievalTextKeepsMemberErrors (0.13s)
    workspace_error_budget_test.go:90: member error was dropped to fit the budget; rendered text:
        [history] acme/healthy/history:00000000  sessions/main/20260801T000000Z_session.jsonl
        ...
--- FAIL: TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrievalJSONKeepsMemberErrors (0.48s)
    workspace_error_budget_test.go:69: member error was dropped to fit the budget: error="" results=0;
        the failed member is now indistinguishable from one with no matches
```

The fixture is two groups: a healthy member with 600 rows (over budget on both surfaces) and a failed member with an error and zero rows. Both tests are deterministic — the trim order is fixed, no maps are involved.

## Fix

Remove `Error` from the trimmable extras in `trimWorkspaceExtrasOnce`. `AbstractPreviews` and the two `Freshness` detail strings stay trimmable; once they are exhausted the caller's loop falls through to dropping ranked rows and, last, whole member groups — a dropped group disappears from `results` entirely rather than misreporting itself as empty-and-healthy.

## Mutation check

Re-add the `case groups[i].Error != "": groups[i].Error = ""` branch → both tests fail again. Remove it → both green at `-count=3`.

`overview` answers "what is this project" with a summary that looks complete while an entire section has been silently deleted by a swallowed error.

`recentDecisionMatches` (internal/cli/agent_surface.go) discarded `loadBrainHistoryIndex`'s error:

```go
index, err := loadBrainHistoryIndex(brainDir, source)
if err != nil {
	return nil
}
```

A source that failed to load is then treated as an empty one. With a corrupt or unreadable `history/index.json` the command exits 0, still reports `sources.history: true`, and the whole "recent decisions" block just disappears:

```

repo: /tmp/... (gh/example/repo)
freshness:
semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
recent decisions:
  [] chose postgres for checkpoint storage

# same brain, index bytes corrupted — no error, no warning, no section
repo: /tmp/... (gh/example/repo)
freshness:
semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
```

Second half of the same problem: `renderBrainOverviewText` never rendered `report.Warnings` at all, so even the warnings `overview` already collects (they ride the JSON contract) never reached a CLI caller.

## Repro

`internal/cli/brain_overview_source_honesty_test.go` builds a brain whose manifest declares a history index that really exists and really holds one decision, proves `overview` carries it, corrupts only the index bytes, and asserts the section's disappearance is explained.

On clean `main` (a812069d):

--- FAIL: TestOverviewReportsUnreadableHistoryIndex
    brain_overview_source_honesty_test.go:87: overview dropped the recent-decisions section with no warning:
        repo: /tmp/.../001 (gh/example/repo)
        freshness:
        semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
FAIL
```

`TestOverviewReportsUnreadableHistoryIndex` is the repro and it compiles and fails unmodified on `main`. The second test in the file, `TestRecentDecisionMatchesReportsUnreadableIndex`, pins the helper seam directly and therefore **cannot** compile on `main` — it asserts the two-value signature this PR introduces. Run the first one to reproduce.

## Fix

- `recentDecisionMatches` returns `([]brainTextMatch, error)`; an unreadable declared index is an error, not an empty decision log.
- `runBrainOverview` records it as `recent decisions unavailable: the manifest declares a history index that could not be read: ...` on `report.Warnings`, so it reaches both the JSON contract and the text surface.
- `renderBrainOverviewText` renders a `warnings:` section, which it never did before.

The rest of the summary is still produced from the sources that do load, so a partly-unreadable brain still answers — it just no longer answers as if nothing were missing.

## What breaks

`entire brain remember --branch <other> "..."` files the fact on `<other>` while the
working tree stays where it is — and then stamps the anchor with `git rev-parse HEAD`,
which is the **current** branch's tip.

The stored fact therefore reads "on `release`, evidenced by `<a commit that is only on
main>`". The pairing never existed. `entire brain verify` cannot catch it either:
`verifyCommitUncached` accepts reachability from *any* local ref, so it reports the
fabricated anchor as `commit exists and is reachable from local refs` → **verified**,
permanently.

This is the authored-fact twin of the same branch-blindness the distilled path has:
the anchor's branch and the anchor's commit are resolved from two different places and
never reconciled.

## Repro

`internal/cli/facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go` runs the real `remember` command with
the working tree on `main` (tip = commit B) and `release` pointing somewhere else
entirely.

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn (0.24s)
    facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go:37: a fact filed on `release` cites bbbb222222222222222222222222222222222222, the tip of the CURRENT branch (main)
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/ashtom/entire-brain/internal/cli	0.990s
```

A second test, `TestRememberKeepsHeadWhenNoBranchOverrideIsGiven`, pins the unchanged
default so the fix cannot be "stop recording a commit".

## Fix

`rememberAnchorCommit` resolves the commit from the branch the fact is actually being
filed on:

* with an explicit `--branch`, `git rev-parse --verify <branch>^{commit}` — the named
  branch's tip is the only honest evidence, and a branch git cannot resolve yields
  **no** commit rather than a wrong one (an absent anchor verifies as unverifiable,
  which is the truth; a wrong one verifies as correct, which is not);
* without one, `git rev-parse HEAD` exactly as before — the branch was derived *from*
  HEAD in the first place, and this also keeps a detached HEAD citing the commit that
  is actually checked out.

The no-override path keeps its original argv byte for byte, so nothing about the
default behavior moves.

## Mutation check

Collapsing `rememberAnchorCommit` back to the unconditional `rev-parse HEAD`
reproduces the original failure:

```
--- FAIL: TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn
    facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go:37: a fact filed on `release` cites bbbb2222...
```

`TestRememberKeepsHeadWhenNoBranchOverrideIsGiven` stays green under that mutation and
under the fix, so it is pinning the default rather than the bug.

## What breaks

A distill run loads a branch's facts **once**, when it first sees the branch, and rewrites the **whole** set at every flush. Its read-modify-write therefore spans the entire run — which the flush comment itself describes as "hours of agent calls".

The brain write lock does not help. Each flush takes it, so the write is serialized, but every other writer already committed and released long before. Everything they did in that window is silently written back over:

- a fact the user added with `entire brain remember` disappears from the store;
- a `facts retract` reverts to `active`;
- a proposal applied in `facts review` is undone;
- a settlement `facts sync` mirrored back from the shared head is undone.

Nothing errors. `remember` printed success, `facts retract` printed success, and the user's next `recall` simply shows the pre-edit state. The longer the run, the wider the window — and a background/scheduled distill makes the window effectively always open.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/incremental (0.83s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/force (2.94s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
FAIL
```

The concurrent writer in the test is a full transaction under the brain write lock — exactly what `facts retract` and `remember` do — committed from inside the fake agent call, i.e. mid-run.

## Fix

The flush rebases the run's in-memory set onto the current on-disk set before writing, under the lock it already holds. The rebase is deliberately **monotone**:

- it adopts on-disk records the run never saw (someone else's addition);
- it adopts a retirement someone else applied to a record the run does hold (`active` -> `retracted`/`superseded` only, never the reverse);
- it changes nothing else.

So it can never undo one of the run's own decisions, and it is idempotent across the repeated mid-run flushes (the second flush re-reads what the first wrote and finds nothing to do).

`--force` is threaded through because a force rebuild deliberately dropped the active distilled facts it is regenerating; re-adopting those would turn the rebuild into an append. `TestDistillForceStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` pins that down and passes both before and after the fix.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both subtests fail again with the messages above, while `TestDistillForceStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` keeps passing.

## What breaks

`distill --force` drops every distilled record before replaying distillation:

```go
if record.Origin != factOriginDistilled {
    kept = append(kept, record)
}
```

That includes **retired** ones. `retracted` and `superseded` record decisions the rebuild does not replay — `facts retract`, an applied review proposal, a `facts promote --strategy prefer-source`, a settlement mirrored back by `facts sync`. With the tombstone gone, the very next chunk re-adds the same statement under the same content-derived id as **active**.

A fact the user explicitly declared no longer true comes back to life and starts being recalled again. A superseded fact comes back active and without its `superseded_by` pointer, so the store now asserts both it and its replacement. Neither prints anything; the run reports a normal rebuild.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestForceDistill' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestForceDistillDoesNotResurrectRetractedFact (0.90s)
    distill_force_retirement_test.go:52: distill --force resurrected a retracted fact as "active":
        {ID:fact:7a63dc1f5dd94ea931920b6c ... Status:active Confidence:1.00 ...}
--- FAIL: TestForceDistillDoesNotResurrectSupersededFact (0.87s)
    distill_force_retirement_test.go:76: distill --force resurrected a superseded fact: {...}
FAIL
```

The tests run the real `runDistillForBrain` with a fake agent that re-emits exactly the retired statement, so the regenerated candidate is guaranteed to collide on the content-derived id.

## Fix

The force filter retains any non-active distilled record. It costs nothing: the regenerated candidate carries the same id, so `upsertFact` lands on the retained tombstone, unions provenance and leaves the status alone — and a supersede the rebuild *does* replay re-marks it identically.

Active distilled facts are still dropped and rebuilt, so `--force` is still a rebuild: `TestForceDistillStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` pins that down and passes both before and after, which is what makes the other two tests specific to the retirement case.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both resurrection tests fail again with the messages above, while `TestForceDistillStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` keeps passing.

## What breaks

`dedupeProposals` collapses review-queue entries on `(action, candidate, target)`. `factsync.ProposalID` — the id the hosted review queue, the shared-proposal ledger and the `facts review` interlock all key on — additionally covers `branch` and `proposed_by`. The two identities disagree, and the queue is written through the narrower one.

distill's private backlog and a cross-member conflict raised by `facts sync` routinely name the same two facts: the shared head holds this member's own previously-synced facts, so the pair repeats. `persistFactsSyncProposals` writes `append(existing, raised...)`, so dedupe keeps the unattributed private entry and drops the member-attributed one.

The consequences are both silent:

- `facts sync` publishes only attributed entries (`if strings.TrimSpace(p.ProposedBy) == "" { continue }`), so the cross-member conflict is **never shared with the team**. Nobody else ever sees it.
- What survives locally looks like a private distill proposal, so the `facts review` shared-proposal interlock does not fire and the member settles it locally — the exact outcome that interlock exists to prevent, since (per its own error text) "a local-only decision would be overridden by the next sync".

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDedupeProposalsKeepsMemberAttribution|TestPersistFactsSyncProposalsKeepsAttributedEntry' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestDedupeProposalsKeepsMemberAttribution (0.00s)
    facts_proposal_attribution_test.go:20: want both the private and the member-attributed proposal,
        got [{Action:supersede CandidateID:fact:c TargetID:fact:t Confidence:0 Branch: ProposedBy:}]
--- FAIL: TestPersistFactsSyncProposalsKeepsAttributedEntry (0.00s)
    facts_proposal_attribution_test.go:64: the cross-member conflict is not publishable after
        persisting; queue = [{... ProposedBy:}]
FAIL
```

The second test goes through the real durable path (`writeFactProposals` -> `persistFactsSyncProposals` -> `loadFactProposals`).

## Fix

The dedupe key now matches `factsync.ProposalID`: action, candidate, target, branch, proposed_by. True duplicates still collapse; entries the sharing machinery treats as distinct rows stay distinct. The sort is extended to a total order over the same fields so the on-disk queue remains deterministic regardless of input order (the test asserts that too).

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/reconcile.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both tests fail again with the messages above.

## What breaks

`factmerge.Promote` copies only **active** source facts (`if sf.Status != StatusActive { continue }`), and `factsync.Sync` is built on it. A member's retirements therefore never reach the shared fact-set head.

Run `entire brain facts retract fact:<id>` and then `entire brain facts sync`. The merge produces bytes identical to the current head, `Advance` short-circuits on `ErrNoChange`, and the command prints:

```
synced 4 local fact(s) on main via local-gitmeta (...): no change; head at facts-... (1 attempt(s))
```

The retraction is gone. Every other member — and every other clone of this member — goes on reading a statement its owner has explicitly declared false, forever: no later sync can ever carry it, because the condition that suppressed it does not change. The same applies to a supersede applied in `facts review`: the replacement fact is promoted, but the head keeps the retired fact **active** and unlinked, so the team sees two contradictory facts with no indication which one won.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/factsync/ -run 'TestSyncPropagates|TestSyncDoesNotRevive' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:50: retraction sync reported no change; the head still carries the fact as active
    retirement_test.go:59: shared head still says "active" after the owner retracted the fact
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesSupersede (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:104: head target not superseded: {ID:fact:306d0675... Status:active ...}
--- FAIL: TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:134: a peer sync revived a retracted fact: [...]
FAIL
```

## Fix

`Sync` folds the member's local retirements onto the merged set before the CAS. The pass is deliberately **monotone**: it only moves a fact from `active` to `retracted`/`superseded`, never back, and only for a record the head already carries.

That gives three properties the tests pin down:

- a retraction reaches the head and the sync publishes (`TestSyncPropagatesRetraction`);
- a peer who still holds the fact as active cannot revive it on their next sync (`TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction`);
- re-syncing the same local state is still a no-op, so the loop converges.

Nothing is deleted — the record, its provenance and its `superseded_by` pointer are retained — so the keep-both guarantee (ADR-P1-G) is unaffected: a fact is retired, never dropped.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/factsync/sync.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes all three tests fail again with the messages above.

## What breaks

A fact id is content-derived (`sha256(normalized text + sorted paths)`), so `entire brain remember "<statement>"` for a statement that was previously retracted lands on the retired record. `upsertFact` matches by id and only unions provenance — it never revives a status, which is exactly right for a re-distill and wrong for an explicit human assertion.

The write is silently lost. The command prints

```
remembered fact:8e83a375b9e7062da881300a [preference] preferences.coding.style on feature
```

and exits 0, while the record on disk stays `retracted`: recall skips it, the fact tree skips it, the manifest's `by_kind` histogram skips it. Short of opening `facts.ndjson` there is no way for the author to know the fact they just wrote down is not in their brain. The same holds for a fact retired by an applied supersede proposal.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestRememberRevives' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestRememberRevivesRetractedFact (0.08s)
    facts_remember_revive_test.go:68: re-authored fact is still "retracted" after
        "remembered fact:8e83a375b9e7062da881300a [preference] preferences.coding.style on feature\n":
        the command reported success but the fact is not recallable
--- FAIL: TestRememberRevivesSupersededFact (0.06s)
    facts_remember_revive_test.go:104: re-authored fact not revived: [{... Status:superseded
        SupersededBy:fact:newer ...}]
FAIL
```

The tests drive the real `runRemember` end to end against a temp brain.

## Fix

Re-authoring now restores the status the author just asserted and clears `superseded_by`. The record is revived, not replaced: `created_at`, provenance and cross-links are kept, and the explicit `--kind` override still wins as before. `upsertFact` itself is untouched, so a re-distill still cannot resurrect a retired fact.

A note on the superseded case: reviving leaves both the revived fact and its replacement active. That is the store's normal keep-both state for two statements a human has asserted, and it is visible in `facts review`/`recall` — unlike today's outcome, where the author's write disappears without trace.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/facts_write_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both revive tests fail again with the messages above, while `TestRememberActiveFactIsStillIdempotent` keeps passing — confirming the tests key on the revival, not on the surrounding upsert path.

## What breaks

`facts reclassify` is the only fact mutator that rewrites `facts.ndjson` without holding the brain write lock. It loads the branch's facts, mutates the records in memory, and writes the whole set back — all outside the lock that `remember`, `facts retract`, `facts review`, `facts promote`, `facts gc`, `facts sync`'s reconcile and distill's flush all take, and that `reclassifyAllFactBranches` (the same operation on the refresh path) takes for its entire pass.

Any writer that commits between reclassify's read and its write is silently overwritten. A fact just added by `entire brain remember`, a retraction just applied by `facts retract`, a settlement just mirrored by `facts sync` — gone from the store, with no error printed by either command and nothing in the manifest to hint at it. The window covers the whole branch, so nothing narrows it.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess -count=1
--- FAIL: TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess (0.52s)
    facts_reclassify_lock_test.go:120: facts reclassify rewrote facts.ndjson while another process
        held the brain write lock: [{ID:fact:inv ... Kind:invariant ...}]
FAIL
```

The test spawns a real second **process** (a re-exec of the test binary) that holds the brain write lock — the lock is an `flock(2)` advisory lock, so an in-process mutex would not exercise it — and checks that `facts reclassify` has not rewritten `facts.ndjson` while that process holds it. It then releases the lock and asserts reclassify completes and persists its work.

## Fix

The load, the mutation, the write and the manifest rebuild now run inside one `withBrainWriteLock`, using `updateFactSourceManifestLocked` so the lock is taken once instead of being re-entered by `updateFactSourceManifest`. That re-entry is also why the old code did not simply deadlock: it wrote the facts unprotected and only then blocked on the lock for the manifest.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes `TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess` fail again with the message above.
