## The drift

The export and verify readers branch on `strategy_options.checkpoints_version` / `checkpoints_v2` and, when either is set, route every checkpoint read at `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main`.

Neither half of that contract has a producer:

- **The setting is ignored by the writer.** The only mention of `checkpoints_version` in `entireio/cli` is `TestNewGitStore_IgnoresCheckpointsVersion` (`cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent_read_store_test.go`), which exists specifically to pin that `ResolveRefs`/`NewGitStore` resolve checkpoint refs *without* consulting it.
- **The ref is never written.** The string `checkpoints/v2` does not appear anywhere in the CLI's Go sources. Checkpoints v2 was a flagged work-in-progress (CHANGELOG, PRs #742/#759/#955) that was removed before it shipped; the surviving backends are `git-branch` (`refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`) and `git-refs` (one ref per checkpoint under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`).

## Which side is wrong

The reader. The writer's behaviour is the contract, and the writer has no v2. There is nothing missing on the CLI side to "finish" — reviving v2 would need both halves built new: a writer for the aggregate ref *and* a store that honours the setting.

## Why it is worth removing rather than leaving

The branch was not merely unreachable, it was actively harmful, which is also what makes it testable. A repository whose `.entire/settings.json` still carries `"checkpoints_version": 2` has ordinary v1 checkpoints on disk, and the reader diverted away from them:

- `--raw` failed with `direct v2 raw transcript export is not implemented`
- `--raw=false` failed reading the non-existent `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main`

Both then fell back to routed discovery, shelling out to `entire checkpoint explain` once per checkpoint for a topology that never existed. And dead code that looks load-bearing is a trap: it reads as "the brain supports two storage generations", which it does not.

## The fix

Removed from `internal/cli/export.go`: `v2MainRef`, `checkpointStorageV2`, `v2TranscriptFileName`, `CheckpointsV2Enabled`, `CheckpointsVersionValue`, the `checkpoints_v2` / `checkpoints_version` settings fields, the `includeV2` plumbing through `localCheckpointRefs`, and the v2 fast path in `loadConfiguredCheckpointSnapshot`. Removed from `internal/cli/verify_cmd.go`: the matching v2 branch in `loadLocalCheckpointSnapshotForVerify`.

## Tests

`internal/cli/export_dead_v2_test.go` (new): a repository carrying `checkpoints_version: 2` now exports the v1 checkpoints it actually has, for both `--raw` and compact, and no export path consults a v2 ref. Both subtests fail on `main` with the two divert errors quoted above.

The existing guards that assert no export reaches for a v2 ref are kept, now anchored on a literal so they keep guarding after the constant is gone. Two tests that existed only to describe the v2 fast path (`...DoesNotMaskGitRefsWithV2FastPath`, `...KeepsCompleteV2OnlyNoEgress`) are removed, and three fixtures that carried the ignored setting incidentally are trimmed.

Mutation-verified: re-adding the v2 ref to `localCheckpointRefs` trips the "v2 ref should not be used" guard in `TestExportUsesCompleteRoutedDiscoveryForConfiguredCheckpointRemote`.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and the full `./internal/cli` suite (2394 tests) are green.","created_at":"2026-08-29T04:20:13Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/export-drop-dead-v2-path","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/163","number":163,"sha":"ed4e0e1ff124c67df02f2ccad4b4419795d2d306","title":"fix(export): drop the checkpoints-v2 reader no writer feeds","updated_at":"2026-08-29T04:20:19Z"}

## The drift

`entireio/cli` is the writer of checkpoint transcripts and `entire-brain` is the reader, and the two disagreed about how a chunked transcript is put back together.

The CLI splits an oversized transcript into `full.jsonl` plus numbered `full.jsonl.NNN` parts (`cmd/entire/cli/agent/chunking.go`, `ChunkTranscript`/`ChunkFileName`) and reassembles them **format-aware** (`ReassembleTranscript`): JSONL agents get a newline join, and Gemini — the one supported agent whose transcript is a standalone JSON document rather than JSONL — gets its per-part `{"messages":[...]}` arrays concatenated into **one** document (`cmd/entire/cli/agent/geminicli/gemini.go`).

The export reader did neither half of that:

1. `readCheckpointSourceTranscript` and `readSnapshotTranscriptFromSource` both returned the base file alone whenever that path was present in the tree, short-circuiting before `snapshotTranscriptChunks` ever ran. Every chunked transcript was therefore exported truncated to its first part.
2. On the path that did read the parts, they were byte-joined with `\n`. For Gemini that yields two top-level JSON documents in one file, so the exported transcript for the only non-JSONL agent did not parse at all.

## Which side is wrong

The reader. The writer's chunking contract is the format that is actually on disk, and the CLI's own reader (`readTranscriptFromTree` in `cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent.go`) treats the unsuffixed file as chunk 0 and reassembles agent-aware. The brain has to match it.

## The fix

`internal/cli/export.go`: both readers now collect every ordered part via `snapshotTranscriptChunks` and hand them to one `readTranscriptChunks` helper, which merges Gemini message arrays into a single document and newline-joins everything else. Gemini detection mirrors the CLI's own content sniff (`DetectAgentTypeFromContent`) — which is what the CLI itself falls back to when the agent type is not recorded — and messages are re-emitted verbatim as `json.RawMessage`, so nothing is normalized away. A single unchunked part is returned byte-for-byte unchanged, which keeps the overwhelmingly common case identical to a plain read.

A later part that does not parse as a Gemini document is now an error rather than a silently malformed export: the first part already parsed, so that is a damaged store, and the caller already degrades an unreadable transcript into a scope-incomplete warning.

## Tests

`internal/cli/export_gemini_chunks_test.go` (new), covering both readers:

- Gemini `full.jsonl` + `full.jsonl.001` reassembles into one valid JSON document with all three messages in order.
- JSONL chunks keep the newline join and no longer lose the trailing part.
- An unchunked transcript is returned verbatim.

Every new test fails on `main`. Mutation-verified: forcing `isGeminiTranscriptDocument` to return `false` fails only the Gemini cases; restoring the base-file early return fails both the Gemini and the JSONL cases.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and the full `./internal/cli` suite (2398 tests) are green.","created_at":"2026-08-29T04:14:23Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/export-gemini-chunk-merge","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/162","number":162,"sha":"cecff70ea980f67600ab28de3337a8925bb6e86d","title":"fix(export): reassemble transcript chunks the way the CLI wrote them","updated_at":"2026-08-29T04:14:28Z"}

## Problem

`checkpointEntriesFromIDs` sorted discovered checkpoint IDs as reversed strings and then truncated to `--checkpoint-limit`, which `discoverCheckpoints` treats as "inspect the most recent N":

```go
sort.Sort(sort.Reverse(sort.StringSlice(sorted)))
if limit > 0 && len(sorted) > limit {
    sorted = sorted[:limit]
}
```

The two ID formats do not share an ordering:

- a **ULID** encodes a millisecond timestamp in its leading characters, so it is genuinely time-sortable — which is what the reversed sort was reaching for;
- a **legacy 12-hex** ID is random throughout and carries no time at all.

Hex is lowercase (`[0-9a-f]`) and a ULID is uppercase Crockford base32, so in descending byte order **every hex ID beginning `a`–`f` outranks every ULID**. Under a limit that systematically discarded the newest checkpoints — the ULIDs the git-refs backend mints — and kept the oldest ones from the pre-migration `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch. In a repo mid-migration, `--checkpoint-limit` returned precisely the wrong end of the history, and the warning it prints ("rerun with a larger limit to inspect more") reads as if the newest were kept.

## Fix

Order by the time the ID actually carries, falling back to descending ID for the legacy IDs that carry none. An ID with a recoverable creation time outranks one without, rather than guessing a legacy ID's era and placing it above checkpoints known to be newer.

`checkpointULIDTime` already existed for exactly this and is already used a few hundred lines away — `loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot` applies the same rule to the same two formats when it sorts by `createdAt`. This brings the two discovery paths into agreement.

A repo that has only ever minted legacy IDs keeps its previous descending-ID order.

## Tests

- `TestCheckpointEntriesFromIDs_LimitKeepsTheNewest` — one legacy hex ID plus two ULIDs, `limit=2`. Fails on `main` (keeps `fedcba987654` and drops the older ULID), passes here.
- `TestCheckpointEntriesFromIDs_LegacyOnlyKeepsDescendingOrder` — unchanged behavior for a legacy-only repo; passes before and after.

`mise run lint` clean. `go test ./internal/cli/` green (2395).","created_at":"2026-08-29T03:54:35Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/export-newest-first-mixed-ids","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/161","number":161,"sha":"1306d9e62f8bd0bfab66b5759c9b435148fea6fe","title":"fix(export): order mixed-format checkpoint IDs by recency, not byte value","updated_at":"2026-08-29T03:54:42Z"}

## Problem

`loadAggregateCheckpointSources` walks the git-branch backend's two aggregate refs:

```go
for _, ref := range []string{v1MainRef, v1OriginRef} {
    ...
    if len(sources) > 0 {
        return sources, warnings   // stops here
    }
}
```

The early return is inside the loop, so the moment `refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1` yields **any** checkpoint, `refs/remotes/origin/entire/checkpoints/v1` is never read.

`entire/checkpoints/v1` is an ordinary branch, and the two refs diverge in both directions:

- the CLI advances the local ref only under its own confinement rules — local-ref advancement is elected-remote-only (`EnsurePrimaryRef`, `SafelyAdvanceLocalRef`), deliberately, so a stale tracking ref cannot replay history onto it;
- checkpoints pushed from another clone land on origin's tracking ref on the next fetch without ever touching this clone's local branch.

So one stale local checkpoint hides **every** origin-only checkpoint, and the export reports success. The caller is `loadLocalCheckpointUnionSnapshot` — the complete-local-union fast path, which labels the manifest `"exporting raw transcripts directly from complete local checkpoint store union"` — so nothing downstream can tell the set was short. Sessions that exist only in origin-side checkpoints are silently absent from the export, and from everything built on it.

## Fix

Read every candidate ref and union the results. **First ref wins per checkpoint ID**, so the local ref keeps its precedence for a checkpoint both refs carry — only checkpoints the earlier ref does not have are added.

Warnings from every ref are now returned, not just the winning ref's.

## Tests

- `TestLoadAggregateCheckpointSources_UnionsEveryCandidateRef` — a local-only and an origin-only checkpoint. Fails on `main` (discovers only the local one), passes here, and asserts each ID resolves to the ref it actually came from.
- `TestLoadAggregateCheckpointSources_LocalRefWinsAConflict` — precedence is unchanged for a checkpoint on both refs; passes before and after.

`mise run lint` clean. `go test ./internal/cli/` green (2395).

## Related, not fixed here

The candidate list itself is still `[local, origin]`, while the CLI's read contract is `[elected sync remote, origin]` (`strategy.CheckpointReadRemotes`). A repo whose checkpoints sync to a non-origin remote has its data on `refs/remotes/<elected>/entire/checkpoints/v1`, which this function does not consult at all. Adding it means resolving the election on the brain side, which is a larger change and a separate call.","created_at":"2026-08-29T03:49:41Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/export-aggregate-ref-union","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/160","number":160,"sha":"b1e244d84ca1ef94498dff95d9eb1d201d94e071","title":"fix(export): union every aggregate checkpoint ref instead of stopping at the first","updated_at":"2026-08-29T03:49:48Z"}

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## The drift

Found by a live round-trip against the real entire-api, not by reading code.

The server now answers a violated cap with an actionable body:

```
400 {"title":"Bad Request","status":400,"detail":"branch is 600 bytes, limit is 512"}
```

The fact-set transport read only the status line. A member hitting a server-side limit got:

```
factsync: POST advance repo/main: unexpected status 400 Bad Request
```

No statement of what was wrong, and no statement of the limit. Six call sites dropped the body: `Current`, `Advance`, `ListProposals`, `GetProposal`, `PublishProposals`, `ResolveProposal`.

## What changed

**`internal/httpx/errbody.go`** — one renderer, next to the outbound HTTP policy the package already owns. Reading an error body has three hazards, solved once rather than at each call site:

| | |
|---|---|
| **size** | The body is not always the small envelope the endpoint documents. An ingress in front of entire-api answers 502/504 with an HTML page; a broken upstream can stream without end. The read is bounded (8 KiB) and the rendered line is bounded again (200 runes). |
| **shape** | JSON when the endpoint answered, HTML when something in front of it did. A gateway page says everything it has to say in its `<title>`; the markup is noise. huma splits a validation failure across a generic `detail` and a specific `errors[]`, so both are kept. |
| **content** | The bytes are attacker-influenced and are about to be printed to a terminal, so control characters (ANSI escapes, NUL, newlines that would forge a log line) and invalid UTF-8 are stripped. |

A body with nothing to say renders `""`, and the suffix form then adds no separator — a message is never left ending in a bare `": "`.

**`internal/factsync`** — all six sites render the body. **`internal/hostedbrain`** — replaces an ad-hoc `io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(…, 4096))` that pasted the raw prefix through. **`internal/cli/publish.go`** — `publishServerDetail` delegates to the shared renderer (it handled huma's envelope correctly and pasted every other shape through as a raw 200-byte slice), and the 503 branch stops dropping the body: the server uses 503 for several distinct reasons and its own sentence is the only thing that says which.

## Semantics are pinned separately from the message

Every status this transport reads is load-bearing control flow. Each mapping has a test asserting `errors.Is`, not the string, so improving the message cannot quietly change the meaning:

- **412 / 409 → `ErrConflict`** — the CAS-loss signal `sync.go` and `proposals.go` re-read and re-merge on. Wrapped with `%w`; a bare 412 (no body) returns the bare sentinel exactly as before.
- **404 / 501 / 503 on the proposal endpoints → `ErrProposalQueueUnsupported`** — "this deployment has no queue", which degrades to the local queue rather than failing a sync whose head-advance already succeeded.
- **404 on one proposal → `ErrProposalNotFound`** — the normal outcome when another member already settled it.
- **The transient-dial retry classifier (#137) is untouched** — it reads a transport error, which exists before any response does. A test re-proves both halves: a local port-table blip is still retried, a refused connection still is not.
- **`brain publish` error classes** (`publish_auth:` / `publish_rejected:` / `publish_unavailable:` / `publish_too_large:` / `publish_failed:`) are unchanged, pinned per status.

## Pre-validate vs surface

**Pre-validated: the branch cap (512 bytes).** The branch is known before a socket is opened, and the request that would learn the limit carries the member's bearer token and, on `Advance`/`ResolveProposal`, the member's whole fact set — a multi-megabyte upload posted only to be told the branch name was too long. The client refuses first, with the same two numbers the server states, at a single chokepoint (`requestTarget`) covering all six methods. `maxBranchBytes` states the residual risk plainly: if the hosted cap is *raised*, this client refuses a branch the server would now accept and cannot detect that on its own. That is accepted only because 512 bytes is far outside the range of any real branch name.

**Surfaced, not mirrored: the publish artifact count and manifest-reference count, and whatever the hosted MCP surface applies to its own branch argument.** The client has no independent basis for those numbers — unlike the publish body-size ceiling, which it must project anyway to avoid building a multi-GB buffer — so a guessed constant would refuse requests the server accepts. The server's own message wins there.

## 5xx and non-JSON

Both covered by tests, on all three surfaces. The surfacing is keyed on "not the success status", not a hand-listed set of 4xx codes, so a 500 with `{"detail":"fact-set store is read-only"}` reaches the member. A 4 MiB HTML error page arrives as `504 Gateway Time-out` and the whole error stays under 1 KiB, with no markup and no control bytes.

## Verification

- Failing-test-first on all three surfaces (stub renderer → assertion failures → implementation).
- Mutation-verified, each reverted independently:
  - drop the surfacing → all 6 factsync surfacing tests fail
  - 412/409 stops wrapping `ErrConflict` → the conflict-semantics test fails (and the pre-existing `TestHTTPServerContract` fails with it)
  - 404/501/503 stops wrapping `ErrProposalQueueUnsupported` → its test fails
  - 404 stops wrapping `ErrProposalNotFound` → its test fails
  - drop the branch pre-validation → the branch tests fail, the at-the-limit control still passes
  - httpx forgets HTML titles and sanitizing → the httpx, factsync and hostedbrain rendering tests fail
  - publish 503 drops the body again → its test fails
- `mise run lint` clean; `go test ./internal/cli ./internal/factsync ./internal/httpx ./internal/hostedbrain` green, plus `-race` on the three transport packages.

Stacked on #154 (`audit/sec-repoid-all-sites`), the tip of the #125 → #121 → #137 → #119 → #154 stack that owns `factsync/httpserver.go`, `factsync/httpproposals.go`, `hostedbrain/client.go` and `cli/publish.go`.","created_at":"2026-08-29T03:22:35Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/http-error-body","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/159","number":159,"sha":"aa5d6fbaa6a63229c264d5f6dce10c48e7bfee34","title":"fix(hostedbrain,factsync,publish): surface the server's error body instead of a bare status","updated_at":"2026-08-29T03:22:42Z"}

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the error-contract half. One handler-side fix, independent of #156/#157 (different file, sibling branch off the same base).

## The drift

`inspectBoundarySpec` is shared by the `boundaries` CLI command (two call sites) and the `brain_boundaries` MCP tool. Its rejection message was written for the CLI:

```
--kind must be route, tool, or workflow
```

So an agent that sent `{"name":"brain_boundaries","arguments":{"kind":"controller"}}` was told to correct a **flag that does not exist on the surface it is calling**. Over MCP the argument is the JSON field `kind`, which the tool's own schema declares and `validateMCPToolArguments` validates by that name. An agent taking the error literally has nowhere to go.

#118 found this and left it as cosmetic. It is small, but it is the error contract of a tool an agent drives blind, and this surface is about to be wrapped — so the misleading string would propagate.

## Fix

The message names the accepted values without naming a flag, which reads correctly from both callers. The CLI still tells the user exactly which values are valid, and cobra supplies the flag context there.

Scope deliberately kept to the shared helper: `facts_read_cmd.go:424` has the same `--kind` phrasing but is CLI-only — no MCP tool exposes a facts kind argument — so it is correct as written and untouched.

## Test

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2 — the description half. Two tools described behaviour their handlers do not implement.

Both matter more than usual: an agent picks a tool by reading these strings, and a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a wrong description propagates into consumers that never see this repo.

## 1. `brain_refresh` promised a worktree semantic index it never builds

The description said, flatly: *"Includes current worktree content by default."*

The `worktree` argument only ever reaches seed and docs. The handler leaves `semanticWorktree` false (`refresh.go:327` reads it, `mcp.go` never sets it), so the semantic index that `semantic=true` rebuilds is built from **committed HEAD**. The refresh command's own `RunE` carries the comment explaining why: *"--worktree belongs to seed/docs. A dirty semantic snapshot must be an explicit `brain index --worktree` operation."*

So an agent calling `brain_refresh(worktree=true, semantic=true)` — the exact combination the description discusses — was left believing its semantic index reflected uncommitted work. It did not.

This is the same drift that shipped in the README as `refresh --worktree` and was corrected in #141. The MCP tool string and the two docs paragraphs describing `brain_refresh` were not part of that fix; they are corrected here.

## 2. `brain_index_repository` claimed a refresh it refuses, and hid its gate

- **"Build or refresh"** — `runSemanticIndex` errors with `semantic index already exists; use --force to replace it` unless `force=true`. The default cannot refresh. (#118 flagged this and left it, on the grounds that the `force` argument's own text disambiguates. I disagree: the top-level description is what an agent reads to *choose* the tool, and "refresh" is the wrong verb at exactly that moment.)
- **Path scoping was undeclared.** The path is confined to the bound repository root unless `ENTIRE_BRAIN_MCP_ALLOW_ANY_PATH` is set, and a relative path resolves against that root rather than the working directory. This was the one path-scoped tool that did not name its gate inline — `brain_delete_project`, `brain_list_projects` and the workspace tools all do, after #133, so an agent that hits the refusal learns the knob from the surface it is already reading. It is documented in README and `docs/limits.md`, but not where the agent is looking.
- **`profile` asserted a closed list.** It claimed *"full, fast, or syntax-only"*. Nothing in this repo validates the value or knows the set — it is forwarded verbatim to the external provider subprocess, and the CLI flag help for the same field says *"e.g. full, syntax-only"*. I could not verify whether `fast` exists, so rather than pick a side I removed the authoritative framing and made the string say what the code actually does. Flagging the two help strings still disagreeing as a follow-up for whoever owns the provider contract.

## Tests that pin declaration to behaviour

`mcpRefreshOptions` is extracted from the `brain_refresh` case block with **no behaviour change**, purely so the claim can be pinned against the handler rather than against a comment.

- **`TestMCPRefreshWorktreeContractMatchesHandler`** asserts in one test that `worktree` reaches `seed.worktree`, that `semanticWorktree` stays false in the `worktree=true, semantic=true` combination, that the default really is `worktree=true`, and that the description says all of this. If `brain_refresh` ever does start indexing the worktree, the test fails and forces the description to move with it.
- **`TestMCPIndexRepositoryDescribesForceAndPathScope`** drives `mcpResolveIndexPath` — absolute path contained, relative path joined onto the bound root, env gate lifting containment — beside the strings that describe it, and fails if the description drifts back to "Build or refresh" or drops the gate name.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

Contract audit of the MCP tool surface, pass 2. #118 compared each tool's declared schema against its handler and fixed three items; this is the adversarial re-check of the rows it marked "none", plus the drift #117 introduced.

## The drift

`mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` reject any integer argument above `mcpIntegerArgMax` (10000) with a `-32000` tool error. The JSON schema declared a floor and **no ceiling** on 27 of the surface's 30 integer arguments.

So a schema-validating MCP client believed `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000}}` was a legal call, sent it, and learned the real bound by being refused at runtime. The declaration understated the contract the handler enforces. #117 added the cap; the schema was never told about it.

`brain_get` was the exception — its `context_before`/`context_after`/`limit` already declared the stricter ceilings their downstream validator enforces (`conversationContextMax`, `conversationOutlineMaxLimit`). Its `after_turn` did not, and is fixed here.

## Fix

`maximum` declared alongside `minimum` in the `integerArg`/`nonNegativeIntegerArg` helpers and on `brain_get`'s inline `after_turn` schema. No handler behaviour changes — this makes the declaration state what the handler already did.

## Tests that pin the two sides together

- **`TestMCPIntegerArgsDeclareTheCeilingTheHandlerEnforces`** walks every integer argument on every tool and requires a declared `maximum` that is never above what the handler accepts. It proves the generic ceiling by calling `mcpPositiveInt`/`mcpNonNegativeInt` at the boundary and one past it, rather than asserting a constant against itself, and it checks the stricter per-tool ceilings against the very constants their downstream validator uses. A new integer argument that forgets its ceiling fails here.
- **`TestMCPToolSurfaceGolden`** pins the whole declared surface — every name, description, and schema — in `testdata/mcp_tool_surface.golden.json`. There was no golden over the full tool-definition JSON; the three existing goldens cover one tool each, chosen for their token budget. This one exists because a separate unified-MCP layer is about to wrap this surface, so a silent edit to a name or a bound propagates into consumers that never see this repo. Regenerate deliberately with `UPDATE_MCP_SURFACE_GOLDEN=1`.

## Cost, measured

The declared ceiling adds 16 bytes per integer argument: **+432 bytes on the `tools/list` result, 26,074 -> 26,506 (+1.7%)**.

The three per-tool byte budgets are re-measured (747->763, 810->826, 987->1003). Their **token** counts in those comments are the earlier measurement and are **not** re-measured here — the pinned o200k_base asset is deliberately not a test dependency, so I could not recompute them honestly rather than estimate.

## Verification

`go build ./...` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli` clean, `go test ./internal/cli -run 'TestMCP|TestDocContract'` green (73 tests). Full suite not re-run on a loaded host.

Stacked on **#116** (`audit/sec-proposal-id-binding`), which is where proposal-id semantics live. Review that first; the diff here is the request-path half of the same subject.

This is the follow-up #154 named. #154 closed the `repoID` segment hole at every request site and left `proposalID` alone on purpose, because it is interpolated into the same two targets and needs its own format rule rather than the repo-id one.

## What is still open after #116

`proposalID` reaches the wire as a path segment at two endpoints:

```
GET  /api/v1/repos/{repo}/brain/facts/proposals/{id}
POST /api/v1/repos/{repo}/brain/facts/proposals/{id}/resolve
```

`newRequest` then attaches the member's bearer token, and the resolve body carries the member's whole fact set. `url.PathEscape` was the only thing between a caller-supplied id and that target, and it cannot perform this check: `.` and `..` are RFC 3986 unreserved, so `url.PathEscape("..") == ".."`, the `..` goes out on the wire, and any dot-segment-normalizing hop (net/http's `ServeMux`, nginx, a CDN, RFC 3986 §5.2.4) collapses the target onto a sibling route.

Demonstrated live against a real `http.ServeMux` — a proposal id of `".."` reaches:

```
ELSEWHERE-head:    /api/v1/repos/{repo}/brain/facts           (the fact-set head, Current's route)
ELSEWHERE-resolve: /api/v1/repos/{repo}/brain/facts/resolve
```

Each with `Authorization: Bearer <token>` attached, and the second with the member's fact set in the body.

## Why #116 does not already cover it

`bindProposalID` constrains the id a **response** may carry — it refuses any served id that is not the value its own content derives, which is exactly right for the confirm-what-you-did-not-see problem #116 is about. It cannot constrain the id a **request** is built from:

- in `GetProposal` the path is assembled and sent *before* any response exists — `bindProposalID` runs on the decoded body, several statements too late to affect the target;
- `ResolveProposal` never reads a proposal back at all, so nothing binds `req.ProposalID`.

Today's in-tree flows happen to be safe, because the CLI resolves a human ref through `FindProposal` over a set that `ListProposals` has already bound, and a bound id is always `prop-` + 16 hex. That is a property of the call sites, not of the transport: `HTTPServer.GetProposal`, `HTTPServer.ResolveProposal` and `hostedbrain.Client.GetProposal` all take an arbitrary string and put it in a path. This is the "every call site remembers" shape #154 refused for the repo id.

## The rule, and why it is not `repoid.Validate`

Deliberately **stricter** than the one-safe-segment rule a repo id gets.

A repo id is an opaque server-issued value, so the most that can be demanded of it is that it stay one segment. A proposal id is not opaque: `ProposalID` derives it from the conflict's content, and #116's `bindProposalID` pins every served id to that derivation. So the set of ids this client can legitimately address is exactly the set `ProposalID` produces — `proposalIDPrefix` followed by `proposalIDHexLen` lowercase hex digits. Anything outside it is a target the member never had, not merely an awkward one, and loosening to the repo-id rule to share code would accept ids no legitimate flow can produce.

The rule is written against the same named constants the derivation uses, and `TestProposalIDRuleIsTheDerivationRule` asserts `validateProposalID(ProposalID(p)) == nil` over a spread of proposals — so a change to the id's shape moves the rule with it instead of silently rejecting every real id.

## How the refusal is enforced

`proposalPath` is the only place a proposal id becomes part of a target, and it returns `(string, error)` rather than a string, so neither endpoint can build a path without handling the refusal — the same structural shape `repoBasePath` gives the repo id in #154. `ResolveProposal` builds it **first thing**, before the fact set is serialized at all: that body is the member's whole fact set, so the id that decides where it is POSTed has to be settled before there is anything to send.

A validated id equals its own `PathEscape`, so it is concatenated raw. `PathEscape` would be a no-op there, and hiding the check behind it is what made this look safe.

## Tests

`internal/factsync/proposalid_segment_test.go`. Every test asserts the **resulting request** — the path that reached the server, or that no request was made at all. None compares an id against an escape of itself.

| test | asserts |
|---|---|
| `TestProposalIDRuleIsTheDerivationRule` | the accepted set is the derived set; a derived id is one normal-form segment (by `path.Join`, not by an escape) |
| `TestProposalIDMustBeDerivable` | 26 hostile ids × both endpoints: refused with `ErrInvalidProposalID`, and **zero requests reach the server** — the token and the fact set never leave the process |
| `TestProposalIDLandsOnItsOwnSegment` | the exact target of both endpoints, the branch still in the query, and the path in normal form (`path.Clean` is a no-op) so no hop can move it |
| `TestProposalIDCannotReachAnotherRoute` | a real `ServeMux` with two handlers no proposal endpoint addresses. One subtest proves the collapse is real (the raw target does reach the fact-set head); the other proves the client will not build it |

`prop-x` / `prop-unknown` / `prop-missing` placeholders in the existing status-mapping tests become well-formed ids — those tests assert response-status mapping, not id shape, and a malformed id no longer gets far enough to have a status.

## Mutation

With `validateProposalID` neutered to `return nil`, both endpoints accept every hostile id and the route test reports the landing:

```
--- FAIL: TestProposalIDMustBeDerivable/GetProposal/dotdot
--- FAIL: TestProposalIDMustBeDerivable/ResolveProposal/dotdot
    ... (26 hostile ids × 2 endpoints)
--- FAIL: TestProposalIDCannotReachAnotherRoute/the_client_refuses
    proposal id ".." was accepted by ResolveProposal
    proposal id ".." moved the target and reached
      ELSEWHERE-head:/api/v1/repos/repo1/brain/facts with the member's bearer token
```

Validator restored: `internal/factsync` (122) and `internal/hostedbrain` (11) green, also under `-race`; `internal/cli` 2385 green. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l` clean.

## Relationship to #154

Orthogonal and non-overlapping: #154 validates the **repo** id at every request site, this validates the **proposal** id at the two sites that carry one. They meet in `httpproposals.go`, where #154 makes `proposalsPath` return an error and this adds `proposalPath` on top of it — a mechanical merge, whichever lands first.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Stacked on #119 (`audit/sec-repoid-escape`), which is itself stacked on #137 → #121 → #125. Review after those; the diff against #119 is the four remaining request sites plus the package move.

## What was still open

#119 fixed one request builder — `hostedbrain.Client.rpc` — and deliberately left the identical hole at the other four to avoid cross-PR conflicts. Each of them interpolated a caller-influenced repo id into its target with `url.PathEscape` and nothing else:

| site | target |
|---|---|
| `factsync.Current` | `/api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts` |
| `factsync.Advance` | `/api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance` |
| `factsync` proposals (`proposalsPath`, 4 endpoints) | `/api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/proposals[/{pid}[/resolve]]` |
| `cli.postBrainArtifacts` | `/api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/artifacts` |

Escaping is not the rule. `.` and `..` are RFC 3986 unreserved, so `url.PathEscape("..") == ".."`, the `..` goes out on the wire, and any dot-segment-normalizing hop collapses the target onto a sibling route.

All four are real holes, demonstrated live against an `http.ServeMux` with the validator disabled — a repo id of `".."` reaches:

```
ELSEWHERE:/api/v1/brain/facts            auth=Bearer secret
ELSEWHERE:/api/v1/brain/facts/advance    auth=Bearer secret
ELSEWHERE:/api/v1/brain/facts/proposals  auth=Bearer secret
ELSEWHERE:/api/v1/brain/artifacts        auth=Bearer secret
```

Each with the bearer token attached, and on the write paths with the member's whole fact set or brain bundle in the body. Nothing upstream constrains the id: `--repo-id` / `ENTIRE_REPO_ID` is only checked for emptiness in `runPublish`, `facts sync` and `facts proposals`.

## Where the validator lives, and why

`internal/repoid` — a new leaf package, standard library only.

Three packages build `/api/v1/repos/{id}/…` targets and carry a bearer token on them: `internal/hostedbrain`, `internal/factsync`, `internal/cli`. They cannot share the rule through each other:

- `internal/hostedbrain` **already imports** `internal/factsync` (`hostedbrain.Client` drives the proposal endpoints over `factsync.HTTPServer`), so `factsync` importing `hostedbrain` back is an **import cycle**, not merely bad layering. The rule physically cannot live in either client.
- `internal/cli` sits above both, so putting it there is upside down.

A rule about the wire format shared by clients at three different layers belongs below all of them. `internal/httpx` (#121) is the same shape for the outbound HTTP policy those same three callers share, so this follows an existing precedent rather than inventing one.

`validRepoID` → `repoid.Validate`, `ErrInvalidRepoID` → `repoid.ErrInvalid`; the rule and its reasoning are unchanged, and #119's call site and test move over. One implementation, not three copies.

## How the refusal is enforced

- **factsync**: one helper, `repoBasePath`, is the only place a repo id becomes part of a target. It returns `(string, error)` rather than a string, so no endpoint can build a path without handling the refusal. `proposalsPath` is built on it, covering all four proposal endpoints at once. `ResolveProposal` checks first thing, before the fact set is serialized at all.
- **cli**: `postBrainArtifacts` checks at the chokepoint — it is the only function that turns an id into a network target and is reachable from callers that did not come through the command. `runPublish` also checks next to the `apiurl.Validate` floor, so a malformed target fails before any git or disk work, with the whole brain still local.

Validated ids equal their own escaped form, so the id is concatenated raw at each site: `PathEscape` would be a no-op, and hiding the check behind it is what made this look safe.

## Tests

Every test asserts the **resulting request** — the path that reached the server, or that no request was made at all. None compares an id against `url.PathEscape` of itself, which is the tautology that let this survive the first fix.

| file | tests |
|---|---|
| `internal/repoid/repoid_test.go` | `TestPathEscapeIsNotTheRule` (pins the premise: the escaped dot segments still yield a rewritable path), `TestValidateRejects`, `TestValidateAcceptsAndYieldsNormalFormSegment` |
| `internal/factsync/repoid_segment_test.go` | `TestFactsyncRepoIDMustBeOneSafeSegment` (6 endpoints × 14 hostile ids, asserting zero requests reach the server), `TestCurrentLandsOnTheIntendedPath`, `TestAdvanceLandsOnTheIntendedPath`, `TestProposalEndpointsLandOnTheIntendedPath`, `TestFactsyncRepoIDCannotReachAnotherRoute` |
| `internal/cli/publish_repoid_segment_test.go` | `TestPostBrainArtifactsRejectsRepoIDThatIsNotOneSafeSegment`, `TestPostBrainArtifactsLandsOnTheIntendedPath`, `TestPublishCannotReachAnotherRoute`, `TestRunPublishRefusesBadRepoIDBeforeTouchingDisk` |

The `LandsOnTheIntendedPath` tests also assert the path is in normal form (`path.Clean` is a no-op on it), which is the property that makes it un-rewritable by any hop between the client and the handler.

## Mutation check

With `repoid.Validate` neutered to `return nil`, every site's test fails:

```
--- FAIL: TestPathEscapeIsNotTheRule
--- FAIL: TestValidateRejects
--- FAIL: TestRPCRejectsRepoIDThatIsNotOneSafeSegment          (hostedbrain, from #119)
--- FAIL: TestRPCCannotReachAnotherRoute                       (hostedbrain, from #119)
--- FAIL: TestFactsyncRepoIDMustBeOneSafeSegment
--- FAIL: TestFactsyncRepoIDCannotReachAnotherRoute
--- FAIL: TestPostBrainArtifactsRejectsRepoIDThatIsNotOneSafeSegment
--- FAIL: TestPublishCannotReachAnotherRoute
--- FAIL: TestRunPublishRefusesBadRepoIDBeforeTouchingDisk
```

Validator restored, all green: `internal/repoid`, `internal/hostedbrain`, `internal/factsync`, `internal/factgitmeta` (225 + 8 tests, also under `-race`), `internal/cli` (2434 tests; the publish subset under `-race`). `gofmt -s` clean, `go vet ./...` clean.

## Deliberately out of scope

`proposalID` is interpolated into the same two paths (`.../proposals/{pid}` and `.../proposals/{pid}/resolve`) and has the identical dot-segment hazard. It is left as `url.PathEscape(proposalID)` here because proposal-id integrity is #116's subject (`bindProposalID`), and a fix would have to decide the id's own format rule rather than reuse the repo-id one. Worth a follow-up on top of #116.

Two defects found while adversarially re-reviewing the `audit/*` campaign. Both are in code the campaign's own PRs touch or depend on, and neither is covered by any open PR.

## 1. `fix(paths)`: the repo-key guards were not applied at every store-path construction

A repo key is untrusted input that becomes a filesystem path. The rules for turning one into a path live in `brainDirForKey`: refuse the reserved `workspaces` segment, refuse a symlinked store root, refuse a symlinked component. Three sites built a store path without going through it, so a key every other command refuses was still accepted there.

- `repoKeyFromRemote` minted the key with no reserved-segment check at all. The generated domain slug is three letters, so this only fires for a hand-edited `DomainSlugs` entry — exactly the case `brainDirForKey`'s refusal exists for — but the failure then surfaced in whichever consumer happened to build a path first, rather than naming the configuration that produced it.
- `brain path <remote>` joined the key onto the store root directly, at both of its remote branches, so it printed a location the reserved-segment and symlink rules exist to keep nothing in: a directory no other verb will read or write.
- `headPathForKey` had no guards. The head file is built from the same key and lands in the same per-key directory shape under `state/`, so accepting a key `brainDirForKey` refuses put the two halves of a repository's storage under different rules.

The reserved-segment test moves into `rejectReservedRepoKeySegment` because it is a property of the key, not of any one consumer.

This is the "same shape, no guard" observation from the #102 thread, applied at every site rather than one.

## 2. `fix(runner)`: a cancelled command could block the runner indefinitely

`exec.CommandContext` kills the child when the context is cancelled, but `cmd.Run`/`cmd.Wait` return only once every writer of the stdout and stderr pipes has closed. A child that backgrounds a grandchild inheriting those descriptors therefore keeps the runner blocked for the grandchild's lifetime, long after the deadline passed and the child was killed.

Every context deadline in this binary is implemented on top of `ExecRunner` — the semantic-provider overall and inactivity timeouts, the distill and seed agent timeouts, the graph-diff bound — so a single stray grandchild made all of them unenforceable. Measured against `main`: a 300 ms deadline returned after 30.0 s.

`cmd.WaitDelay` is set on both the buffered and the streaming path. It is a cancellation backstop rather than a timeout: the delay only starts counting once the context is already cancelled, so a command that exits normally is unaffected. With the fix the same probe returns in 2.3 s on both paths.

## Verification

Both commits are mutation-checked: reverting the non-test hunk fails the added tests at all four assertions. `go build ./...` clean; `go test ./internal/cli` = 2392 passed.

**First-run failure on any repository without a github.com origin.** Running `setup` in a local repo with no remote failed the semantic phase with:

```
semantic snapshot repo_key "local/repo" does not match current repo "local/repo-<hash>"
```

**Root cause: two independent derivations of repository identity that are not the same rule, by design.**

| | rule |
|---|---|
| brain storage key | the `origin` remote for **any** host; with no origin, `local/<base>-<sha256(abs dir)[:12]>`. The hash suffix is **load-bearing** — the key *is* the on-disk directory name under `<data>/repos/`, so two checkouts sharing a basename must not collide onto one brain. |
| provider label | the first **github.com** remote. No hash, no suffix. |

So demanding equality was wrong in principle, not just in this case: it fails for every repository whose origin is not github.com, including a brand-new local repo — the exact first-run path.

**Fix:** the brain mirrors the provider's rule to compute the key the provider *should* emit for this repository and accepts that, keeping its own hashed key for storage. A genuinely foreign snapshot is still rejected (pinned by `TestSemanticIndexRejectsForeignProviderRepoKey`).

**Diagnosability:** a mismatch that survives both checks now names both keys, the expected key, the repository, the provider binary, and two concrete remedies — instead of failing bare mid-phase.

**Tests (5):** accepts a repo with no remote; accepts a non-GitHub remote; rejects a foreign key; the mirror matches entire-graph's documented rule; and `TestProviderRepoKeyMatchesInstalledEntireGraph` checks the rule against the **actually installed** binary, so drift between the two implementations fails a test rather than a user's first run.

**Fixes a standing flake generator, with measurements rather than a guess.**

The windows `-race` lane runs against `-timeout 20m`. Measured on **green** runs, `internal/cli` alone takes **811-997s against that 1200s cap** — a healthy suite routinely consuming 68-83% of its budget. Runner draws vary widely: the `phase1-semantic (windows)` job, an identical test subset, ranges **4m46s to 13m10s across PRs (2.75x)**.

So a slow draw tips an otherwise passing PR into `panic: test timed out`. That is not hypothetical — two audit PRs (#104, #108) failed exactly this way during the audit campaign, and **both passed on an unchanged re-run**. Local timings under `-race` across main, #108 and #104 were within **1.6%** of each other, and #108 touches **zero** `internal/cli` lines, so the failures were runner variance, not code.

**Change:** 20m → 30m on that one lane.

**Why this is the right shape of fix:** a timeout is a guard against a *wedged* test, not a performance budget. 30m still surfaces a genuine hang promptly, while leaving a normal run real margin instead of a coin flip. The structural fix is splitting `internal/cli` (it is by far the largest package and dominates every lane); that is worth doing separately and is noted in the commit.

No test was weakened and no assertion was skipped to achieve this.","created_at":"2026-08-28T22:28:15Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/ci-windows-timeout","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/149","number":149,"sha":"93254e821b8e794c01fa3aff545aa7c4cb401a5f","title":"ci: give the windows race suite a timeout that is a hang guard, not a budget","updated_at":"2026-08-28T22:28:21Z"}

**Two things: permanent fuzz infrastructure, plus one new bug it found.**

### The targets
The campaign's crashers were each fixed on their own branch (#126, #127, #128, #129) but the *targets that found them* were not kept, so nothing stops the same classes returning. This adds them as the permanent regression surface, each with its minimized seed corpus: canonical encoding + signature verification (`FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper`, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, `FuzzSignatureEnvelope`, `FuzzCheckCompatibility`), the fact-set NDJSON round trip, git-meta tree paths and target sharding, the hosted client's response handling, the entity-index document, and agent transcript scanning (`FuzzScanConversationTranscript`, `FuzzDistillDocumentConversation`, …).

**This branch is stacked on #126–#129** — those fixes are merged in, so the targets run green here. On bare main two of them correctly fail, which is the point.

### The new finding
Running them turned up one more, fixed in this commit: **`encoding/json` does not fail on invalid UTF-8, it substitutes U+FFFD.** A record written with such a byte **read back changed, with no error on either side** — silent corruption. Fact paths come from real filenames and POSIX permits arbitrary bytes there, so an ordinary repository reaches this; on the shared cross-member head the mangled path would then merge into every other member.

`WriteNDJSON` now refuses such a record with `ErrInvalidUTF8`, naming the offending field, on exactly the rule already established by `ErrRecordTooLarge`: never persist what this package cannot faithfully return.

**Tests:** refusal across paths/text/locus/provenance, each asserting the field is named and nothing was written; plus `TestWriteNDJSONAcceptsValidUTF8` so the guard cannot start rejecting legitimate non-ASCII (`café/日本語.go`, `naïve — ünïcode ✓`).

**Mutation-verified:** disabling the guard reproduces the original fuzz failure — `Paths:[]string{"\x85"}` written, `Paths:[]string{"�"}` read back.","created_at":"2026-08-28T08:32:26Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fuzz-targets","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/140","number":140,"sha":"db6a7ef60f809bcfa601710e26f89d360902fa52","title":"test(fuzz): keep the fuzz targets, and refuse records JSON would mangle","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:44:41Z"}

**Fixes a real product failure and the load-sensitive test flake behind it.** Under load the local dial can fail with `EADDRNOTAVAIL` (ephemeral ports exhausted) or a reset **before the request is ever sent**. Every hosted call turned that into a hard sync failure.

- `TestHTTPServerRetriesTransientDialFailureOnPOSTWithoutDoublingTheMutation` — a POST is retried only when the *dial* failed, so a mutation cannot be applied twice.

**Severity: MED (availability / self-DoS).** `brain_ingest_traces` accepted any path from the caller. A size ceiling does not bound a read: `open(2)` on a FIFO with no writer blocks *inside the syscall* before a single byte is read, and a character device yields bytes forever. Worse, the read happened **while holding the semantic index lock**, so one such call wedges the brain for every other caller — daemon, hook, and human alike.

**Fix, three independent layers:**
1. `os.Lstat` (never `os.Stat`) so a symlink pointing at a FIFO cannot slip through the type check a resolving stat would pass.
2. A post-open `SameFile` + `IsRegular` recheck, closing the regular-to-FIFO swap-during-open TOCTOU window.
3. A read deadline on descriptors that support one, so a pollable file that never yields EOF cannot park the caller. Regular files do not support deadlines and are unaffected.

Plus: the trace file is now read **before** the index lock is taken, so even a slow regular file cannot hold the lock.

**Tests (4):** FIFO rejected promptly; FIFO does not wedge the index lock; trace read happens before the lock is taken; regular-to-FIFO swap during open is rejected.

**Mutation-verified honestly:** disabling any *single* guard still fails safe — the other layers catch it, which is the point of defense in depth. Disabling **all three** fails `TestIngestTracesRejectsRegularToFIFOSwapDuringOpen` with `swap rejection error = <nil>, want it to name the regular-file requirement`. Reported this way rather than claiming a single-guard mutation proved the tests.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

**Severity: HIGH (code execution).** A repository is data, not a trust boundary — but git resolves several configuration keys to *commands it executes*, honoured from the target repository's own `.git/config` and in-tree `.gitattributes`. Indexing or fingerprinting an untrusted repo ran code that repo carried.

**Three vectors, each confirmed against git 2.54.0 by arming a scratch repo and watching the payload run:**
- `diff.external` / `GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF` — runs for every `git diff` form. It also *replaces* the diff, so an armed repo makes `git diff --binary HEAD` return nothing: silent corruption of any fingerprint computed from that output.
- `diff.<driver>.textconv`, selected by an in-tree `.gitattributes` entry — runs for every command that renders patch text.
- `core.fsmonitor` — runs for `status`, all `diff` forms, `ls-files`, `diff-tree`.

**Why flags, not config:** neutralizing with `-c diff.external=` does NOT work — git still takes the external-diff path and aborts ("external diff died"), losing the output. `--no-ext-diff`/`--no-textconv` both stop execution and preserve correct output. `core.fsmonitor=false` is behaviour-preserving (pure perf cache) so it is applied globally.

**Why it is unbypassable:** the rewrite lives at the single point where this binary spawns git, so every call site in every package — including `internal/entityindex`, which receives `ExecRunner` straight through — is covered without each one having to remember. Flags are inserted after the subcommand (before any `--` pathspec separator) and skipped if the caller already passed them; the dedup check deliberately ignores pathspecs, since `.brainignore` feeds repo-controlled pathspecs and a repo shipping a literal `--no-ext-diff` pattern must not suppress its own neutralizer.

**Tests:** 9 added, 6 of them real exploit tests (arm the vector in a scratch repo, assert the payload never runs) across worktree fingerprinting, `gitDiffBinary`, changed-range/file detection, status, and seed collection.

**Mutation-verified:** removing the two rewrite hooks in `runner.go` fails the exploit tests with `SECURITY: repo-local core.fsmonitor executed an attacker-controlled program during indexing`.

**Verification:** `go build ./...` clean; targeted `internal/cli` hardening + exploit tests pass. Full-suite not re-run on a heavily loaded host — stated plainly rather than overclaimed.","created_at":"2026-08-28T08:14:35Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-git-no-ext-diff","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/130","number":130,"sha":"e3aff9e0a41810c1485af1ff4284f12913465200","title":"fix(git): stop repo-local git config turning a read into code execution","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:35:15Z"}
{"base":"audit/ndjson-line-cap","body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/57
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

Canonical form passes unknown members through on purpose (ADR 0001, additive-only: an older verifier must be able to canonicalize and verify a **newer** producer's artifact). "Unknown" was decided by **exact** match against the contract keys — but Go's `encoding/json` matches object members to struct fields **case-insensitively**.

So a member like `manIfest` is unknown to this canonicalizer and **is** the manifest to `encoding/json`. The same signed bytes then carry two different meanings depending on which decoder reads them:

```go
raw := `{"manIfest":{"repo_key":"EVIL","generated_at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05Z","brain_schema_version":"1.0"}}`

json.Unmarshal(raw, &BrainArtifact{})   // RepoKey == "EVIL"
CanonicalUnmarshal(raw, &artifact)      // RepoKey == ""      (zero-filled)
```

and `VerifyBytes` accepts the bytes either way, because canonicalization preserves the unknown key verbatim. One signature, two readings, decided by the consumer's parser rather than by the signer.

This is the same class of cross-parser differential `canonical.go` already rejects duplicate members for, and it is not hypothetical: the artifact is consumed across a repo boundary (`entire-api`) by a Go decoder this repo does not control.

## The fix

`normalizeObject` rejects an unknown member that case-folds to a contract field. Every contract key is lowercase ASCII, so no legitimate artifact carries one. Genuinely unknown newer-minor fields still pass through untouched, and canonical form is still a fixed point over them — `TestUnknownFieldsStillPassThrough` pins both. Unknown keys are visited in sorted order so input with several collisions produces a deterministic error.

`strings.EqualFold` is a superset of `encoding/json`'s own fold matching for ASCII contract keys, so nothing the decoder would fold slips past.

## How it was found

`FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, which states the ADR 0001 obligation as a testable property: for any two byte strings that verify under the same signature, the decoded `BrainArtifact` must be identical. It failed in ~3 s. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestCanonicalizeRejectsCaseFoldedContractKeys` and `TestSignedArtifactCannotBeReinterpretedByFolding` are the standalone regressions; the latter reproduces the full smuggling scenario end to end.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/brainwire/` (173 tests) — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle` ran 11.0M execs and `FuzzVerifyBytesRejectsTamper` 19.8M execs with no crasher. <!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`ParseNDJSON` scanned with a 64 KiB line bound. `WriteNDJSON` enforced nothing. A fact whose serialized record exceeded that bound wrote cleanly and then failed to load:

```
bufio.Scanner: token too long
```

So the store could persist a fact-set it could not read back — with no position and no bound in the error to act on.

On the shared cross-member head this is worse than local corruption. `factsync.Sync` parses the pulled blob with `ParseNDJSON`, so **one** member's oversized fact permanently fails **every other** member's sync, and the affected members cannot repair it, because the fact only exists on the head they cannot read.

## The fix

- `MaxLineBytes` is **16 MiB**, matching the ceiling the rest of the brain applies to untrusted inputs it reads whole (`safe_read.go`).
- `WriteNDJSON` refuses a record whose line would exceed it (`ErrRecordTooLarge`), so the two halves can never disagree again. Nothing is written when it refuses.
- An oversized line already on disk is reported as a `*ParseError` naming the line number and the bound, not as an opaque `bufio` error.

## How it was found

`FuzzNDJSONWriteReadRoundTrip`, which asserts the property directly: any record the store is willing to write, the reader must be able to read back. It failed on the first non-trivial size. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestWriteReadRoundTripAtRealisticSizes`, `TestWriteRefusesUnreadableRecord`, and `TestParseReportsOversizedLineWithPosition` are the standalone regressions.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factmerge/ ./internal/factsync/` — all green. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:44Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/ndjson-line-cap","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/128","number":128,"sha":"64f62e43548093efe2235ab84028ceb4379f3700","title":"fix(factmerge): stop the fact-set writer emitting lines its own reader rejects","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:12Z"}

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`ValidateTargetValue` returned early for path targets, so **no** rule applied to them. Path values legitimately contain `/` — they are stored as nested, escaped segments under the `__target__` sentinel — but that exemption also skipped every segment-level check the format needs.

A value with an empty segment (`"/"`, `"a//b"`, a leading or trailing slash) encodes to a tree path with an empty component:

```
path:"/"  key:"0"   ->   "path///__target__/0/__value"
```

`BuildTree` then refuses that path — and it refuses the **whole `Serialize` call**, not just the offending record. One such record therefore makes the entire store unwritable for every writer that materializes it, with no repair path from the reading side.

## The fix

`ValidatePathTargetValue` restores the segment rules: no empty segment, no `.` or `..` segment, no NUL. Values that legitimately contain slashes are unaffected (`src/main.rs`, `a/b/c`, `~weird`, `__reserved/x` all still serialize).

`parseLeafPath` validates the path target it reconstructs from a tree, for the same reason the other target types do: on a shared ref the tree is untrusted input, and a value the serializer could not have produced belongs to `ErrMalformedTree` at the read boundary.

The `entire-api` copy of this vendored engine already carries a check of this name; this copy had lost it — the divergence note at the top of the file already flagged exactly this.

## How it was found

`FuzzTreePath`, from the fuzzing campaign, after 7.4M execs: `encoded path "path///__target__/0/__value" has an empty component (type="path" value="/" key="0")`. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factgitmeta/...` — all green. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.

## Note

Touches the same two files as #126 (a separate defect: a commit target value too short to shard, which panics). Both are independently valid off `main`; whichever lands second will need a small conflict resolution in `ValidateTargetValue` and `parseLeafPath`.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:29Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fuzz-path-target-validation","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/127","number":127,"sha":"2334f0415d4f2cb657cdd2e00af7dc74e46540e4","title":"fix(gitmeta): validate path-target values instead of exempting them","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:10Z"}

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/54
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`TreeBasePath` shards a commit target on its own first two hex characters (`t.Value[:2]`). `ParseTarget` enforced a 3-character minimum — but nothing else did, and the `Target` `materialize.go` rebuilds from a tree leaf path never goes through `ParseTarget`.

A metadata tree carrying `commit/ab/a/k/__value` materialized into a `State` with a one-character commit value, and the very next write re-serialized it:

```
panic: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:2] with length 1
    gitmeta.TreeBasePath      treepath.go:40
    gitmeta.buildKeyTreePath
    gitmeta.TreePath
    gitmeta.Serialize         <- MetaStore.updateLocked, every write
```

That is the whole read-materialize-CAS loop `MetaStore` runs, so one such record crashes the process on every subsequent pass. The store is local today; once git-meta records are exchanged over a shared ref (P1), the tree is bytes another member wrote.

## The fix

Three changes, at the three places that can stop it:

- **`ValidateTargetValue` enforces `MinTargetValueLen`**, the minimum `ParseTarget` has always documented. `Serialize` is the only gate between a materialized `State` and the tree, so the rule belongs where every write path passes through it. `ParseTarget` now delegates rather than keeping a second copy.
- **`parseLeafPath` validates the target it reconstructs**, so a hostile tree is classified as `ErrMalformedTree` at the READ boundary — the permanent failure a consumer is already documented to drop — instead of being carried into `State`.
- **`TreeBasePath` shards through `shardPrefix`.** It returns no error, so a caller that somehow reaches it unvalidated must get a wrong-but-total path rather than a panic.

## Blast radius

Nothing in this repo builds a branch or change-id target, and the only commit target is `entityindex.commitTarget(sha)` with a 40-hex SHA, so the minimum cannot regress real usage.

## How it was found

`FuzzTreePath`, from the fuzzing campaign. The minimized inputs ship as seed corpus entries for `FuzzTreePath` and `FuzzMaterializeRoundTrip` (inert until those harnesses land in the fuzz-targets PR). `TestShortTargetValueIsRejectedNotPanic` and `TestMaterializeRejectsShortTargetValue` are the standalone regressions; both fail on the pre-fix code.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/factgitmeta/... ./internal/entityindex/...` — all green. Post-fix, `FuzzTreePath` ran 16.5M execs and `FuzzMaterializeRoundTrip` 7.5M execs with no crasher. The full suite was not run on this host: it is under heavy load from a parallel audit fleet and long runs are timing out environmentally.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:34:14Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/gitmeta-shard-panic","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/126","number":126,"sha":"84173018bb1b67c02c33ffeb510fc9a9e52403dc","title":"fix(gitmeta): reject a target value too short to shard instead of panicking","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:38:48Z"}

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Summary

`ENTIRE_API_URL` (and the `--api-url` flag that overrides it) had **no scheme floor and no host allowlist**. Any value it was given received brain content — and the member's bearer token — in the clear. This adds a single shared validator (`internal/apiurl`) that requires `https://`, carves out loopback for local dev, and fails closed on everything else.

## What actually egressed over `http://` today (measured, not asserted)

I stood up a plaintext HTTP server bound to a **non-loopback** address (this machine's LAN IP, `192.168.1.121`), pointed `ENTIRE_API_URL` at it, and drove the real `publish` and `facts sync` code paths on the pre-fix tree. Both succeeded. Captured:

**`entire brain publish` → `POST http://192.168.1.121:PORT/api/v1/repos/{repo_id}/brain/artifacts`**

```
Authorization: "Bearer SECRET-BEARER-TOKEN-abc123"     <-- token crosses plaintext: YES
body: 2437 bytes, 4 artifacts
  kind=manifest  ref=<HEAD sha>   -> repo_key "gh/example/repo", default_branch, generated_at,
                                     provider/provider_version, and the full content index:
                                     sha256 digests, sizes, media types and on-disk PATHS of every
                                     snapshot / overlay / facts blob
  kind=snapshot  ref=<commit>     -> semantic snapshot NDJSON: {"symbol":"Foo","kind":"func"}
  kind=overlay   ref=<base>..<head> -> {"base":...,"head":...,"branch":"feature/x"}
  kind=facts     ref=main         -> durable fact text: {"branch":"main","text":"the repo uses go"}
```

**`entire brain facts sync --facts-backend http` → three plaintext calls, all bearing the token**

```
GET  .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts?branch=main            Authorization: Bearer <token>
POST .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/advance                Authorization: Bearer <token>
     body.data (303 bytes) = the merged fact-set NDJSON, in the clear:
       {"id":"fact:60e95c57ed6370b3f79e74a5","paths":["ops.deploy.secret"],
        "text":"the prod deploy key lives in vault path kv/prod/deploy","branch":"main",
        "origin":"distilled","status":"active","provenance":[{"session_id":"session-EV"}],
        "created_at":...,"updated_at":...}
GET  .../api/v1/repos/{id}/brain/facts/proposals?branch=main  Authorization: Bearer <token>
```

So: **the whole brain artifact bundle, the merged durable fact-set (fact text, paths, provenance session ids), and the bearer token all crossed plaintext to an arbitrary attacker-named host.** `internal/cli/publish_test.go` already did `t.Setenv("ENTIRE_API_URL", server.URL)` against an `httptest` (plain http) server — the plaintext path was live and exercised.

Two aggravating details found while verifying:

- The refusal for a malformed URL happened *after* the whole bundle was built. `publish.go`'s own doc comment promises a refusal "BEFORE any resolution, disk read, or HTTP request"; with `ENTIRE_API_URL=http://evil.example` the pre-fix run got as far as `no brain found for this repo`, i.e. it had already resolved storage and read local state for an unsafe target.
- Non-HTTP schemes were passed straight to `http.Client` — `ftp://`, `file:///etc/passwd`, `//api.entire.io` and bare `api.entire.io` all produced a built request and a confusing transport error rather than a config refusal.

## The fix

New `internal/apiurl` — one validator, no I/O of any kind (no DNS, no disk, no network), so callers run it as their first act after resolving the flag/env and every refusal is egress-free:

- `https://` — always allowed.
- `http://` — allowed **only** when the URL's literal host is loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, `localhost`). This is what local dev and every `httptest`-based test in the repo use, so they keep passing unchanged. The name carve-out is exactly `localhost`, matching the plugin's existing `isLoopbackHTTPURL` check for the local model server; `api.localhost` is RFC 6761 loopback in principle but resolver-dependent in practice, so it takes the opt-in.
- `http://` anywhere else — refused (`insecure_api_url:`) unless the new documented opt-in **`ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_INSECURE_API_URL`** is explicitly truthy.
- Anything else — empty, relative, schemeless, protocol-relative, `ftp`, `file`, garbage — refused (`invalid_api_url:`), and the opt-in does **not** rescue it.

Loopback is decided from the URL's literal host only. No DNS: resolving would be a TOCTOU check, would need the network to validate a URL, and would let a hostile DNS answer widen the carve-out.

**Fail-closed direction.** `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_INSECURE_API_URL` uses the *opt-in* spelling — only `1/true/yes/on/enable/enabled` unlocks plaintext; anything unrecognized (a typo'd `ture`) leaves the floor in place, with a deduped stderr warning so the operator learns their value was not understood. This is deliberately the mirror image of `securityToggleEnabled` / `toggleOn`, which fail an unrecognized value **ON**: those switch a protection *on*, so a typo must not disable it; this one switches a protection *off*, so the same fail-closed principle resolves the other way. It matches the existing `ENTIRE_BRAIN_ALLOW_HOSTED` publish opt-in.

Wired at every site that accepts a base URL:

| site | where |
|---|---|
| `internal/cli/publish.go` | right after the base URL is resolved — before `repoStoragePaths`, before the brain is read, before the bundle is built. Restores the doc-comment promise. |
| `internal/cli/facts_sync_cmd.go` | in the `http` fact backend resolution, before the backend is constructed. |
| `internal/cli/facts_proposals_cmd.go` | in `resolveHostedProposalTarget`, which is documented to make no network call. |
| `internal/factsync/httpserver.go` | in `newRequest`, the single request chokepoint for **both** `httpserver.go` (fact-set `Current`/`Advance`) and `httpproposals.go` (list/get/publish/resolve). Defense in depth: a caller that bypasses the CLI is still covered. |
| `internal/hostedbrain/client.go` | in `rpc`, the hosted MCP query chokepoint, next to the existing no-egress gate. |

`Validate` is idempotent, so the CLI-level check and the transport-level check compose without changing or re-rejecting the value.

## Tests (failing-first, then mutation-verified)

Written and shown failing against the pre-fix tree, then made to pass:

- `internal/cli/https_floor_test.go` — `ENTIRE_API_URL=http://evil.example` is refused for `publish`, `facts sync`, and `facts proposals`; each asserts the error is *not* a dial/DNS error, which would prove a request had already been attempted (pre-fix, `facts sync` and `facts proposals` failed exactly that way: `dial tcp: lookup evil.example: no such host`). Also: publish refuses **before** the disk read (it must not reach `no brain found`); the malformed-URL table; and the carve-out fence — loopback v4/v6/`localhost` stay allowed, the opt-in works, and a garbage opt-in value fails closed.
- `internal/factsync/https_floor_test.go` — `Current`, `Advance`, `ListProposals`, `PublishProposals` all refuse, with a counting `http.RoundTripper` proving **zero** requests reached the transport; loopback still round-trips.
- `internal/hostedbrain/https_floor_test.go` — same, for `CallTool`.
- `internal/apiurl/apiurl_test.go` — the validator table (schemes, loopback literals, `localhost` subdomains and lookalikes, opt-in truthiness incl. fail-closed garbage, malformed input), idempotence, and `IsLoopbackHost`.

Mutation check: with the floor neutered, the refusal tests fail; restored, they pass.

## Compatibility

- Every existing `httptest`-based test passes unchanged — they bind `127.0.0.1`, which is the loopback carve-out.
- Local dev against `http://localhost:8787` is unaffected.
- Breaking only for an operator pointing at a non-loopback plaintext endpoint, who now gets a clear error naming the opt-in.
- `--api-url` help text, the `publish` long help, and the README env table document the floor and the new variable.

## Green gate

`gofmt -l .` empty · `go vet ./...` · `go build ./...` · `go test ./internal/cli/... ./internal/factsync/... ./internal/hostedbrain/... ./internal/apiurl/...`

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Impact

ADR 0001 (`docs/adr/0001-ga-schema-contract.md` in entire-graph) states the tolerant-reader duty this consumer owes:

> Consumers ignore unknown fields within a supported major, and **warn (not fail) when they see a newer supported-major minor**, since additive facts may have been skipped.
> `entire-brain` ingestion MUST follow the tolerant-reader rules above: accept any `1.x`, ignore unknown fields, warn on a newer minor.

`validateSemanticSchema` (`internal/cli/semantic.go`) implemented only half of that:

```go
major, _, ok := strings.Cut(version, ".")
if !ok { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema version %q", version) }
if major != semanticSupportedMajor { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema major version %q", major) }
return nil
```

Three defects:

1. **No newer-minor warning anywhere.** A `1.2` snapshot from a newer entire-graph is accepted in silence. The resulting index is quietly less complete than the snapshot it came from — additive facts this build cannot ingest are dropped with nothing recorded. That is precisely the case the ADR requires a warning for. (`brainwire.CheckCompatibility`, `internal/brainwire/version.go:36`, implements the same ADR policy correctly one layer over; this path did not reuse it.)
2. **Only the text before the first dot is examined,** so `"1.abc"` and `"1."` are accepted as ordinary 1.x minors and a malformed header rides straight into the store.
3. **The rejection message never says what this build supports** — only what it received — collapsing "upgrade the provider" and "upgrade the brain" into one unactionable string.

## Fix

- `parseSemanticSchemaVersion` requires a well-formed `major.minor` (a trailing patch component is tolerated and ignored, since refusing it would itself violate the tolerant-reader rule).
- `validateSemanticSchema` keeps the major as the compatibility boundary and now names the supported range in every rejection.
- `semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` emits `provider_schema_newer_minor` for a newer minor within the supported major, naming both versions and the remedy.

### Applied at every point a provider `schema_version` crosses into this build

Recording the warning at index time alone is not enough — each of these is an independent way for an under-ingested snapshot to be trusted as complete:

| site | sink |
|---|---|
| `runSemanticIndex` | live `entire graph snapshot` header → warning recorded on the persisted manifest |
| `semanticStaleReport` | the `provider` freshness axis read by `brain doctor`/`status` and every semantic query/context/impact/changes/boundary/tests command → **degraded**, not a clean `ok` |
| `validateImportedBundle` | imported bundle manifest → warning appended to the semantic source that is then persisted |

`semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` is the single implementation behind all three. `validateSemanticSchema` remains the sole authority on rejecting an unparseable or unsupported-major version, and runs first at each site.

> Supersedes #120, which wired the same three sinks behind a weaker parser (`validateSemanticSchema` left lenient, and a minor parse that silently gave up on `1.2.3`). This PR carries the union: #123's strict parser plus #120's full call-site coverage. #120 is closed.

## Verification

- `TestValidateSemanticSchemaFollowsTheTolerantReaderContract` — accept `1.0`/`1.1`/`1.2`/`1.17`/`1.2.3`; refuse `""`/`1`/`2.0`/`0.9`/`1.abc`/`1.`/`x.1`.
- `TestSemanticSchemaNewerMinorWarns`, `TestSemanticSchemaErrorsNameTheSupportedRange`.
- One positive and one negative test per sink: `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`; `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor` / `TestSemanticStaleReportSilentAtSupportedMinor`; `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning` / `TestBundleImportSilentAtSupportedMinor`.
- **Mutation-verified per site:** disabling the warning at each of the three sites in turn fails exactly one test — index → `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`, stale-report → `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor`, bundle-import → `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning`. Restoring the lenient major-only parse, computing the warning but dropping it, and stripping the supported range from the message each also fail a test.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/cli/`, `go test ./internal/cli/` (2413 tests, green).

### Known gap, deliberately out of scope

`readSemanticSnapshotSummary` also calls `validateSemanticSchema` on a snapshot header, but it is a pure read helper returning `(semanticHeader, semanticCounts, error)` with no warning sink, and it only re-reads a snapshot whose manifest was already warned on at one of the three sites above. Wiring it needs a signature change and is not required for ADR 0001 compliance here.
