<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Finding

Two production HTTP clients fell back to `http.DefaultClient`, which has **no timeout**:

- `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:55-60` — used by every hosted-brain RPC (`rpc`, and through it `Initialize`/`ListTools`/`CallTool`/`Search`/`Get`/`MultiGet`/`Status`).
- `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:39-44` — used by `Current`, `Advance`, and all four proposal calls in `httpproposals.go`.

The factsync one is **live today**, not only on the P1 hosted path: `internal/cli/facts_sync_cmd.go:573` constructs `&factsync.HTTPServer{BaseURL: baseURL, Token: token}` with no `Client`, so `entire brain facts sync --backend http` ran on an untimed client on both its read and its write path.

The realistic caller is the CLI or the workspace daemon passing `context.Background()`. With no caller deadline, the client's own bound is the only thing that can end the call.

## Proof

A test server that accepts the request and never responds, called with `context.Background()`:

```
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHang (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002033333s against a wedged endpoint (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHangFactsync (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002050125s (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
```

Both calls never return. The endpoint completes the TCP dial and only then stalls, so a dial-phase bound would not have helped either — the bound has to cover the wait for the response, which `http.Client.Timeout` does.

## Audit of every HTTP client construction (non-test)

| site | bound before | action |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:59` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 60s |
| `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:43` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 5m |
| `internal/cli/publish.go:543` | `Timeout: publishRequestTimeout` (5m) | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/embed_ollama.go:73` | `Timeout: 60s` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:1992` | `Timeout: timeout` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |

No `http.Get`/`http.Post`/`http.Head` call sites and no other `&http.Client{}` exist outside tests.

## Fix

Each package gets a documented default bound and keeps the caller-supplied-client override:

- `hostedbrain`: 60s. The hosted tools are bounded reads (search / get / status).
- `factsync`: 5m. `Advance` uploads the whole merged fact-set, so the bound matches the five minutes the hosted publish path already allows for a body-carrying request (`cli.publishRequestTimeout`) rather than a short read timeout.

Both are plain `http.Client.Timeout`, the same shape `publish.go` already uses, so `http.DefaultTransport` and its connection pool stay shared. Both are `var`, not `const`, so tests can shorten them.

An earlier draft also set `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout` on a cloned transport; that was dropped after it was measured to cause connection churn and ephemeral-port exhaustion in the existing suite. `Client.Timeout` already covers the response wait, which is the property under test.

## Tests

Per package: a direct assertion that the default client carries a non-zero `Timeout` (and that a caller-supplied client still wins), plus a behavioural test driving a wedged server with `context.Background()` and asserting the call returns.

Mutation-verified: restoring `return http.DefaultClient` in each package fails all four tests (the behavioural ones by hanging out their 15s budget); restoring the fix passes them.

## Finding

`internal/hostedbrain/client.go:116` built the brain MCP endpoint by raw string concatenation:

```go
url := strings.TrimRight(c.BaseURL, "/") + "/api/v1/repos/" + repoID + "/brain/mcp"
```

`repoID` was not escaped. Every sibling call in the repo already escapes it — `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:63,107`, `internal/factsync/httpproposals.go:46,105,252`, `internal/cli/publish.go:534` all use `url.PathEscape`. This was the one that did not, so it was an oversight rather than a convention.

## Proof

An `httptest` server recording the request target, driven through `Client.Initialize`, observes the request going somewhere other than the brain MCP route (unfixed code):

| repo id | observed path | observed query |
|---|---|---|
| `a/b` | `/api/v1/repos/a/b/brain/mcp` | — |
| `../../admin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `..%2f..%2fadmin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `x?admin=1` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | `admin=1/brain/mcp` |
| `x#frag` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | — |
| `x/brain/facts/advance` | `/api/v1/repos/x/brain/facts/advance/brain/mcp` | — |

The `?` and `#` cases are the sharpest: the POST — carrying the member's `Authorization: Bearer` token — lands on `/api/v1/repos/x`, a different endpoint entirely, and the rest of the intended path is smuggled into the query string. The dot-segment cases reach the wire un-normalized, so any server or proxy that normalizes resolves them above the `/api/v1` prefix.

## Fix

`url.PathEscape(repoID)`, matching the siblings. The local variable is renamed `endpoint` (as in `publish.go`) so it no longer shadows the `net/url` package.

## Test

`TestRPCEscapesRepoID` asserts, for each payload above plus a benign id, that the server sees the `/api/v1/repos/` prefix and `/brain/mcp` suffix intact with the repo id occupying exactly one path segment and no query string smuggled out of it. It asserts on `r.URL.EscapedPath()`, which is what an HTTP router matches on, so a percent-encoded separator is correctly seen as staying inside one segment.

Mutation-verified: reverting the one-line fix fails 6 of the 7 subtests; restoring it passes all 7.

## Verification

`gofmt -l .` clean, `go vet ./...` clean, `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/hostedbrain/...` green.","created_at":"2026-08-28T05:00:41Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-repoid-escape","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/119","number":119,"sha":"1300dc7df94fa43fe01effedcd16f732909749ce","title":"fix(hostedbrain): escape repo id in the brain MCP request path","updated_at":"2026-08-28T23:13:50Z"}

Three real drift items found and fixed (smallest complete fix on the side judged wrong — see notes):

- **`brain_search_graph`'s `offset` and `brain_get_code_snippet`'s `context_lines`** declared `minimum: 1` in their JSON schema, but both handlers (`mcpNonNegativeInt`) accept and default to `0`. - **`docs/semantic_mcp_guide.md`'s tool catalog** was missing `brain_entity_history` — registered in code and documented in `README.md`, but absent from the guide's "Available tools" list.

Added regression tests for each: schema-minimum lock for the two zero-accepting params, a description lock for `brain_get_architecture`, and a doc-contract test that every registered MCP tool name appears in the guide (would have caught the `brain_entity_history` gap).

## Impact

`mcpPositiveInt` and `mcpNonNegativeInt` (`internal/cli/mcp.go:1378`, `:1396`) enforced a floor and nothing else — `typed <= float64(math.MaxInt)` is not a bound, it is a type check.

An MCP client is not a trusted peer in this design: the agent driving it carries repository text in its context that an untrusted checkout can influence, and a `tools/call` is one line of JSON.

The argument is not merely a result count. It reaches allocation sizing:

- `internal/cli/history_fts.go:581` — `out := make([]scoredHistoryRecord, 0, limit)`
- `internal/cli/doc_fts.go:199,204` — `LIMIT ?` with `limit*4`, and `make([]scoredDocRecord, 0, limit*4)`
- `internal/cli/retrieve.go:209,322` — the history arm scales the same value by 2 then 3 (with overflow guards, but no ceiling)

So `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000000}}` decides how many elements the server asks the runtime for. Depending on element size that is either a panic the request recovery turns into an opaque `-32603 internal error` (what I observed end to end), or an allocation request under the `makeslice` cap that the process attempts and does not survive. Either way an unauthenticated argument, not the server, picks the number.

`context_lines` on `brain_get_code_snippet` has the same shape — `semantic_graph.go:894` adds it to `record.EndLine`, and `math.MaxInt64` there overflows the sum negative.

## Repro

`internal/cli/mcp_int_bounds_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestMCPIntegerArgumentsAreCapped
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1e+09; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpNonNegativeInt accepted limit=1e+09
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1.099511627776e+12; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=2147483647; it sizes a slice capacity
--- FAIL: TestMCPToolCallRejectsOversizedLimit
    error = {"code":-32603,"message":"internal error handling \"tools/call\""}
```

That last line is the whole point: on `main` an oversized `limit` does not produce a validation error, it produces a recovered internal failure. After the fix it is a clean `-32000 limit must be an integer between 1 and 10000`.

## Fix

`mcpIntegerArgMax = 10000`, enforced in both decoders. Far above any useful result count, depth, offset or context window; far below the point where the value becomes an allocation problem.

Enforced in the decoders rather than declared as `"maximum"` in each `inputSchema` **on purpose**: the tool definitions are sent on every `tools/list` and their size is budgeted in tokens — `TestMCPBrainBriefToolDefinitionGolden` asserts an exact 747-byte definition and documents the tokenizer accounting for the whole `tools/list` payload. Adding a `maximum` to ~25 integer properties would spend that budget restating a bound the server must check itself regardless. `brain_get_conversation` and `brain_concepts`, which already declare real semantic maxima, keep them.

Two existing assertions in `mcp_test.go` move from `"limit must be an integer greater than zero"` to `"limit must be an integer between 1 and"`. The rejection behaviour they cover is unchanged; only the message is more accurate.

## Mutation

Restoring `math.MaxInt` in either decoder reproduces the failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli/` clean.","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:46:27Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-mcp-int-bounds","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/117","number":117,"sha":"5d54f0d9083828e5ec2821aec996a04352c16609","title":"fix(mcp): integer tool arguments have no upper bound, so a tool call chooses an allocation size","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:40:37Z"}

## Impact

A proposal id is content-derived — `ProposalID` (`internal/factsync/proposals.go:82`) hashes action, candidate id, target id, branch and proposer. That is the entire basis for showing an id to a member and accepting it back: `facts proposals apply prop-abc123` is meant to name one decision and nothing else.

The open set, though, is served by the hosted brain, and a server-supplied non-empty id was taken verbatim. Only an **empty** id was recomputed:

```go
for i := range set.Proposals {
    if set.Proposals[i].ID == "" {
        set.Proposals[i].ID = ProposalID(set.Proposals[i].Proposal)
    }
}
```

(`httpproposals.go:93-97`, and the same at `:129-131` for `GetProposal`.)

Settling is not read-only:

- accept marks the **target** fact superseded, and a `merge` action calls `removeFactByID` on the candidate (`factmerge/admin.go:36-46`);
- the settled proposal is then mirrored into the member's **local** fact store — `facts_proposals_cmd.go:261` → `applySettlementLocally` at `:320` — and the same mirror runs unattended from `facts sync` via `reconcileLocalProposalQueue`;
- `FindProposal` (`proposals.go:109-118`) resolves the member's reference against that same server-supplied id.

So a hosted brain could display one decision under an id and execute a different one when the member confirmed it, against local facts of the server's choosing. The id a human sees is not bound to what applying it does — confirm-what-you-did-not-see.

## Repro

`internal/factsync/proposal_id_binding_test.go` drives the real `HTTPServer` adapter over the existing `hostedContractServer` fake. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestListProposalsRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    proposal id prop-c92b6250535b7a6c does not derive from the decision it names
    ({Action:supersede CandidateID:fact:attacker TargetID:fact:victim Branch:main})
--- FAIL: TestGetProposalRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    GetProposal returned {ID:prop-c92b6250535b7a6c Proposal:{Action:supersede ...}}
    under an id that does not derive from it
```

## Fix

`bindProposalID` derives an absent id exactly as before (older/looser servers omit it — pinned by `TestProposalsStillAcceptDerivedAndOmittedIDs/omitted`), and requires a present one to equal the derived value. A mismatch is refused with `ErrProposalIDMismatch` rather than silently corrected: correcting the id would leave it no longer resolving the reference the member was handed.

## Mutation

Dropping the mismatch branch reproduces both failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet` clean.

## Related

This is the proposal-side counterpart to #95, which binds *fact* ids to their content on the same transport. Neither is subsumed by the other: `VerifyIdentities` checks records, and a proposal carries no record — only ids.","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:43:15Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-proposal-id-binding","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/116","number":116,"sha":"83fa0675340573bd17cff8fc23cb7ab191427ce6","title":"fix(factsync): hosted proposal ids are not bound to the decision they name","updated_at":"2026-08-28T04:43:20Z"}

https://entire.io/gh/entireio/entire-brain/trails/43
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

A graft truncates `git log --format=%P`, so in a shallow clone the boundary commit reports **no parents** and is indistinguishable from a real root to the walk:

```
$ git clone --depth=1 file://origin clone && cd clone
$ git log -1 --format=%P            # empty
$ git cat-file commit HEAD | head -2
tree   b7130d30b0ce47edf9a8f30a0a38d3c22f953d5e
parent ab142df864ba9d51317289381fc969732e35baa4   # the parent is right there
```

A root commit is diffed against the empty tree so its entities are recorded as `added`. The boundary therefore gets a forward delta document declaring that it **added every entity in the whole tree**, plus one reverse-index entry per entity pointing at it.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. Those records are durable git-meta, and from then on `entities history` answers "this symbol was introduced by `<boundary>`" — naming a commit that introduced none of them. The same join is what fact provenance anchors to, so the fabricated commit propagates into stored facts.

Any CI checkout (`actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`) or any `git clone --depth=N` hits this.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_shallow_test.go` makes a real 3-commit origin, `git clone --depth=2` off it, verifies the boundary really is grafted (`%P` empty), and indexes the clone.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_shallow_test.go:142: the shallow boundary 3a000de3 was indexed against the empty tree:
    base=4b825dc6 entities=[{Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_first ... Path:first.go ...}
    {Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_second ... Path:second.go ...}]
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit (4.08s)
```

`first.go` was added three commits before the boundary, in history this clone does not have.

## Fix

A shallow boundary is not a root: its parent exists, it is just not in this clone, so its delta genuinely cannot be computed. Treat it as the hole it is — exactly the way a commit the provider could not diff is already treated. Nothing is written for it, no cursor steps over it (so the window keeps its "every first-parent commit from floor to tip carries a document" claim honest), and the pass reports it in `Warnings`.

Telling a boundary from a root is one `cat-file commit`: the raw object still carries its parent lines even when the graft hides them from `%P`. The check only runs for commits the walk reported as parentless, and `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` is memoized per pass, so a full clone pays one extra `git rev-parse` at most and a repository with no parentless commits in range pays nothing at all.

The tradeoff, stated plainly: a `--depth=1` clone now indexes nothing rather than indexing one fabricated document. That is the correct direction for a store whose contents are durable and feed provenance — a deeper clone indexes everything except its boundary, which is exactly right.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, disabling the guard (`if false && commit.Parent == "" && b.isGraftedBoundary(...)`) makes the new test fail again with the identical "indexed against the empty tree" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass.

## What breaks

Workspace retrieval reports a member repo whose retrieval **failed** as:

```json
{"repo_key": "acme/broken", "results": [], "error": "load history index: parse history/index.json: unexpected end of JSON input"}
```

When the 128 KiB response budget binds, `trimWorkspaceExtrasOnce` resolved the overage by **clearing that error** — and it did so *before* dropping a single ranked row. The member then serializes as:

```json
{"repo_key": "acme/broken", "results": []}
```

which is byte-identical to a healthy member that simply had no matches. The only signal left is the envelope-level `response_truncated: true`, which says *rows were dropped*, not *a member's failure was suppressed*. So a caller searching a workspace reads a broken repo as "searched successfully, nothing found" — a wrong answer with no error, and the wrongness is worst exactly when the workspace is large enough for the budget to bind.

The same trimmer backs the text surface, which renders `"<repo> error <detail>"` per member; the line disappears there too.

The priority was also inverted: a member's failure is small and load-bearing, a marginal ranked row is neither, yet the error was sacrificed first.

## Repro

```
go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1 -run 'TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrieval'
```

On `origin/main` @ `a812069d`:

```
--- FAIL: TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrievalTextKeepsMemberErrors (0.13s)
    workspace_error_budget_test.go:90: member error was dropped to fit the budget; rendered text:
        [history] acme/healthy/history:00000000  sessions/main/20260801T000000Z_session.jsonl
        ...
--- FAIL: TestBoundedWorkspaceRetrievalJSONKeepsMemberErrors (0.48s)
    workspace_error_budget_test.go:69: member error was dropped to fit the budget: error="" results=0;
        the failed member is now indistinguishable from one with no matches
```

The fixture is two groups: a healthy member with 600 rows (over budget on both surfaces) and a failed member with an error and zero rows. Both tests are deterministic — the trim order is fixed, no maps are involved.

## Fix

Remove `Error` from the trimmable extras in `trimWorkspaceExtrasOnce`. `AbstractPreviews` and the two `Freshness` detail strings stay trimmable; once they are exhausted the caller's loop falls through to dropping ranked rows and, last, whole member groups — a dropped group disappears from `results` entirely rather than misreporting itself as empty-and-healthy.

## Mutation check

Re-add the `case groups[i].Error != "": groups[i].Error = ""` branch → both tests fail again. Remove it → both green at `-count=3`.

## What breaks

`overview` answers "what is this project" with a summary that looks complete while an entire section has been silently deleted by a swallowed error.

`recentDecisionMatches` (internal/cli/agent_surface.go) discarded `loadBrainHistoryIndex`'s error:

```go
index, err := loadBrainHistoryIndex(brainDir, source)
if err != nil {
	return nil
}
```

A source that failed to load is then treated as an empty one. With a corrupt or unreadable `history/index.json` the command exits 0, still reports `sources.history: true`, and the whole "recent decisions" block just disappears:

```
# healthy
repo: /tmp/... (gh/example/repo)
freshness:
semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
recent decisions:
  [] chose postgres for checkpoint storage

# same brain, index bytes corrupted — no error, no warning, no section
repo: /tmp/... (gh/example/repo)
freshness:
semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
```

Second half of the same problem: `renderBrainOverviewText` never rendered `report.Warnings` at all, so even the warnings `overview` already collects (they ride the JSON contract) never reached a CLI caller.

## Repro

`internal/cli/brain_overview_source_honesty_test.go` builds a brain whose manifest declares a history index that really exists and really holds one decision, proves `overview` carries it, corrupts only the index bytes, and asserts the section's disappearance is explained.

On clean `main` (a812069d):

```
$ go test -count=1 -run 'TestOverviewReportsUnreadableHistoryIndex' ./internal/cli/
--- FAIL: TestOverviewReportsUnreadableHistoryIndex
    brain_overview_source_honesty_test.go:87: overview dropped the recent-decisions section with no warning:
        repo: /tmp/.../001 (gh/example/repo)
        freshness:
        semantic: 0 files, 0 symbols, 0 relations
FAIL
```

`TestOverviewReportsUnreadableHistoryIndex` is the repro and it compiles and fails unmodified on `main`. Run the first one to reproduce.

## Fix

- `recentDecisionMatches` returns `([]brainTextMatch, error)`; an unreadable declared index is an error, not an empty decision log.
- `runBrainOverview` records it as `recent decisions unavailable: the manifest declares a history index that could not be read: ...` on `report.Warnings`, so it reaches both the JSON contract and the text surface.
- `renderBrainOverviewText` renders a `warnings:` section, which it never did before.

The rest of the summary is still produced from the sources that do load, so a partly-unreadable brain still answers — it just no longer answers as if nothing were missing.

## What breaks

`entire brain remember --branch <other> "..."` files the fact on `<other>` while the
working tree stays where it is — and then stamps the anchor with `git rev-parse HEAD`,
which is the **current** branch's tip.

The stored fact therefore reads "on `release`, evidenced by `<a commit that is only on
main>`". The pairing never existed. `entire brain verify` cannot catch it either:
`verifyCommitUncached` accepts reachability from *any* local ref, so it reports the
fabricated anchor as `commit exists and is reachable from local refs` → **verified**,
permanently.

This is the authored-fact twin of the same branch-blindness the distilled path has:
the anchor's branch and the anchor's commit are resolved from two different places and
never reconciled.

## Repro

`internal/cli/facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go` runs the real `remember` command with
the working tree on `main` (tip = commit B) and `release` pointing somewhere else
entirely.

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn (0.24s)
    facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go:37: a fact filed on `release` cites bbbb222222222222222222222222222222222222, the tip of the CURRENT branch (main)
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/ashtom/entire-brain/internal/cli	0.990s
```

A second test, `TestRememberKeepsHeadWhenNoBranchOverrideIsGiven`, pins the unchanged
default so the fix cannot be "stop recording a commit".

## Fix

`rememberAnchorCommit` resolves the commit from the branch the fact is actually being
filed on:

* with an explicit `--branch`, `git rev-parse --verify <branch>^{commit}` — the named
  branch's tip is the only honest evidence, and a branch git cannot resolve yields
  **no** commit rather than a wrong one (an absent anchor verifies as unverifiable,
  which is the truth; a wrong one verifies as correct, which is not);
* without one, `git rev-parse HEAD` exactly as before — the branch was derived *from*
  HEAD in the first place, and this also keeps a detached HEAD citing the commit that
  is actually checked out.

The no-override path keeps its original argv byte for byte, so nothing about the
default behavior moves.

## Mutation check

Collapsing `rememberAnchorCommit` back to the unconditional `rev-parse HEAD`
reproduces the original failure:

```
--- FAIL: TestRememberAnchorsToTheBranchItFilesTheFactOn
    facts_write_branch_anchor_test.go:37: a fact filed on `release` cites bbbb2222...
```

`TestRememberKeepsHeadWhenNoBranchOverrideIsGiven` stays green under that mutation and
under the fix, so it is pinning the default rather than the bug.

## What breaks

A distill run loads a branch's facts **once**, when it first sees the branch, and rewrites the **whole** set at every flush. Its read-modify-write therefore spans the entire run — which the flush comment itself describes as "hours of agent calls".

The brain write lock does not help. Each flush takes it, so the write is serialized, but every other writer already committed and released long before. Everything they did in that window is silently written back over:

- a fact the user added with `entire brain remember` disappears from the store;
- a `facts retract` reverts to `active`;
- a proposal applied in `facts review` is undone;
- a settlement `facts sync` mirrored back from the shared head is undone.

Nothing errors. `remember` printed success, `facts retract` printed success, and the user's next `recall` simply shows the pre-edit state. The longer the run, the wider the window — and a background/scheduled distill makes the window effectively always open.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/incremental (0.83s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/force (2.94s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
FAIL
```

The concurrent writer in the test is a full transaction under the brain write lock — exactly what `facts retract` and `remember` do — committed from inside the fake agent call, i.e. mid-run.

## Fix

The flush rebases the run's in-memory set onto the current on-disk set before writing, under the lock it already holds. The rebase is deliberately **monotone**:

- it adopts on-disk records the run never saw (someone else's addition);
- it adopts a retirement someone else applied to a record the run does hold (`active` -> `retracted`/`superseded` only, never the reverse);
- it changes nothing else.

So it can never undo one of the run's own decisions, and it is idempotent across the repeated mid-run flushes (the second flush re-reads what the first wrote and finds nothing to do).

`--force` is threaded through because a force rebuild deliberately dropped the active distilled facts it is regenerating; re-adopting those would turn the rebuild into an append. `TestDistillForceStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` pins that down and passes both before and after the fix.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both subtests fail again with the messages above, while `TestDistillForceStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` keeps passing.

## What breaks

`distill --force` drops every distilled record before replaying distillation:

```go
if record.Origin != factOriginDistilled {
    kept = append(kept, record)
}
```

That includes **retired** ones. `retracted` and `superseded` record decisions the rebuild does not replay — `facts retract`, an applied review proposal, a `facts promote --strategy prefer-source`, a settlement mirrored back by `facts sync`. With the tombstone gone, the very next chunk re-adds the same statement under the same content-derived id as **active**.

A fact the user explicitly declared no longer true comes back to life and starts being recalled again. A superseded fact comes back active and without its `superseded_by` pointer, so the store now asserts both it and its replacement. Neither prints anything; the run reports a normal rebuild.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestForceDistill' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestForceDistillDoesNotResurrectRetractedFact (0.90s)
    distill_force_retirement_test.go:52: distill --force resurrected a retracted fact as "active":
        {ID:fact:7a63dc1f5dd94ea931920b6c ... Status:active Confidence:1.00 ...}
--- FAIL: TestForceDistillDoesNotResurrectSupersededFact (0.87s)
    distill_force_retirement_test.go:76: distill --force resurrected a superseded fact: {...}
FAIL
```

The tests run the real `runDistillForBrain` with a fake agent that re-emits exactly the retired statement, so the regenerated candidate is guaranteed to collide on the content-derived id.

## Fix

The force filter retains any non-active distilled record. It costs nothing: the regenerated candidate carries the same id, so `upsertFact` lands on the retained tombstone, unions provenance and leaves the status alone — and a supersede the rebuild *does* replay re-marks it identically.

Active distilled facts are still dropped and rebuilt, so `--force` is still a rebuild: `TestForceDistillStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` pins that down and passes both before and after, which is what makes the other two tests specific to the retirement case.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both resurrection tests fail again with the messages above, while `TestForceDistillStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` keeps passing.

## What breaks

`dedupeProposals` collapses review-queue entries on `(action, candidate, target)`. `factsync.ProposalID` — the id the hosted review queue, the shared-proposal ledger and the `facts review` interlock all key on — additionally covers `branch` and `proposed_by`. The two identities disagree, and the queue is written through the narrower one.

distill's private backlog and a cross-member conflict raised by `facts sync` routinely name the same two facts: the shared head holds this member's own previously-synced facts, so the pair repeats. `persistFactsSyncProposals` writes `append(existing, raised...)`, so dedupe keeps the unattributed private entry and drops the member-attributed one.

The consequences are both silent:

- `facts sync` publishes only attributed entries (`if strings.TrimSpace(p.ProposedBy) == "" { continue }`), so the cross-member conflict is **never shared with the team**. Nobody else ever sees it.
- What survives locally looks like a private distill proposal, so the `facts review` shared-proposal interlock does not fire and the member settles it locally — the exact outcome that interlock exists to prevent, since (per its own error text) "a local-only decision would be overridden by the next sync".

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDedupeProposalsKeepsMemberAttribution|TestPersistFactsSyncProposalsKeepsAttributedEntry' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestDedupeProposalsKeepsMemberAttribution (0.00s)
    facts_proposal_attribution_test.go:20: want both the private and the member-attributed proposal,
        got [{Action:supersede CandidateID:fact:c TargetID:fact:t Confidence:0 Branch: ProposedBy:}]
--- FAIL: TestPersistFactsSyncProposalsKeepsAttributedEntry (0.00s)
    facts_proposal_attribution_test.go:64: the cross-member conflict is not publishable after
        persisting; queue = [{... ProposedBy:}]
FAIL
```

The second test goes through the real durable path (`writeFactProposals` -> `persistFactsSyncProposals` -> `loadFactProposals`).

## Fix

The dedupe key now matches `factsync.ProposalID`: action, candidate, target, branch, proposed_by. True duplicates still collapse; entries the sharing machinery treats as distinct rows stay distinct. The sort is extended to a total order over the same fields so the on-disk queue remains deterministic regardless of input order (the test asserts that too).

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/reconcile.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both tests fail again with the messages above.

## What breaks

`factmerge.Promote` copies only **active** source facts (`if sf.Status != StatusActive { continue }`), and `factsync.Sync` is built on it. A member's retirements therefore never reach the shared fact-set head.

Run `entire brain facts retract fact:<id>` and then `entire brain facts sync`. The merge produces bytes identical to the current head, `Advance` short-circuits on `ErrNoChange`, and the command prints:

```
synced 4 local fact(s) on main via local-gitmeta (...): no change; head at facts-... (1 attempt(s))
```

The retraction is gone. Every other member — and every other clone of this member — goes on reading a statement its owner has explicitly declared false, forever: no later sync can ever carry it, because the condition that suppressed it does not change. The same applies to a supersede applied in `facts review`: the replacement fact is promoted, but the head keeps the retired fact **active** and unlinked, so the team sees two contradictory facts with no indication which one won.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/factsync/ -run 'TestSyncPropagates|TestSyncDoesNotRevive' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:50: retraction sync reported no change; the head still carries the fact as active
    retirement_test.go:59: shared head still says "active" after the owner retracted the fact
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesSupersede (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:104: head target not superseded: {ID:fact:306d0675... Status:active ...}
--- FAIL: TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:134: a peer sync revived a retracted fact: [...]
FAIL
```

## Fix

`Sync` folds the member's local retirements onto the merged set before the CAS. The pass is deliberately **monotone**: it only moves a fact from `active` to `retracted`/`superseded`, never back, and only for a record the head already carries.

That gives three properties the tests pin down:

- a retraction reaches the head and the sync publishes (`TestSyncPropagatesRetraction`);
- a peer who still holds the fact as active cannot revive it on their next sync (`TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction`);
- re-syncing the same local state is still a no-op, so the loop converges.

Nothing is deleted — the record, its provenance and its `superseded_by` pointer are retained — so the keep-both guarantee (ADR-P1-G) is unaffected: a fact is retired, never dropped.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/factsync/sync.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes all three tests fail again with the messages above.

## What breaks

A fact id is content-derived (`sha256(normalized text + sorted paths)`), so `entire brain remember "<statement>"` for a statement that was previously retracted lands on the retired record. `upsertFact` matches by id and only unions provenance — it never revives a status, which is exactly right for a re-distill and wrong for an explicit human assertion.

The write is silently lost. The command prints

```
remembered fact:8e83a375b9e7062da881300a [preference] preferences.coding.style on feature
```

and exits 0, while the record on disk stays `retracted`: recall skips it, the fact tree skips it, the manifest's `by_kind` histogram skips it. Short of opening `facts.ndjson` there is no way for the author to know the fact they just wrote down is not in their brain. The same holds for a fact retired by an applied supersede proposal.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestRememberRevives' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestRememberRevivesRetractedFact (0.08s)
    facts_remember_revive_test.go:68: re-authored fact is still "retracted" after
        "remembered fact:8e83a375b9e7062da881300a [preference] preferences.coding.style on feature\n":
        the command reported success but the fact is not recallable
--- FAIL: TestRememberRevivesSupersededFact (0.06s)
    facts_remember_revive_test.go:104: re-authored fact not revived: [{... Status:superseded
        SupersededBy:fact:newer ...}]
FAIL
```

The tests drive the real `runRemember` end to end against a temp brain.

## Fix

Re-authoring now restores the status the author just asserted and clears `superseded_by`. The record is revived, not replaced: `created_at`, provenance and cross-links are kept, and the explicit `--kind` override still wins as before. `upsertFact` itself is untouched, so a re-distill still cannot resurrect a retired fact.

A note on the superseded case: reviving leaves both the revived fact and its replacement active. That is the store's normal keep-both state for two statements a human has asserted, and it is visible in `facts review`/`recall` — unlike today's outcome, where the author's write disappears without trace.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/facts_write_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes both revive tests fail again with the messages above, while `TestRememberActiveFactIsStillIdempotent` keeps passing — confirming the tests key on the revival, not on the surrounding upsert path.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## What breaks

`facts reclassify` is the only fact mutator that rewrites `facts.ndjson` without holding the brain write lock. It loads the branch's facts, mutates the records in memory, and writes the whole set back — all outside the lock that `remember`, `facts retract`, `facts review`, `facts promote`, `facts gc`, `facts sync`'s reconcile and distill's flush all take, and that `reclassifyAllFactBranches` (the same operation on the refresh path) takes for its entire pass.

Any writer that commits between reclassify's read and its write is silently overwritten. A fact just added by `entire brain remember`, a retraction just applied by `facts retract`, a settlement just mirrored by `facts sync` — gone from the store, with no error printed by either command and nothing in the manifest to hint at it. The window covers the whole branch, so nothing narrows it.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess -count=1
--- FAIL: TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess (0.52s)
    facts_reclassify_lock_test.go:120: facts reclassify rewrote facts.ndjson while another process
        held the brain write lock: [{ID:fact:inv ... Kind:invariant ...}]
FAIL
```

The test spawns a real second **process** (a re-exec of the test binary) that holds the brain write lock — the lock is an `flock(2)` advisory lock, so an in-process mutex would not exercise it — and checks that `facts reclassify` has not rewritten `facts.ndjson` while that process holds it. It then releases the lock and asserts reclassify completes and persists its work.

## Fix

The load, the mutation, the write and the manifest rebuild now run inside one `withBrainWriteLock`, using `updateFactSourceManifestLocked` so the lock is taken once instead of being re-entered by `updateFactSourceManifest`. That re-entry is also why the old code did not simply deadlock: it wrote the facts unprotected and only then blocked on the lock for the manifest.

## Mutation check

Reverting `internal/cli/facts_admin_cmd.go` to the pre-fix version (test file kept) makes `TestFactsReclassifyWaitsForOtherProcess` fail again with the message above.

## What breaks

The reverse index records a commit under the entity's **post-change** key, and the alias record points `old key -> new key`. So everything a symbol did before a rename or a move lives under its *old* key, and the rename commit itself is the first entry under the new one.

Resolution only ever followed that chain forward (`AliasChain`), which means the answer depends on which spelling you happen to ask by:

- ask by the **old** key -> the full history
- ask by the **current** key -> the rename/move commit, alone

The current key is the only spelling that still exists in the tree, so it is the one a human types and the one a ranked search returns. `entities history` and `brain_entity_history` therefore print a short, plausible, wrong history for every renamed or moved symbol, with nothing anywhere reporting that anything was dropped — "this function was first touched in the commit that moved it" is wrong in the direction that looks right.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/query_alias_family_test.go` builds a real repository (`git mv internal/pay/charge.go internal/billing/charge.go` after two commits), indexes it, then asks for the same entity by both spellings.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory -v
```

On `main`:

```
    query_alias_family_test.go:155: history depends on the spelling asked by:
          current key internal/billing/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
          old key     internal/pay/charge.go#function#fn_charge -> [b1497049f78d22b724a01138cc669b9068619af0 753dbe598088443d3e09842d4e443d14dff484ce 806d8850f0c0bb9ce6f3518327a03e6857419ede]
--- FAIL: TestCommitsByCurrentKeyKeepThePreRenameHistory (4.26s)
```

The test also goes through `Snapshot.Search`, which is the surface the CLI and the MCP tool actually call.

## Fix

Resolve the whole alias **family** rather than the forward chain: the earlier spellings that resolve *into* a key as well as the chain forward from it. `AliasFamily` walks both directions breadth-first with a visited set, so:

- a symbol renamed and then renamed back (`A -> B -> A`) terminates instead of looping,
- predecessors are sorted at every level, so the result is deterministic (pinned by `TestAliasFamilyIsTotalAndDeterministic`, including 25 repeated calls and a two-old-keys-into-one-current-key fold),
- the family is bounded by the alias map itself rather than by a hop budget that could silently clip a long chain,
- a linear chain still comes out oldest-spelling-first.

Both call sites move over: `Snapshot.Commits` and `entityHistory` in `internal/cli/entities_cmd.go`. `AliasChain` is removed rather than left sitting beside `AliasFamily` — it had no remaining caller, and a forward-only chain is the exact shape of this bug.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing the backward frontier seed (`frontier := []string{entityKey}` -> `var frontier []string`) makes both new tests fail again — the real-git one with the same "history depends on the spelling asked by" output, and the unit one on the `A -> B -> A` cycle. The rest of the package (and `internal/cli`) still passes, so the tests pin the backward walk specifically.

<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

## Problem

`entire-brain semantic repair` is meant to regenerate a missing/corrupt semantic generation from the durable snapshot. It never checked whether the *current* generation was already healthy before rebuilding — it always read the snapshot and called `buildSemanticGeneration`, which writes a brand-new generation directory (a full copy of `semantic.sqlite`, `metrics.json`, `parse-cache/`).

Nothing prevents `repair` from running against a healthy store (`doctor` can suggest it defensively; a user or agent can run it speculatively "just in case"). Repair derives its generation id from the *snapshot's* existing directory name, so a repair against unchanged content asks `semanticAvailableGenerationID` to place a generation at an id that's already taken — the same one written on the original build. Collision handling there assumes any existing id means genuinely different content needing disambiguation, so it appends the content-hash suffix again, producing a fresh, permanently-duplicated ~180MB generation directory that nothing automatically cleans up (`semantic gc` is a manual command, defaults to a 30-day age cutoff, so a same-day duplicate is never pruned).

## Evidence (real fixture: entireio/entire-brain's own repo)

`semantic/generations/` held two generation directories ~54 minutes apart: `58b0c54e...-bef1b268c57d94ca` (179,859,456 bytes) and `58b0c54e...-bef1b268c57d94ca-bef1b268c57d94ca` (179,879,936 bytes, double-suffixed) — same content, from a `repair` run against an already-good store. `du -sh semantic/` = 475M; only ~180M of that is the live generation.

## Fix

Before reading the snapshot and rebuilding, `runSemanticRepair` now validates the manifest's *currently active* generation with `validateSemanticSQLiteStore` — the same integrity+count check `status`/`doctor` already use — and, if it passes, reports "semantic generation already valid; nothing to repair" and returns without writing anything. Any failure of that check (missing file, symlink, integrity/count mismatch, invalid manifest paths) falls straight through to the existing full-rebuild path, unchanged.

## Test

`TestSemanticRepairIsNoOpWhenGenerationAlreadyValid` (`internal/cli/semantic_test.go`): indexes a fresh brain, confirms one generation directory exists, runs `repair` and asserts (a) the output is the new no-op message rather than "repaired", (b) the generations directory still has exactly one entry with the same name, (c) the manifest's generation/store pointers are untouched, then removes the store file and re-runs `repair` to confirm the existing rebuild-when-actually-broken behavior is unchanged. The existing `TestSemanticRepairRebuildsMissingStoreFromActiveSnapshot` and the full semantic suite (190 tests) pass unchanged.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `gofmt -s -l` are clean. **Verification note:** the full `go test ./...` run did not complete locally (shared/loaded machine; a prior attempt showed 1563 passed/1 failed/6 skipped in internal/cli but the specific failing test could not be captured before the log truncated, and re-runs did not finish in time) -- verified by targeted tests only (the suites named above), not a full-suite green run.

## Problem

`history_records.id` carried a `UNIQUE` constraint. `conversationExchangeID` derives id from `(repo_key, session_id, ordinal, request_digest)` with no branch/path component, so the *same* exchange legitimately produces the same id once per branch it's retained under — a session captured on a feature branch and later retained under `sessions/main` after merge indexes as two branch-scoped rows sharing one id.

On any repo with that (common) shape, `buildHistoryFTSIdentity`'s INSERT hits a UNIQUE violation partway through, the whole transaction rolls back via the deferred `tx.Rollback()`, and the derived BM25 cache (`history/index-fts.sqlite`) never persists. Because `openHistoryFTS`/`rankHistoryLexicalFromSourceWithLoader` fall back silently to the substring scorer on any build failure ("the index is an optimization, never load-bearing"), this is invisible to the user — every `search`/`query`/`inspect`-history call just quietly re-attempts and re-fails the same rebuild, forever, with zero feedback that anything is wrong.

## Evidence (real fixture: entireio/entire-brain's own repo, checked out at 1,179 files / 618 checkpoints / 185 sessions — 136,661 history records)

- Reproduced deterministically: `UNIQUE constraint failed: history_records.id (2067)` at record 69354/136661, id `conversation:18f1a5aa61c158a02485f03ebca4e62b` — the same exchange retained under two feature branches (`claude/pr49-review-fixes`, `codex/full-plan-implementation`) and again under `sessions/main` after merge. 243 distinct duplicated ids / 442 duplicate rows total in this repo's history.
- Before: `history/index-fts.sqlite` never accumulates its schema (`sqlite3 index-fts.sqlite .tables` → empty) no matter how many times `search` runs; each call pays a partial build (up to ~69k rows) then a full rollback.
- After: the same fixture builds and persists all 136,661 rows on the first call (`select count(*) from history_records` → 136661; `history_fts_meta` present with the matching content fingerprint); `openHistoryFTSIfFresh` returns non-nil on every subsequent call, so later `search`/`query`/`brief` calls skip the rebuild entirely instead of repeating it.

## Fix

- Drop the `UNIQUE` constraint on `history_records.id` (kept `NOT NULL`). Nothing queries this table by `id` — both join sites go through `fts_rowid`/`rec_order`, which already carry the real per-row uniqueness used everywhere in this file.
- The "corrupt derived payload" detector on the direct-read fast path (`rankHistoryViaFreshFTSCutoffOnce`) treated a repeated `id` within one query's result set as corruption under the same wrong assumption. Removed it; kept the `seenOrders` check (a repeated `rec_order`/`fts_rowid` really would mean a broken join/scan, which is still guarded against).

## Test

`TestBuildHistoryFTS_DuplicateIDAcrossBranches` (`internal/cli/history_fts_test.go`): builds an index with two records sharing an id under different branches, asserts the build succeeds, both rows persist as distinct storage rows (queried directly by branch, not just a row count), BM25 ranking still works, and the store reports fresh afterward (proving no perpetual rebuild). The existing `history_fts_test.go` suite (22 tests, including the "aliased record order" corruption case, which still passes) and the broader search/query/brief/retrieve suite (330 tests) pass unchanged.

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, and `gofmt -s -l` are clean. **Verification note:** the full `go test ./...` run did not complete locally (shared/loaded machine; a prior attempt showed 1563 passed/1 failed/6 skipped in internal/cli but the specific failing test could not be captured before the log truncated, and re-runs did not finish in time) -- verified by targeted tests only (the suites named above), not a full-suite green run.

## Impact

`rejectSymlinkPathComponents` and `rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents` (`internal/cli/semantic.go:5385`, `:5415`) are the shared containment guards for repo-relative paths. Their prefix test was:

```go
if filepath.IsAbs(clean) || clean == "." || strings.HasPrefix(clean, ".."+string(filepath.Separator)) {
```

`filepath.Clean("..")` is `".."` — not `"."`, and not prefixed with `"../"` — so a bare `..` fell through the entire test. (`"../x"` and `"../../x"` are both caught; `".."` alone was not.)

The per-component symlink walk then Lstats `filepath.Join(root, "..")`, the **parent of root** — a real directory, not a symlink — and passes it. The only remaining check is the closing containment test, and that returns `nil` early whenever `EvalSymlinks(root)` reports `ENOENT` (`semantic.go:5441-5445`), which is the ordinary state before the store directory has been created.

`brainDirForKey` (`internal/cli/env.go:286`) hands the guard the **repo key** as its relative path, and `runMCPDeleteProject` (`internal/cli/mcp.go:1204`) passes the result straight to `os.RemoveAll`. A repo key of `..` therefore resolved to the plugin **data root itself** — every project's brain and every workspace, not just the named one. `brain_delete_project` takes `repo_key` as an MCP tool argument.

## Repro

`internal/cli/path_guard_dotdot_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestRejectExistingSymlinkPathComponentsRejectsBareDotDot
    guard accepted "..", which resolves to the parent of root
--- FAIL: TestBrainDirForKeyRejectsDotDot
    brainDirForKey resolved repo key ".." to <data-root>
    — os.RemoveAll on that wipes the whole brain data root
```

`TestRejectSymlinkPathComponentsRejectsBareDotDot` (the read guard) passes on `main` because its root exists in that fixture, so the containment check catches it there. It is kept as a regression pin: that guard has the same hole and only the ordering of an unrelated precondition hides it.

## Fix

Both guards list `clean == ".."` explicitly. That is the form the majority of this repo's other path checks already use — `semantic.go:1208`, `dash.go:570`, `export.go:2141`/`2776`/`2884`, `agent_surface.go:3257`, `brain.go:309` — so this closes a consistent omission rather than inventing a new rule.

Every call site that delegates containment to these two guards is covered by the same change: `export.go:2764` (`ensureExportDirectories` at `:2801`), `seed.go:501`, `brainDirForKey`, and the bundle import path. The call sites that carry their own `Contains(name, "..")` pre-check or an exact-path allowlist (`semantic.go:6367`, `history.go:3128`, `memory_receipts.go:345`) were already safe.

## Mutation

Reverting either `clean == ".."` reproduces the two failures above.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, exit 0, no failures), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli/` clean.","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:13:39Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-dotdot-path-guard","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/102","number":102,"sha":"9e655cbf359330cd10e59fe265549ec842d4e1d8","title":"fix(paths): shared path guards accept a bare "..", letting a repo key escape the brain store root","updated_at":"2026-08-28T21:01:10Z"}

## What breaks

The brain reports a live facts source with real counts while every recall surface serves nothing from it.

`loadFacts` treats an absent `facts.ndjson` as an empty branch, deliberately, so first-run callers do not have to special-case it. The cost is that a deleted or never-restored fact store is **indistinguishable from "this branch has no facts"** on every read surface. With the manifest still declaring the branch:

- `status` / MCP `brain_status`: `sources: ... facts=true` and `counts: 1 (0 distilled, 1 authored, 0 superseded) across 1 branch(es)`
- `brief` / `brain_brief`: the embedded status block reports the facts source as present, `facts` comes back empty, and `warnings` says nothing about it
- `recall`: `no facts for "postgres" on main` plus the note `the answer may genuinely not be in the brain` — a confident claim that is false
- `doctor`: passes; it had no facts check at all

An agent reading that brief concludes the brain holds one fact and that fact simply did not match the task. It holds none, because the store is gone.

## Repro

`internal/cli/brain_facts_store_availability_test.go` writes one authored fact on the checked-out branch, derives the fact source manifest from disk, proves the healthy path (status counts it, brief carries it, doctor says ok), then deletes only `facts/<branch>/facts.ndjson`, proves `recall` no longer returns it, and asserts what the surfaces must say.

On clean `main` (a812069d):

```
$ go test -count=1 -run 'TestStatusReportsDeclaredFactBranchWithMissingStore|TestBrainBriefWarnsWhenFactStoreIsMissing|TestDoctorReportsDeclaredFactBranchWithMissingStore' ./internal/cli/
--- FAIL: TestStatusReportsDeclaredFactBranchWithMissingStore
    brain_facts_store_availability_test.go:97: status facts.missing_branches = [], want [feature]
--- FAIL: TestBrainBriefWarnsWhenFactStoreIsMissing
    (brief packet still reports a present facts source, contributes zero facts, and warns only "semantic index missing")
--- FAIL: TestDoctorReportsDeclaredFactBranchWithMissingStore
    brain_facts_store_availability_test.go:147: healthy doctor facts = "" present=false, want ok
FAIL
```

All three compile and run unmodified on `main`; the status assertion reads `missing_branches` out of the serialized contract precisely so it does.

## Fix

The manifest names exactly which branches the store is supposed to hold, so the claim is checkable against disk.

- `missingFactBranchStores` / `missingFactStoreWarning` (facts.go): compare `sources.facts.branches` against the `facts.ndjson` each branch resolves to.
- `buildBrainStatusReportWithAvailability`: additive `facts.missing_branches` on the status contract plus a warning, so `status` text, status JSON, and MCP `brain_status` (compact preserves `facts` and `warnings`) all carry it.
- `runBrainBriefWithRawHistoryMatcher`: the same warning on the packet, before the facts arm reports a present source that contributed nothing.
- `brainDoctorReadOnlyReport`: a `facts` check, so doctor can no longer pass while a declared source is silently dead.

Reads still degrade gracefully — nothing new fails hard, and a branch the manifest does not declare still reads as legitimately empty. They just no longer degrade silently.

## Mutation check

Making `missingFactBranchStores` return `nil` unconditionally makes all three tests fail again. Restoring it makes them pass.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l .` (empty) all clean. `go test ./...` green: every non-`internal/cli` package, plus `internal/cli` run in four `-run '^Test[A-E]' / '[F-M]' / '[N-R]' / '[S-Z]'` shards (the package exceeds the default 10m `go test` timeout on this machine).","created_at":"2026-08-28T04:09:40Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fix-facts-store-missing","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/101","number":101,"sha":"0376c34ffb5eb4a3d40e9bcfabe00e137d72f1c9","title":"fix(status): report declared fact branches whose store is missing from disk","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:45:46Z"}

## What breaks

Two `brain_query` / `brain_search` calls with the same query, against the same unchanged brain, can return the history and conversation hits in a **different order**. Nothing errors; both rankings look authoritative. An agent that reruns a query to check its own work sees a different answer, and a `--limit` cut can keep a different record.

`fuseScoredRankLists` is the shared RRF merge behind `rankFreshHistory` (every retrieval whose brain has a short-term overlay) and `rankHistoryFused`. It fuses by `historyRecordReplacementKey` — a seven-field identity — but its final tie-break compares only five of them:

```go
if left.ID != right.ID { ... }
if left.Branch != right.Branch { ... }
if left.SessionID != right.SessionID { ... }
if left.Path != right.Path { ... }
return left.Line < right.Line
```

`Kind` and `SourceDigest` are missing. Two entries that the fusion key *deliberately* keeps distinct therefore compare equal, and `sort.SliceStable` leaves comparator-equal elements in input order — which here is a `for ... range` over the `fused` map, re-randomized by the runtime on every iteration.

The reachable case is the one `recordReplacementKey` documents. For a conversation record with no session id it falls back to the source digest, so that "two degraded sessions [do not] replace one another merely because an old producer emitted the same exchange ID". Both degraded copies survive fusion as separate entries, tie on id, branch, session id, path and line, and permute. `Kind` is part of the key for every record, degraded or not.

## Repro

Two tests, both failing on `origin/main` @ `a812069d`:

```
go test ./internal/cli/ -count=1 -run 'TestFuseScoredRankLists'
```

```
--- FAIL: TestFuseScoredRankListsOrdersDegradedCopiesDeterministically (0.00s)
    history_fusion_tiebreak_test.go:82: run 0: fused order = "d03 d04 d05 d06 d07 d08 d01 d02",
        want "d01 d02 d03 d04 d05 d06 d07 d08"; the same input produced a different ranking
--- FAIL: TestFuseScoredRankListsTieBreakCoversTheFusionKey (0.00s)
    history_fusion_tiebreak_test.go:120: run 0: fused order = "k6 k7 k8 k1 k2 k3 k4 k5",
        want "k1 k2 k3 k4 k5 k6 k7 k8"; the same input produced a different ranking
```

Each test builds an **exact 8-way tie** (one record per list, all at rank 0, so the RRF score is identical) and asserts the order over 500 calls in one process. With an incomplete comparator a single call has a 1/8! (~1 in 40,320) chance of landing on the sorted order, so both tests fail on run 0 on every invocation — `-count=5` gives 10/10 failures on main, not a 1-in-N flake. In-process repetition is the stronger probe here because Go re-randomizes each `range` over a map, not just the per-process seed.

## Fix

Extend the comparator with the two remaining components of the key it fuses by, so the ordering is total over that key:

```go
if left.Kind != right.Kind {
    return left.Kind < right.Kind
}
return left.SourceDigest < right.SourceDigest
```

Records that were already ordered are unaffected — the new comparisons only run once every earlier field is equal.

## Mutation check

- Replace `return left.SourceDigest < right.SourceDigest` with `return false` → `TestFuseScoredRankListsOrdersDegradedCopiesDeterministically` fails again (5/5 runs).
- Delete the `left.Kind != right.Kind` branch → `TestFuseScoredRankListsTieBreakCoversTheFusionKey` fails again (5/5 runs).
- Restore both → green at `-count=20`.

## What breaks

A distilled fact can be anchored to a commit that is **not on the branch the fact
was distilled on** — and nothing downstream catches it.

The entity → checkpoint reverse index is **project-scoped**: `brain:entity:<key>`
lists every commit that ever touched an entity, on every branch. A cherry-pick or a
rebase copies a checkpoint's `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer onto a *second* commit, so
one checkpoint id resolves to two (or more) commits — the original and the copy that
landed elsewhere — and the copy usually has the **newer committer date**.

`entityProvenanceResolver` scopes candidates by session and picks the newest one
(`betterProvenance`). Nothing checks that the winning commit is reachable from the
fact's branch. So:

* `entire brain facts read --branch main` shows an anchor commit that
  `git log main` will never contain;
* when that commit is a live copy on another branch, `entire brain verify` reports
  it **verified**: `verifyCommitUncached` (verify_cmd.go:392) accepts reachability
  from *any* local ref (`refs/heads`, `refs/remotes`, `refs/tags`) rather than from
  the fact's branch, so nothing downstream ever objects;
* the fact's own header comment already names this class as the thing that must
  not happen: *"a provenance triple that never existed and that verification would
  then have to either reject or launder."*

**Scope, precisely.** A commit that *no* ref contains is a different case, and verify
already catches that one — it reports `commit is not reachable from local refs` →
orphaned. The laundering claim above is only about the live-but-off-branch commit.
The guard still improves the orphan case, by keeping the honest coarse anchor instead
of writing a dangling one, but that half was never silent.

The sibling read path already does the right thing — `entities history` filters its
answers through `branchReachableCommits`/`filterOccurrencesToBranch`. Provenance did
not.

## Repro

`internal/cli/entities_provenance_branch_test.go` builds the index over the standard
entity fixture, then says commit B is not on `main` — it lives on a feature branch, or
it is the pre-rewrite copy a rebase left behind. The object still exists and still
carries the session's checkpoint trailer, so the index still lists it.

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestEntityProvenanceRefusesACommitThatIsNotOnTheFactsBranch' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestEntityProvenanceRefusesACommitThatIsNotOnTheFactsBranch (0.08s)
    entities_provenance_branch_test.go:60: a fact on main was anchored to bbbb222222222222222222222222222222222222, a commit that is not reachable from main
FAIL
FAIL	github.com/ashtom/entire-brain/internal/cli	0.924s
```

Three tests ship with the fix:

* `TestEntityProvenanceRefusesACommitThatIsNotOnTheFactsBranch` — the bug, plus a
  control asserting an on-branch anchor **still sharpens** (so the guard cannot pass
  by disabling the feature).
* `TestEntityProvenanceKeepsSharpeningWhenReachabilityIsUnknown` — a failed
  `rev-list` must not silently downgrade a whole run to the coarse anchor.
* `TestEntityProvenanceTreatsATruncatedReachabilityWalkAsUnknown` — the walk is
  bounded at `entityBranchRevWalkMax`, so on a deep history it returns the branch's
  *newest* commits, not its commits; reading that as a reachability set would call
  every older indexed commit off-branch.

## Fix

`buildEntityProvenanceResolver` now takes a `provenanceBranchReachability` lookup and
drops a candidate whose commit is not reachable from that session's branch, at build
time — so the winner is the newest **on-branch** candidate rather than the newest
candidate anywhere, instead of merely rejecting a bad winner after the fact.

`newEntityProvenanceResolver` supplies `branchReachabilityLookup`, which memoizes the
existing `branchReachableCommits` walk per branch: one `rev-list` per branch a distill
run touches, not one per candidate.

Unknown reachability is deliberately **not** a refusal. A branch that is gone locally,
a walk git refused, and a walk that hit its bound all resolve to nil, and refusing on
nil would silently downgrade every fact in the run to the coarse anchor. A *known* set
that does not contain the commit is a refusal. When every candidate is dropped the
resolver is nil and distill keeps the exact pre-index anchor, byte for byte — property
1 of the file header ("non-breaking") is preserved.

## Mutation check

Reverting the guard (deleting the `provenanceCommitOnBranch` skip) reproduces the
original failure verbatim:

```
--- FAIL: TestEntityProvenanceRefusesACommitThatIsNotOnTheFactsBranch (0.09s)
    entities_provenance_branch_test.go:60: a fact on main was anchored to bbbb222222222222222222222222222222222222, a commit that is not reachable from main
```

Removing the `set == nil` escape hatch fails
`TestEntityProvenanceKeepsSharpeningWhenReachabilityIsUnknown`; disabling the
`len(set) >= entityBranchRevWalkMax` clause fails
`TestEntityProvenanceTreatsATruncatedReachabilityWalkAsUnknown`. Each test dies when
its own line is reverted.

## What breaks

The indexed window is the index's coverage claim: *every first-parent commit from `floor` to `tip` inclusive carries a forward delta document*. A freshness tick extends the tip by walking `<tip>..<head>`, and the only thing guarding that walk is `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.

Ancestry is not first-parent ancestry. Take the most ordinary sequence there is:

```
git checkout feature && git merge main     # main's tip becomes M's SECOND parent
git checkout main    && git merge --ff-only feature
```

main's stored tip is now still an ancestor of the new head, so the window survives the divergence check — but the head's **first-parent** chain runs through the feature commits. `<tip>..<head>` excludes everything reachable from the tip by *any* parent, which is exactly those commits. The walk returns only the merge, the tip advances to it, and the window now claims a first-parent run containing commits that were never indexed.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. `entities backfill` prints `indexed window: <floor>..<head>`, and from then on every `entities history` / `brain_entity_history` query for a symbol that only changed in the hole answers "that entity was never touched" — confidently, and permanently, because the window says the range is already covered so no later pass ever revisits it.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_firstparent_test.go` drives a real git repository (real commits, real merges, real fast-forward) and asserts the window's actual claim: walk `rev-list --first-parent <tip>` down to `<floor>` and require a forward document on every commit.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_firstparent_test.go:195: window 97cbfd46..cbae47a7 claims coverage but 4b153ff1 has no
    forward delta document (first-parent chain [cbae47a7f1475d4b7c7f9f1eaca973292ec71d04
    4b153ff1e993869a1b6cac6619701ef2146e62c0 3dc545894ca1b75b674ff62c4b9b93f74102102e
    97cbfd46eb920f3bb425d59d0770a3271eff94af])
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotClaimCoverageOverASecondParentTip (6.98s)
```

Two of the four commits the window claims have no delta document at all.

## Fix

Check contiguity using data the walk has already parsed. `walkForward` bounds the range from the **newest** end (it counts first, then skips past what the budget cannot reach), so its oldest element is always the oldest commit of the range — and when the range really does sit on top of the tip, that commit's first parent *is* the tip.

`contiguousWithTip` asserts exactly that. When it fails, the tip is not on the head's first-parent chain, so the walk cannot be used to advance the cursor: drop the window and re-cover from the head, which is the path a diverged tip already takes. An empty range with `tip != head` means the same thing and is treated the same way — if the tip were on the head's first-parent chain there would be at least one commit above it, and no commit above the tip is reachable from it.

The repair is cheap: `alreadyIndexed` skips every commit that already has a document, so re-covering costs one probe per commit, not one `graph diff` per commit.

## Mutation check

With the fix in place, replacing `return commits[0].Parent == tip` with `return true` makes the new test fail again with the identical "claims coverage but ... has no forward delta document" message. The other 23 tests in the package still pass, so the test is pinning the check itself rather than something incidental.

## What breaks

The brain reports a healthy, fresh docs layer while serving nothing from it.

`status`, MCP `brain_status`, and `doctor` decide the docs layer is fine from the **manifest alone**. Retrieval reads the index off disk and skips it when it is missing — `loadDocIndex`'s `os.IsNotExist` is swallowed by `case derr != nil && !os.IsNotExist(derr)` in `retrieveUnifiedWithOptions` (internal/cli/retrieve.go:448), not raised. So once `docs/index.json` is gone (partial restore, interrupted write, a manual "reset", a half-synced brain directory), the whole docs layer contributes zero and every surface still says it is present and current:

```
sources: seed=true sessions=false semantic=false history=false facts=false docs=true

Retrieval
  docs: 1 records from 1 files (generated 2026-08-10T02:00:00Z)
  freshness: ok
    docs: ok (docs index was built from the current seed)
```

and the same query that used to return the doc now answers with a confidently wrong diagnosis:

```
no results for "postgres"
note: the brain has no distilled facts; run `entire brain refresh`, then `distill`
```

`doctor` had no docs check at all, so it passed too. History already behaves correctly here (a declared-but-missing `history/index.json` raises a real error and a health issue); docs was the inconsistent one.

## Repro

`internal/cli/brain_status_docs_availability_test.go` builds a brain whose manifest declares a docs index **and** whose index is really on disk, proves the healthy path, deletes only the index file, proves retrieval no longer returns the record, and then asserts what status/doctor must say.

On clean `main` (a812069d), with **only that new file** applied:

```
$ go test -count=1 -run 'TestStatusReportsDeclaredDocsIndexMissing|TestDoctorReportsDeclaredDocsIndexMissing' ./internal/cli/
--- FAIL: TestStatusReportsDeclaredDocsIndexMissing
    brain_status_docs_availability_test.go:102: docs axis still reports ok while docs/index.json is absent: {State:ok Detail:docs index was built from the current seed Current: Indexed:}
--- FAIL: TestDoctorReportsDeclaredDocsIndexMissing
    brain_status_docs_availability_test.go:131: healthy doctor docs_index = "" present=false, want ok
FAIL
```

Note for anyone replaying this: the new test file compiles and fails on `main` on its own, but the other test change in this PR (`semantic_audit_test.go`) does **not** — it is a fixture update to the fix's `buildBrainRetrievalStatus` signature, so applying all `_test.go` changes at once will not build on `main`. Apply the new file alone to reproduce.

## Fix

- `verifyDeclaredDocIndex` (doc.go) probes the exact file `loadDocIndex` opens — no new path semantics, so a "docs: ok" status is now a statement about the bytes retrieval will actually rank.
- `buildBrainRetrievalStatus` consults it before the timestamp comparisons: an absent index is a `missing` axis naming `docs/index.json`, an unreadable one is `unsafe`. Both make the retrieval freshness severity non-ok, which `status` text, the status JSON contract, MCP `brain_status` (compact preserves `retrieval`), and `brief`'s embedded status block all read.
- `brainDoctorReadOnlyReport` grows the matching `docs_index` check, mirroring the existing `history_index` wording, so doctor can no longer pass while the layer is dead.
- The existing `TestBuildBrainRetrievalStatus` fixture now writes a real index, because its cases are about *freshness*, not availability.

The docs layer still degrades gracefully — retrieval keeps answering from the remaining sources. It just says so now.

## Mutation check

Making `verifyDeclaredDocIndex` return `nil` unconditionally makes both tests fail again with the original messages (`docs axis still reports ok while docs/index.json is absent`, `doctor docs_index still ok with docs/index.json absent`). Restoring it makes them pass.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `gofmt -l .` (empty) all clean. `go test ./...` green: every non-`internal/cli` package, plus `internal/cli` run in four `-run '^Test[A-E]' / '[F-M]' / '[N-R]' / '[S-Z]'` shards (the package exceeds the default 10m `go test` timeout on this machine).","created_at":"2026-08-28T03:50:39Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/fix-status-docs-index-missing","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/97","number":97,"sha":"7fafbeecb7311507eb4daf8b82bd2733bb6590ea","title":"fix(status): report a declared docs index that is absent or unreadable","updated_at":"2026-08-28T20:46:15Z"}

Two defects on the same write path (`entire brain patterns skills form <task-id> --yes`). A `SKILL.md` is an agent-instruction file, so landing one at a chosen path is **persistent prompt injection into every later session**.

## Impact

**1. Path traversal through the synthesized skill name.**
`name` comes from `skillNameFromFrontmatter` (`internal/cli/skill_synthesis.go:85`), which reads the synthesis agent's `name:` line with only whitespace/quote trimming — no charset or traversal validation. That agent's input is `buildSkillEvidence`: recurring commands and real session excerpts, i.e. text a hostile repo can reach through a captured session.

`skillDestinations` then did `path.Join("skills", name, "SKILL.md")`. `path.Join` **collapses** `..`, it does not reject it, so the name walked straight out of the skills directory.

**2. CWE-59 symlink write at the destination.**
The overwrite guard was `os.Stat(skillFilePath(d.Path))`. `os.Stat` resolves the link and reports a **dangling** symlink as `ENOENT`, so the "refusing to overwrite existing skill file" guard passed, and `os.WriteFile` then created the file the link pointed at — **no `--force` needed**. With `--force` the guard was skipped entirely, so an existing link was truncated and written through. The destination's parent directories are in the repo working tree (repo scope) or a home agent config (global scope) — both places an untrusted checkout can pre-seed.

Same bug class as the `entire-graph` `os.Stat`/`os.Lstat` finding. `skill_cmd.go` is the one write path in this repo that the earlier hardening sweep missed: every other writer already goes through `rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents` / `rejectOpenFileAlias` / `writeFileAtomic`.

## Repro

`internal/cli/skill_write_escape_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestSkillDestinationsRejectTraversalInSynthesizedName
    name "../../../../../../../../tmp/pwn" escaped the skills dir: /var/tmp/pwn/SKILL.md
--- FAIL: TestSkillFileExistsSeesDanglingSymlink
    overwrite guard does not see a dangling symlink at the destination
--- FAIL: TestSkillWriteRefusesSymlinkedDestination
    writeSkillFile followed a symlink out of the skills dir
```

## Fix

- `skillDestinations` reduces the name to a single safe path component with `safePathComponent` — the helper branch directories already use, so no separator can survive.
- `skillDestination` keeps `base` and `rel` apart (unexported, JSON shape unchanged) so the write boundary can prove where the file lands.
- `writeSkillFile` checks every component from the agent root to the leaf with `rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents`, before **and** after `MkdirAll`, then writes. The leaf is in that check, which is what stops a dangling link being written through.
- `skillFileExists` replaces the guard's `os.Stat` with `os.Lstat`.

`TestSkillWriteAcceptsHonestDestination` pins that a normal install still works.

## Mutation

Reverting each half individually reproduces the corresponding failure above; restoring makes all four pass.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go test ./...` (full suite, 0 failures), `gofmt -l internal/` clean, `go vet ./internal/cli/` clean.","created_at":"2026-08-28T03:32:47Z","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-skill-write-escape","head_repo":"entireio/entire-brain","html_url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/96","number":96,"sha":"0769e6314bce225d2dc8a69399f4d51a43db0009","title":"fix(skills): skill-form writes escape the skills directory via synthesized name and symlinked destination","updated_at":"2026-08-28T04:51:27Z"}
