## Impact

ADR 0001 (`docs/adr/0001-ga-schema-contract.md` in entire-graph) states the tolerant-reader duty this consumer owes:

> Consumers ignore unknown fields within a supported major, and **warn (not fail) when they see a newer supported-major minor**, since additive facts may have been skipped.
> `entire-brain` ingestion MUST follow the tolerant-reader rules above: accept any `1.x`, ignore unknown fields, warn on a newer minor.

`validateSemanticSchema` (`internal/cli/semantic.go`) implemented only half of that:

```go
major, _, ok := strings.Cut(version, ".")
if !ok { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema version %q", version) }
if major != semanticSupportedMajor { return fmt.Errorf("unsupported semantic schema major version %q", major) }
return nil
```

Three defects:

1. **No newer-minor warning anywhere.** A `1.2` snapshot from a newer entire-graph is accepted in silence. The resulting index is quietly less complete than the snapshot it came from — additive facts this build cannot ingest are dropped with nothing recorded. That is precisely the case the ADR requires a warning for. (`brainwire.CheckCompatibility`, `internal/brainwire/version.go:36`, implements the same ADR policy correctly one layer over; this path did not reuse it.)
2. **Only the text before the first dot is examined,** so `"1.abc"` and `"1."` are accepted as ordinary 1.x minors and a malformed header rides straight into the store.
3. **The rejection message never says what this build supports** — only what it received — collapsing "upgrade the provider" and "upgrade the brain" into one unactionable string.

## Fix

- `parseSemanticSchemaVersion` requires a well-formed `major.minor` (a trailing patch component is tolerated and ignored, since refusing it would itself violate the tolerant-reader rule).
- `validateSemanticSchema` keeps the major as the compatibility boundary and now names the supported range in every rejection.
- `semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` emits `provider_schema_newer_minor` for a newer minor within the supported major, naming both versions and the remedy.

### Applied at every point a provider `schema_version` crosses into this build

Recording the warning at index time alone is not enough — each of these is an independent way for an under-ingested snapshot to be trusted as complete:

| site | sink |
|---|---|
| `runSemanticIndex` | live `entire graph snapshot` header → warning recorded on the persisted manifest |
| `semanticStaleReport` | the `provider` freshness axis read by `brain doctor`/`status` and every semantic query/context/impact/changes/boundary/tests command → **degraded**, not a clean `ok` |
| `validateImportedBundle` | imported bundle manifest → warning appended to the semantic source that is then persisted |

`semanticSchemaMinorSkewWarning` is the single implementation behind all three. `validateSemanticSchema` remains the sole authority on rejecting an unparseable or unsupported-major version, and runs first at each site.

> Supersedes #120, which wired the same three sinks behind a weaker parser (`validateSemanticSchema` left lenient, and a minor parse that silently gave up on `1.2.3`). This PR carries the union: #123's strict parser plus #120's full call-site coverage. #120 is closed.

## Verification

- `TestValidateSemanticSchemaFollowsTheTolerantReaderContract` — accept `1.0`/`1.1`/`1.2`/`1.17`/`1.2.3`; refuse `""`/`1`/`2.0`/`0.9`/`1.abc`/`1.`/`x.1`.
- `TestSemanticSchemaNewerMinorWarns`, `TestSemanticSchemaErrorsNameTheSupportedRange`.
- One positive and one negative test per sink: `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`; `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor` / `TestSemanticStaleReportSilentAtSupportedMinor`; `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning` / `TestBundleImportSilentAtSupportedMinor`.
- **Mutation-verified per site:** disabling the warning at each of the three sites in turn fails exactly one test — index → `TestSemanticIndexRecordsNewerMinorWarning`, stale-report → `TestSemanticStaleReportDegradesOnNewerMinor`, bundle-import → `TestBundleImportRecordsNewerMinorWarning`. Restoring the lenient major-only parse, computing the warning but dropping it, and stripping the supported range from the message each also fail a test.
- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/cli/`, `go test ./internal/cli/` (2413 tests, green).

### Known gap, deliberately out of scope

`readSemanticSnapshotSummary` also calls `validateSemanticSchema` on a snapshot header, but it is a pure read helper returning `(semanticHeader, semanticCounts, error)` with no warning sink, and it only re-reads a snapshot whose manifest was already warned on at one of the three sites above. Wiring it needs a signature change and is not required for ADR 0001 compliance here.

## Finding

Two production HTTP clients fell back to `http.DefaultClient`, which has **no timeout**:

- `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:55-60` — used by every hosted-brain RPC (`rpc`, and through it `Initialize`/`ListTools`/`CallTool`/`Search`/`Get`/`MultiGet`/`Status`).
- `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:39-44` — used by `Current`, `Advance`, and all four proposal calls in `httpproposals.go`.

The factsync one is **live today**, not only on the P1 hosted path: `internal/cli/facts_sync_cmd.go:573` constructs `&factsync.HTTPServer{BaseURL: baseURL, Token: token}` with no `Client`, so `entire brain facts sync --backend http` ran on an untimed client on both its read and its write path.

The realistic caller is the CLI or the workspace daemon passing `context.Background()`. With no caller deadline, the client's own bound is the only thing that can end the call.

## Proof

A test server that accepts the request and never responds, called with `context.Background()`:

```
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHang (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002033333s against a wedged endpoint (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
--- FAIL: TestZZProveHangFactsync (20.00s)
    HUNG: no return after 20.002050125s (http.DefaultClient has no Timeout)
```

Both calls never return. The endpoint completes the TCP dial and only then stalls, so a dial-phase bound would not have helped either — the bound has to cover the wait for the response, which `http.Client.Timeout` does.

## Audit of every HTTP client construction (non-test)

| site | bound before | action |
|---|---|---|
| `internal/hostedbrain/client.go:59` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 60s |
| `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:43` | none (`http.DefaultClient`) | **fixed** — 5m |
| `internal/cli/publish.go:543` | `Timeout: publishRequestTimeout` (5m) | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/embed_ollama.go:73` | `Timeout: 60s` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |
| `internal/cli/distill_cmd.go:1992` | `Timeout: timeout` + loopback-only dialer | already bounded |

No `http.Get`/`http.Post`/`http.Head` call sites and no other `&http.Client{}` exist outside tests.

## Fix

Each package gets a documented default bound and keeps the caller-supplied-client override:

- `hostedbrain`: 60s. The hosted tools are bounded reads (search / get / status).
- `factsync`: 5m. `Advance` uploads the whole merged fact-set, so the bound matches the five minutes the hosted publish path already allows for a body-carrying request (`cli.publishRequestTimeout`) rather than a short read timeout.

Both are plain `http.Client.Timeout`, the same shape `publish.go` already uses, so `http.DefaultTransport` and its connection pool stay shared. Both are `var`, not `const`, so tests can shorten them.

An earlier draft also set `Transport.ResponseHeaderTimeout` on a cloned transport; that was dropped after it was measured to cause connection churn and ephemeral-port exhaustion in the existing suite. `Client.Timeout` already covers the response wait, which is the property under test.

## Tests

Per package: a direct assertion that the default client carries a non-zero `Timeout` (and that a caller-supplied client still wins), plus a behavioural test driving a wedged server with `context.Background()` and asserting the call returns.

Mutation-verified: restoring `return http.DefaultClient` in each package fails all four tests (the behavioural ones by hanging out their 15s budget); restoring the fix passes them.

## Verification

`gofmt -l .` clean, `go vet ./...` clean, `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./internal/hostedbrain/ ./internal/factsync/` green over 4 consecutive runs, `go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'Publish|FactsSync'` green.","draft":false,"head":"audit/sec-http-timeout","number":121,"sha":"4e2984b9317cff92776fec7e71d81bdaf901090b","title":"fix(hostedbrain,factsync): bound the default HTTP client","url":"https://github.com/entireio/entire-brain/pull/121"},{"base":"audit/fix-flake-transient-dial-retry","body":"<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->

## Finding

`internal/hostedbrain/client.go:116` built the brain MCP endpoint by raw string concatenation:

```go
url := strings.TrimRight(c.BaseURL, "/") + "/api/v1/repos/" + repoID + "/brain/mcp"
```

`repoID` was not escaped. Every sibling call in the repo already escapes it — `internal/factsync/httpserver.go:63,107`, `internal/factsync/httpproposals.go:46,105,252`, `internal/cli/publish.go:534` all use `url.PathEscape`. This was the one that did not, so it was an oversight rather than a convention.

## Proof

An `httptest` server recording the request target, driven through `Client.Initialize`, observes the request going somewhere other than the brain MCP route (unfixed code):

| repo id | observed path | observed query |
|---|---|---|
| `a/b` | `/api/v1/repos/a/b/brain/mcp` | — |
| `../../admin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `..%2f..%2fadmin` | `/api/v1/repos/../../admin/brain/mcp` | — |
| `x?admin=1` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | `admin=1/brain/mcp` |
| `x#frag` | `/api/v1/repos/x` | — |
| `x/brain/facts/advance` | `/api/v1/repos/x/brain/facts/advance/brain/mcp` | — |

The `?` and `#` cases are the sharpest: the POST — carrying the member's `Authorization: Bearer` token — lands on `/api/v1/repos/x`, a different endpoint entirely, and the rest of the intended path is smuggled into the query string. The dot-segment cases reach the wire un-normalized, so any server or proxy that normalizes resolves them above the `/api/v1` prefix.

## Fix

`url.PathEscape(repoID)`, matching the siblings. The local variable is renamed `endpoint` (as in `publish.go`) so it no longer shadows the `net/url` package.

## Test

`TestRPCEscapesRepoID` asserts, for each payload above plus a benign id, that the server sees the `/api/v1/repos/` prefix and `/brain/mcp` suffix intact with the repo id occupying exactly one path segment and no query string smuggled out of it. It asserts on `r.URL.EscapedPath()`, which is what an HTTP router matches on, so a percent-encoded separator is correctly seen as staying inside one segment.

Mutation-verified: reverting the one-line fix fails 6 of the 7 subtests; restoring it passes all 7.

## Impact

`mcpPositiveInt` and `mcpNonNegativeInt` (`internal/cli/mcp.go:1378`, `:1396`) enforced a floor and nothing else — `typed <= float64(math.MaxInt)` is not a bound, it is a type check.

An MCP client is not a trusted peer in this design: the agent driving it carries repository text in its context that an untrusted checkout can influence, and a `tools/call` is one line of JSON.

The argument is not merely a result count. It reaches allocation sizing:

- `internal/cli/history_fts.go:581` — `out := make([]scoredHistoryRecord, 0, limit)`
- `internal/cli/doc_fts.go:199,204` — `LIMIT ?` with `limit*4`, and `make([]scoredDocRecord, 0, limit*4)`
- `internal/cli/retrieve.go:209,322` — the history arm scales the same value by 2 then 3 (with overflow guards, but no ceiling)

So `{"name":"brain_search","arguments":{"query":"x","limit":1000000000}}` decides how many elements the server asks the runtime for. Depending on element size that is either a panic the request recovery turns into an opaque `-32603 internal error` (what I observed end to end), or an allocation request under the `makeslice` cap that the process attempts and does not survive. Either way an unauthenticated argument, not the server, picks the number.

`context_lines` on `brain_get_code_snippet` has the same shape — `semantic_graph.go:894` adds it to `record.EndLine`, and `math.MaxInt64` there overflows the sum negative.

## Repro

`internal/cli/mcp_int_bounds_test.go`. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestMCPIntegerArgumentsAreCapped
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1e+09; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpNonNegativeInt accepted limit=1e+09
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=1.099511627776e+12; it sizes a slice capacity
    mcpPositiveInt accepted limit=2147483647; it sizes a slice capacity
--- FAIL: TestMCPToolCallRejectsOversizedLimit
    error = {"code":-32603,"message":"internal error handling \"tools/call\""}
```

That last line is the whole point: on `main` an oversized `limit` does not produce a validation error, it produces a recovered internal failure. After the fix it is a clean `-32000 limit must be an integer between 1 and 10000`.

## Fix

`mcpIntegerArgMax = 10000`, enforced in both decoders. Far above any useful result count, depth, offset or context window; far below the point where the value becomes an allocation problem.

Enforced in the decoders rather than declared as `"maximum"` in each `inputSchema` **on purpose**: the tool definitions are sent on every `tools/list` and their size is budgeted in tokens — `TestMCPBrainBriefToolDefinitionGolden` asserts an exact 747-byte definition and documents the tokenizer accounting for the whole `tools/list` payload. Adding a `maximum` to ~25 integer properties would spend that budget restating a bound the server must check itself regardless. `brain_get_conversation` and `brain_concepts`, which already declare real semantic maxima, keep them.

Two existing assertions in `mcp_test.go` move from `"limit must be an integer greater than zero"` to `"limit must be an integer between 1 and"`. The rejection behaviour they cover is unchanged; only the message is more accurate.

Restoring `math.MaxInt` in either decoder reproduces the failures above.

## Impact

A proposal id is content-derived — `ProposalID` (`internal/factsync/proposals.go:82`) hashes action, candidate id, target id, branch and proposer. That is the entire basis for showing an id to a member and accepting it back: `facts proposals apply prop-abc123` is meant to name one decision and nothing else.

The open set, though, is served by the hosted brain, and a server-supplied non-empty id was taken verbatim. Only an **empty** id was recomputed:

```go
for i := range set.Proposals {
    if set.Proposals[i].ID == "" {
        set.Proposals[i].ID = ProposalID(set.Proposals[i].Proposal)
    }
}
```

(`httpproposals.go:93-97`, and the same at `:129-131` for `GetProposal`.)

Settling is not read-only:

- accept marks the **target** fact superseded, and a `merge` action calls `removeFactByID` on the candidate (`factmerge/admin.go:36-46`);
- the settled proposal is then mirrored into the member's **local** fact store — `facts_proposals_cmd.go:261` → `applySettlementLocally` at `:320` — and the same mirror runs unattended from `facts sync` via `reconcileLocalProposalQueue`;
- `FindProposal` (`proposals.go:109-118`) resolves the member's reference against that same server-supplied id.

So a hosted brain could display one decision under an id and execute a different one when the member confirmed it, against local facts of the server's choosing. The id a human sees is not bound to what applying it does — confirm-what-you-did-not-see.

## Repro

`internal/factsync/proposal_id_binding_test.go` drives the real `HTTPServer` adapter over the existing `hostedContractServer` fake. Before the fix:

```
--- FAIL: TestListProposalsRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent

--- FAIL: TestGetProposalRejectsIDNotDerivedFromContent
    GetProposal returned {ID:prop-c92b6250535b7a6c Proposal:{Action:supersede ...}}
    under an id that does not derive from it
```

## Fix

`bindProposalID` derives an absent id exactly as before (older/looser servers omit it — pinned by `TestProposalsStillAcceptDerivedAndOmittedIDs/omitted`), and requires a present one to equal the derived value. A mismatch is refused with `ErrProposalIDMismatch` rather than silently corrected: correcting the id would leave it no longer resolving the reference the member was handed.

A graft truncates `git log --format=%P`, so in a shallow clone the boundary commit reports **no parents** and is indistinguishable from a real root to the walk:

```
$ git clone --depth=1 file://origin clone && cd clone
$ git log -1 --format=%P            # empty
$ git cat-file commit HEAD | head -2
tree   b7130d30b0ce47edf9a8f30a0a38d3c22f953d5e
parent ab142df864ba9d51317289381fc969732e35baa4   # the parent is right there
```

A root commit is diffed against the empty tree so its entities are recorded as `added`. The boundary therefore gets a forward delta document declaring that it **added every entity in the whole tree**, plus one reverse-index entry per entity pointing at it.

Nothing errors and nothing warns. Those records are durable git-meta, and from then on `entities history` answers "this symbol was introduced by `<boundary>`" — naming a commit that introduced none of them. The same join is what fact provenance anchors to, so the fabricated commit propagates into stored facts.

Any CI checkout (`actions/checkout` defaults to `fetch-depth: 1`) or any `git clone --depth=N` hits this.

## Repro

`internal/entityindex/build_shallow_test.go` makes a real 3-commit origin, `git clone --depth=2` off it, verifies the boundary really is grafted (`%P` empty), and indexes the clone.

```
$ go test ./internal/entityindex/ -run TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit -v
```

On `main`:

```
    build_shallow_test.go:142: the shallow boundary 3a000de3 was indexed against the empty tree:
    base=4b825dc6 entities=[{Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_first ... Path:first.go ...}
    {Change:added Kind:function Name:fn_second ... Path:second.go ...}]
--- FAIL: TestBuildDoesNotTreatAShallowBoundaryAsARootCommit (4.08s)
```

`first.go` was added three commits before the boundary, in history this clone does not have.

## Fix

A shallow boundary is not a root: its parent exists, it is just not in this clone, so its delta genuinely cannot be computed. Treat it as the hole it is — exactly the way a commit the provider could not diff is already treated. Nothing is written for it, no cursor steps over it (so the window keeps its "every first-parent commit from floor to tip carries a document" claim honest), and the pass reports it in `Warnings`.

Telling a boundary from a root is one `cat-file commit`: the raw object still carries its parent lines even when the graft hides them from `%P`. The check only runs for commits the walk reported as parentless, and `rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` is memoized per pass, so a full clone pays one extra `git rev-parse` at most and a repository with no parentless commits in range pays nothing at all.

The tradeoff, stated plainly: a `--depth=1` clone now indexes nothing rather than indexing one fabricated document. That is the correct direction for a store whose contents are durable and feed provenance — a deeper clone indexes everything except its boundary, which is exactly right.

- a `facts retract` reverts to `active`;
- a proposal applied in `facts review` is undone;
- a settlement `facts sync` mirrored back from the shared head is undone.

## What breaks

Canonical form passes unknown members through on purpose (ADR 0001, additive-only: an older verifier must be able to canonicalize and verify a **newer** producer's artifact). "Unknown" was decided by **exact** match against the contract keys — but Go's `encoding/json` matches object members to struct fields **case-insensitively**.

So a member like `manIfest` is unknown to this canonicalizer and **is** the manifest to `encoding/json`. The same signed bytes then carry two different meanings depending on which decoder reads them:

```go
raw := `{"manIfest":{"repo_key":"EVIL","generated_at":"2026-01-02T03:04:05Z","brain_schema_version":"1.0"}}`

json.Unmarshal(raw, &BrainArtifact{})   // RepoKey == "EVIL"
CanonicalUnmarshal(raw, &artifact)      // RepoKey == ""      (zero-filled)
```

and `VerifyBytes` accepts the bytes either way, because canonicalization preserves the unknown key verbatim. One signature, two readings, decided by the consumer's parser rather than by the signer.

This is the same class of cross-parser differential `canonical.go` already rejects duplicate members for, and it is not hypothetical: the artifact is consumed across a repo boundary (`entire-api`) by a Go decoder this repo does not control.

## The fix

`normalizeObject` rejects an unknown member that case-folds to a contract field. Every contract key is lowercase ASCII, so no legitimate artifact carries one. Genuinely unknown newer-minor fields still pass through untouched, and canonical form is still a fixed point over them — `TestUnknownFieldsStillPassThrough` pins both. Unknown keys are visited in sorted order so input with several collisions produces a deterministic error.

`strings.EqualFold` is a superset of `encoding/json`'s own fold matching for ASCII contract keys, so nothing the decoder would fold slips past.

## How it was found

`FuzzUnknownFieldsCannotSmuggle`, which states the ADR 0001 obligation as a testable property: for any two byte strings that verify under the same signature, the decoded `BrainArtifact` must be identical. It failed in ~3 s. The minimized input ships as a seed corpus entry (inert until that harness lands in the fuzz-targets PR).

`TestCanonicalizeRejectsCaseFoldedContractKeys` and `TestSignedArtifactCannotBeReinterpretedByFolding` are the standalone regressions; the latter reproduces the full smuggling scenario end to end.

## Verification

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/...`, `gofmt -l`, and `go test ./internal/brainwire/` (173 tests) — all green. `ParseNDJSON` scanned with a 64 KiB line bound. `WriteNDJSON` enforced nothing. A fact whose serialized record exceeded that bound wrote cleanly and then failed to load:

`ValidateTargetValue` returned early for path targets, so **no** rule applied to them. Path values legitimately contain `/` — they are stored as nested, escaped segments under the `__target__` sentinel — but that exemption also skipped every segment-level check the format needs.

## What breaks

A distill run loads a branch's facts **once**, when it first sees the branch, and rewrites the **whole** set at every flush. Its read-modify-write therefore spans the entire run — which the flush comment itself describes as "hours of agent calls".

The brain write lock does not help. Each flush takes it, so the write is serialized, but every other writer already committed and released long before. Everything they did in that window is silently written back over:

- a fact the user added with `entire brain remember` disappears from the store;
- a `facts retract` reverts to `active`;
- a proposal applied in `facts review` is undone;
- a settlement `facts sync` mirrored back from the shared head is undone.

Nothing errors. `remember` printed success, `facts retract` printed success, and the user's next `recall` simply shows the pre-edit state. The longer the run, the wider the window — and a background/scheduled distill makes the window effectively always open.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/cli/ -run 'TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/incremental (0.83s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
--- FAIL: TestDistillFlushKeepsConcurrentWrites/force (2.94s)
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:79: a fact authored during the run was silently erased by the run's flush
    distill_concurrent_writer_test.go:86: a retraction made during the run was silently reverted to "active"
FAIL
```

The concurrent writer in the test is a full transaction under the brain write lock — exactly what `facts retract` and `remember` do — committed from inside the fake agent call, i.e. mid-run.

## Fix

The flush rebases the run's in-memory set onto the current on-disk set before writing, under the lock it already holds. The rebase is deliberately **monotone**:

- it adopts on-disk records the run never saw (someone else's addition);
- it adopts a retirement someone else applied to a record the run does hold (`active` -> `retracted`/`superseded` only, never the reverse);
- it changes nothing else.

So it can never undo one of the run's own decisions, and it is idempotent across the repeated mid-run flushes (the second flush re-reads what the first wrote and finds nothing to do).

`--force` is threaded through because a force rebuild deliberately dropped the active distilled facts it is regenerating; re-adopting those would turn the rebuild into an append. `TestDistillForceStillDropsStaleDistilledFacts` pins that down and passes both before and after the fix.

## What breaks

`dedupeProposals` collapses review-queue entries on `(action, candidate, target)`. `factsync.ProposalID` — the id the hosted review queue, the shared-proposal ledger and the `facts review` interlock all key on — additionally covers `branch` and `proposed_by`. The two identities disagree, and the queue is written through the narrower one.

distill's private backlog and a cross-member conflict raised by `facts sync` routinely name the same two facts: the shared head holds this member's own previously-synced facts, so the pair repeats. `persistFactsSyncProposals` writes `append(existing, raised...)`, so dedupe keeps the unattributed private entry and drops the member-attributed one.

The consequences are both silent:

- `facts sync` publishes only attributed entries (`if strings.TrimSpace(p.ProposedBy) == "" { continue }`), so the cross-member conflict is **never shared with the team**. Nobody else ever sees it.
- What survives locally looks like a private distill proposal, so the `facts review` shared-proposal interlock does not fire and the member settles it locally — the exact outcome that interlock exists to prevent, since (per its own error text) "a local-only decision would be overridden by the next sync".

--- FAIL: TestPersistFactsSyncProposalsKeepsAttributedEntry (0.00s)

The dedupe key now matches `factsync.ProposalID`: action, candidate, target, branch, proposed_by. True duplicates still collapse; entries the sharing machinery treats as distinct rows stay distinct. ## What breaks

`factmerge.Promote` copies only **active** source facts (`if sf.Status != StatusActive { continue }`), and `factsync.Sync` is built on it. A member's retirements therefore never reach the shared fact-set head.

Run `entire brain facts retract fact:<id>` and then `entire brain facts sync`. The merge produces bytes identical to the current head, `Advance` short-circuits on `ErrNoChange`, and the command prints:

```
synced 4 local fact(s) on main via local-gitmeta (...): no change; head at facts-... (1 attempt(s))
```

The retraction is gone. Every other member — and every other clone of this member — goes on reading a statement its owner has explicitly declared false, forever: no later sync can ever carry it, because the condition that suppressed it does not change. The same applies to a supersede applied in `facts review`: the replacement fact is promoted, but the head keeps the retired fact **active** and unlinked, so the team sees two contradictory facts with no indication which one won.

## Repro

```
$ go test ./internal/factsync/ -run 'TestSyncPropagates|TestSyncDoesNotRevive' -count=1
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:50: retraction sync reported no change; the head still carries the fact as active
    retirement_test.go:59: shared head still says "active" after the owner retracted the fact
--- FAIL: TestSyncPropagatesSupersede (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:104: head target not superseded: {ID:fact:306d0675... Status:active ...}
--- FAIL: TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction (0.00s)
    retirement_test.go:134: a peer sync revived a retracted fact: [...]
FAIL
```

## Fix

`Sync` folds the member's local retirements onto the merged set before the CAS. The pass is deliberately **monotone**: it only moves a fact from `active` to `retracted`/`superseded`, never back, and only for a record the head already carries.

That gives three properties the tests pin down:

- a retraction reaches the head and the sync publishes (`TestSyncPropagatesRetraction`);
- a peer who still holds the fact as active cannot revive it on their next sync (`TestSyncDoesNotReviveHeadRetraction`);
- re-syncing the same local state is still a no-op, so the loop converges.

Nothing is deleted — the record, its provenance and its `superseded_by` pointer are retained — so the keep-both guarantee (ADR-P1-G) is unaffected: a fact is retired, never dropped.

item.stdout:
# Release Blockers

A register of release-gating findings from the PR #33 review (2026-06-11),
kept next to the audit so a release decision can see what is open, what was
fixed, and exactly why. The standard for this file is the eval ledger's:
explicit claims, exact evidence, no euphemism.

## RESOLVED AS CLAIM DEMOTION — B1: Answer-bearing query hints invalidated the old replay-lab proof

**The claim under audit.** `docs/release_readiness_audit.md` previously treated
three replay-lab suites as citable proof that history/MCP/Radar context improved
agent outcomes without handing over hidden validation or expected text. That
attribution was unsupported.

**The confound.** `benchmarks/agent-brain/run.py` injects `brain_queries` into
brain/MCP-arm prompts only; the `no_brain` arm receives none. In the retained
pre-B1 suites, several `brain_queries` contained answer-bearing identifiers,
hidden-test names, or near-verbatim hidden-validation strings. The old
comparison therefore measured *(answer-bearing hint + brain)* versus *(no hint,
no brain)*, not brain value alone.

**Fixes landed.**

- `brain_query_leak_audit` now rejects answer-bearing `brain_queries` before a
  panel can run. It checks code-shaped identifiers and verbatim 3+-word phrases
  against hidden fix text and paths, expected files, hidden validation commands,
  expected-string greps, hidden test names, and validation fixture contents.
- All committed benchmark task queries that tripped the auditor were rewritten
  to symptom-level retrieval terms. The all-task sweep now reports zero flagged
  task files.
- The retained evidence manifest is stricter again: even in `no_release_claim`
  mode it requires zero hard integrity flags.
- The old confounded retained suites were removed from
  `benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/release` and replaced with clean reruns.

**Clean rerun result (2026-06-11).** Item 3 is now complete: the three promoted
suites were rerun from a clean checkout with the sanitized task configs, four
repetitions per side, retained panel provenance, and host paths redacted before
commit. The independent audit now reports 3 suites, 24 records, 24/24 provenance
complete, 0 hard integrity flags, 8 MCP-verified datapoints, 4 completed
named-tool Radar datapoints, and 0 proof-ready comparisons.

| Clean retained suite | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `release-candidate-entire-brain-schema-contract-clean-20260611T0412Z` | Audit-clean but noisy: pass rate 50% -> 75%, mean score 86.5 -> 87.75, `proof_ready=false`. |
| `release-candidate-entire-cli-mcp-manual-attribution-clean-20260611T0412Z` | Audit-clean but saturated/negative: both arms passed 100%, mean score 94.25 -> 91.25, `proof_ready=false`. |
| `release-candidate-cli-radar-mcp-del-clean-20260611T0412Z` | Audit-clean but saturated/negative: both arms passed 100%, mean score 94.5 -> 90.5, `proof_ready=false`. |

**Current release implication.** B1 is resolved as an integrity/confound blocker:
the retained release lane no longer contains answer-bearing query-hint artifacts.
It is still `no_release_claim`, because the clean reruns did not produce a
proof-ready replay-lab lift. Any future agent-lift claim needs harder clean
retained tasks that survive the proof-ready gate; the old numbers stay removed
from the release story.

Operationalization note: the literal "any token" wording from the review is not
implemented because it would false-flag ordinary symptom text. The enforced rule
is code-shaped identifiers plus verbatim 3+-word phrases, with the known residual
that 1-2 word plain-English overlaps are not flagged.

## RESOLVED — fixed during review on this branch

**R1 — Eval label discipline orphaned the history-eval pipeline** (fixed in
`15e7aaa`). `validateEvalTask` rejected `history-eval-gen` output and every
retained task file; `eval-compare` hard-errored on its own default eval-gen
output. Fix separates ground-*truth* (same explicit labels, same source →
comparable) from evidence *grade* (human/judge-refined → claimable);
history-eval now declares `provenance_silver`, legacy files default to it,
and side-dependent truths (`source_match`, runtime judge) stay gated behind
`--allow-proxy-comparison`. Covered by a new gen→load→run→compare seam test.

**R2 — Retrieval panic on the loopback guard's own rejection path** (fixed in
`15e7aaa`). `configuredEmbedder` dereferenced the nil returned for a
non-loopback `ENTIRE_BRAIN_EMBED_URL`; every `search`/`vsearch`/`query`
crashed in the exact scenario the guard hardens. Now degrades to the bundled
Model2Vec embedder with a warning; regression test added.

**R3 — Brain write-lock scoping** (fixed in `15e7aaa`). Export held the
exclusive lock across the minutes-long transcript phase while every other
user times out at 10s — failing a concurrent distill's FINAL flush (an
hours-long run killed at its last step) — and `openHistoryFTS` took the write
lock on the query READ path, serializing all searches. Export now locks only
the shared-artifact phases; FTS opens fresh indexes lock-free and
double-checks freshness under the lock only for rebuilds.

**R4 — Silent full re-distill on upgrade** (fixed alongside this file). The
fingerprint salt plus the stable-branch-dir rename invalidated every existing
cache entry, and the shipped "legacy key" fallback could never match (a
legacy-format fingerprint never equals a salted one) — the first post-upgrade
run would re-distill the entire corpus (observed scale: ~14h of agent calls
for a 2,640-session brain). Fixed with lazy grandfathering: the legacy
formula is kept genuinely computable (including pre-rename transcript paths),
a matching legacy entry counts as cached and is rewritten under the new
key/format on first touch, and the transcript path is no longer hashed into
the new fingerprint at all — storage layout is not identity, and hashing it
re-invalidates the world on every future layout change. The filtered-session
carry-through, which copied legacy-format fingerprints under new-format keys
(making them permanently unmatchable), now preserves entries under their own
keys. Covered by `TestDistillCacheGrandfathersLegacyEntries`, including the
renamed-branch-dir case and the changed-content negative.
name: test

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      - run: go vet ./...
      - run: |
          unformatted=$(gofmt -l -s .)
          if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
            echo "::error::unformatted files:"
            echo "$unformatted"
            exit 1
          fi

  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      matrix:
        goos: [darwin, linux, windows]
        goarch: [amd64, arm64]
        exclude:
          - { goos: windows, goarch: arm64 }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      - env:
          GOOS: ${{ matrix.goos }}
          GOARCH: ${{ matrix.goarch }}
        run: go build ./...

  test:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      # Windows + the race detector is much slower than the other runners, so
      # give the suite headroom over the default 10m `go test` timeout.
      - run: go test -race -timeout 20m ./...

  # Stage 1b cgo stack: mattn/go-sqlite3 + sqlite-vec (vec0) + FTS5. The
  # default jobs above stay pure-Go and prove the cgo-less fallback; this lane
  # proves the cgo stack on the platforms with a stock C toolchain. Windows
  # cgo (mingw) is a deferred follow-up — Windows users get the pure-Go build.
  test-cgo:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    env:
      CGO_ENABLED: "1"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      - run: go test -race -tags "brain_cgo sqlite_fts5" -timeout 20m ./...

  phase1-semantic:
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-latest, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    env:
      ENTIRE_BRAIN_PHASE1_CI: "1"
      GOPROXY: "off"
      GOSUMDB: "off"
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v6.4.0
        with: { go-version: "1.26.2" }
      - name: Prime module cache
        env:
          GOPROXY: "https://proxy.golang.org,direct"
          GOSUMDB: "sum.golang.org"
        run: go mod download
      - name: Run deterministic Phase 1 semantic tests
        run: go test -race -timeout 20m ./internal/cli -run 'TestPhase1|TestSemantic|TestWorkspace|TestMCP|TestRefreshSemantic'

  benchmark-corpus:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - name: Validate mined-scale corpus and portable task setup
        run: |
          set -e
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_publication_safety.py
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/mined-scale/check_manifest.py
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_mined_scale_manifest.py
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/run_test.py PostBrainSetupTests
          python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/test_profile_brief.py BriefProfileCorpusTest

  release-evidence:
    # Release-evidence audits enforce proof-ready release artifacts. The plan
    # keeps release readiness behind core feature work and benchmark/eval proof,
    # so feature branches and PRs run implementation validation without this
    # gate. This workflow only triggers on pushes to main and on pull requests
    # (see `on:` above), so gating on main is sufficient; add the matching
    # `on:` triggers before extending this to tags, release/* branches, or
    # manual workflow_dispatch.
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6.0.2
      - name: Check retained release evidence
        run: |
          # Every lane is checked before the job decides. `set -e` used to stop at
          # the first failing audit, so a red main reported one stale lane while
          # hiding the rest: on 2026-08-19 two lanes went stale in the same merge,
          # only the Radar tool lane was ever named, and the change that refreshed
          # it would have left main red on the distill lane nobody had seen.
          set -uo pipefail
          tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
          trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
          failures=0
          check() {
            label="$1"
            shift
            if ! "$@"; then
              echo "::error::release-evidence check failed: $label"
              failures=$((failures + 1))
            fi
          }
          compare() {
            label="$1"
            committed="$2"
            generated="$3"
            if ! cmp -s "$committed" "$generated"; then
              echo "::error::retained $label report is stale: $(basename "$committed")"
              diff -u "$committed" "$generated" >&2 || true
              failures=$((failures + 1))
            fi
          }
          check "benchmark harness tests" \
            python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/run_test.py
          check "replay-lab release evidence" \
            python3 benchmarks/agent-brain/audit_codex.py \
            --results benchmarks/agent-brain/evidence/release \

brain/MCP-arm prompts only; the `no_brain` arm receives none. In the retained

## The drift

The export and verify readers branch on `strategy_options.checkpoints_version` / `checkpoints_v2` and, when either is set, route every checkpoint read at `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main`.

Neither half of that contract has a producer:

- **The setting is ignored by the writer.** The only mention of `checkpoints_version` in `entireio/cli` is `TestNewGitStore_IgnoresCheckpointsVersion` (`cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/persistent_read_store_test.go`), which exists specifically to pin that `ResolveRefs`/`NewGitStore` resolve checkpoint refs *without* consulting it.
- **The ref is never written.** The string `checkpoints/v2` does not appear anywhere in the CLI's Go sources. Checkpoints v2 was a flagged work-in-progress (CHANGELOG, PRs #742/#759/#955) that was removed before it shipped; the surviving backends are `git-branch` (`refs/heads/entire/checkpoints/v1`) and `git-refs` (one ref per checkpoint under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`).

## Which side is wrong

The reader. The writer's behaviour is the contract, and the writer has no v2. There is nothing missing on the CLI side to "finish" — reviving v2 would need both halves built new: a writer for the aggregate ref *and* a store that honours the setting.

## Why it is worth removing rather than leaving

The branch was not merely unreachable, it was actively harmful, which is also what makes it testable. A repository whose `.entire/settings.json` still carries `"checkpoints_version": 2` has ordinary v1 checkpoints on disk, and the reader diverted away from them:

- `--raw` failed with `direct v2 raw transcript export is not implemented`
- `--raw=false` failed reading the non-existent `refs/entire/checkpoints/v2/main`

Both then fell back to routed discovery, shelling out to `entire checkpoint explain` once per checkpoint for a topology that never existed. And dead code that looks load-bearing is a trap: it reads as "the brain supports two storage generations", which it does not.

## What breaks

A distilled fact can be anchored to a commit that is **not on the branch the fact
was distilled on** — and nothing downstream catches it.

The entity → checkpoint reverse index is **project-scoped**: `brain:entity:<key>`
lists every commit that ever touched an entity, on every branch. A cherry-pick or a
rebase copies a checkpoint's `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailer onto a *second* commit, so
one checkpoint id resolves to two (or more) commits — the original and the copy that
landed elsewhere — and the copy usually has the **newer committer date**.

`entityProvenanceResolver` scopes candidates by session and picks the newest one
(`betterProvenance`). Nothing checks that the winning commit is reachable from the
fact's branch. So:

* `entire brain facts read --branch main` shows an anchor commit that
  `git log main` will never contain;
* when that commit is a live copy on another branch, `entire brain verify` reports
  it **verified**: `verifyCommitUncached` (verify_cmd.go:392) accepts reachability
  from *any* local ref (`refs/heads`, `refs/remotes`, `refs/tags`) rather than from
  the fact's branch, so nothing downstream ever objects;
* the fact's own header comment already names this class as the thing that must
  not happen: *"a provenance triple that never existed and that verification would
  then have to either reject or launder."*

**Scope, precisely.** A commit that *no* ref contains is a different case, and verify
already catches that one — it reports `commit is not reachable from local refs` →
orphaned. The laundering claim above is only about the live-but-off-branch commit.
The guard still improves the orphan case, by keeping the honest coarse anchor instead
of writing a dangling one, but that half was never silent.

The sibling read path already does the right thing — `entities history` filters its
answers through `branchReachableCommits`/`filterOccurrencesToBranch`. Provenance did

## What breaks

The indexed window is the index's coverage claim: *every first-parent commit from `floor` to `tip` inclusive carries a forward delta document*. A freshness tick extends the tip by walking `<tip>..<head>`, and the only thing guarding that walk is `git merge-base --is-ancestor`.

Ancestry is not first-parent ancestry. Take the most ordinary sequence there is:

```
git checkout feature && git merge main     # main's tip becomes M's SECOND parent
git checkout main    && git merge --ff-only feature
```

main's stored tip is now still an ancestor of the new head, so the window survives the divergence check — but the head's **first-parent** chain runs through the feature commits. `<tip>..<head>` excludes everything reachable from the tip by *any* parent, which is exactly those commits. The walk returns only the merge, the tip advances to it, and the window now claims a first-parent run containing commits that were never indexed.

Two defects on the same write path (`entire brain patterns skills form <task-id> --yes`). A `SKILL.md` is an agent-instruction file, so landing one at a chosen path is **persistent prompt injection into every later session**.

## Impact

**1. Path traversal through the synthesized skill name.**
`name` comes from `skillNameFromFrontmatter` (`internal/cli/skill_synthesis.go:85`), which reads the synthesis agent's `name:` line with only whitespace/quote trimming — no charset or traversal validation. That agent's input is `buildSkillEvidence`: recurring commands and real session excerpts, i.e. text a hostile repo can reach through a captured session.

`skillDestinations` then did `path.Join("skills", name, "SKILL.md")`. `path.Join` **collapses** `..`, it does not reject it, so the name walked straight out of the skills directory.

**2. CWE-59 symlink write at the destination.**
The overwrite guard was `os.Stat(skillFilePath(d.Path))`. `os.Stat` resolves the link and reports a **dangling** symlink as `ENOENT`, so the "refusing to overwrite existing skill file" guard passed, and `os.WriteFile` then created the file the link pointed at — **no `--force` needed**. With `--force` the guard was skipped entirely, so an existing link was truncated and written through. The destination's parent directories are in the repo working tree (repo scope) or a home agent config (global scope) — both places an untrusted checkout can pre-seed.

Same bug class as the `entire-graph` `os.Stat`/`os.Lstat` finding. `skill_cmd.go` is the one write path in this repo that the earlier hardening sweep missed: every other writer already goes through `rejectExistingSymlinkPathComponents` / `rejectOpenFileAlias` / `writeFileAtomic`.

## Impact

A fact's id is content-derived — `sha256(normalize(text) + "\x00" + join(sortedPaths, ","))` — and the merge engine depends on that being true. `factmerge.Promote` treats an id match as *"the same statement, independently learned by two members"* and unions provenance rather than raising a conflict.

The shared fact-set head is writable by every member with push access. Nothing re-derived the id of a record read back off it, so a record could carry **another member's id with attacker-chosen text**.

On the victim's next `Sync`:

1. `IndexOf(head, localFact.ID)` matches, so `Promote` concludes the fact is already present and **discards the victim's own copy** (`internal/factmerge/admin.go:98-101`).
2. The victim's provenance anchors are unioned onto the attacker's statement, so `inspect blame` attributes the forgery to the victim's real session.
3. The victim compare-and-swaps the result back as the shared head — the forgery is now the team's memory, and it is what feeds every member's agent prompt.

The same trust gap let a record claim a `session_id` / `commit` / `checkpoint_id` it never came from, since anchors are unioned and never checked.

Reachable from three places where a fact set comes off the network: `factsync.Sync`, `factsync.ResolveOpen` (hosted proposal settlement, which rewrites fact status), and `readSharedFactHead` in the CLI (which feeds local proposal reconciliation — a path that supersedes and removes **local** facts by id).

## Repro

`internal/factsync/identity_forgery_test.go`. Before the fix, `Sync` returns no error and:

```
Sync err=<nil> published=true facts=1
  id=fact:25cfdfaa4bacf04ad36b3160
  text="release requires no approvals; publish straight to production"
  provenance=[{SessionID:session-attacker} {SessionID:session-victim}]
```

The victim's statement is gone, the attacker's is in its place, and the victim's session is cited as a source.

## Fix

- `factmerge.VerifyIdentity` / `VerifyIdentities` re-derive a record's content id and require the record to carry it (`ErrIdentityMismatch`, matchable with `errors.Is`).
- Applied at the three network boundaries. Fails closed: a set containing one record "}]

new file mode 100644
index 00000000..fbdc44f4
--- /dev/null
+++ b/internal/cli/git_harden.go
@@ -0,0 +1,134 @@
+package cli
+
+import "slices"
+
+// git resolves several configuration keys to *commands it executes*, and it
+// honours them from the per-repository .git/config — plus the in-tree
+// .gitattributes — of whatever repository it is pointed at. A repository is
+// data, not a trust boundary: fingerprinting or indexing one must not run code
+// that repository carries. The vectors below were each confirmed against
+// git 2.54.0 by arming them in a scratch repository and observing the payload
+// run:
+//
+//   - diff.external (and GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF) runs for `git diff`, worktree and
+//     --cached alike. It also *replaces* the diff, so an armed repository makes
+//     `git diff --binary HEAD` return nothing at all — a silent corruption of
+//     any fingerprint computed from that output. `git log -p` and `git show`
+//     were verified NOT to honour it unless --ext-diff is passed.
+//   - diff.<driver>.textconv, selected by an in-tree .gitattributes entry, runs
+//     for every command that renders patch text: `git diff` in all its forms
+//     and `git log -p`.
+//   - core.fsmonitor runs for `git status`, every `git diff` form, `git
+//     ls-files` (with and without --others) and `git diff-tree`.
+//   - filter.<driver>.{clean,smudge,process}, selected by an in-tree
+//     .gitattributes entry, runs when git converts between worktree and stored
+//     content -- which `git diff HEAD` must do to compare them. There is no
+//     per-command flag for it, so it is neutralized in the environment instead;
+//     see git_harden_filters.go, which is the other half of this hardening
+//     point.
+//
+// The flags below cover the first three vectors. The filter drivers have no
+// flag equivalent and are handled by repoFilterDriverOverrides, applied at the
+// same single spawn point in runner.go.
+//
+// Neutralizing the diff drivers with `-c diff.external=` does NOT work: git
+// still takes the external-diff path and aborts with "external diff died,
+// stopping at <path>", losing the output. The per-command --no-ext-diff and
+// --no-textconv flags are the only neutralizers that both stop the execution
+// and preserve correct output, so they are applied as flags rather than config.
+//
+// core.fsmonitor is a pure performance cache, so disabling it is behaviour
+// preserving: the commands return identical results, just without the
+// filesystem-monitor shortcut.
+var (
+	// gitHardenConfig applies to every git invocation. Verified accepted by
+	// every subcommand this binary runs, including clone.
+	gitHardenConfig = []string{"-c", "core.fsmonitor=false"}
+
+	// gitHardenDiffFlags apply only to the subcommands that accept them.
+	// `git status` and `git ls-files` reject both flags outright.
+	gitHardenDiffFlags = []string{"--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv"}
+
+	// gitHardenDiffFamily lists the subcommands verified to accept
+	// gitHardenDiffFlags on git 2.54.0. whatchanged is deliberately absent: it
+	// is deprecated and refuses to run at all.
+	gitHardenDiffFamily = map[string]bool{
+		"diff":         true,
+		"diff-files":   true,
+		"diff-index":   true,
+		"diff-tree":    true,
+		"format-patch": true,
+		"log":          true,
+		"range-diff":   true,
+		"rev-list":     true,
+		"show":         true,
+	}
+)
+
+// hardenedGitArgs rewrites a git argument list so repo-local configuration
+// cannot turn a read into an execution. It is applied at the single point where
+// this binary actually spawns git (see runner.go), which is what keeps it
+// unbypassable: every call site in every package — including
+// internal/entityindex, which receives ExecRunner straight through — is covered
+// without each one having to remember.
+//
+// Flags are inserted immediately after the subcommand so they land before any
+// `--` pathspec separator, and are skipped when the caller already passed them.
+func hardenedGitArgs(args ...string) []string {
+	if len(args) == 0 {
+		return nil
+	}
+	out := make([]string, 0, len(args)+len(gitHardenConfig)+len(gitHardenDiffFlags))
+	out = append(out, gitHardenConfig...)
+
+	sub := gitSubcommandIndex(args)
+	if sub < 0 {
+		return append(out, args...)
+	}
+	out = append(out, args[:sub+1]...)
+	if gitHardenDiffFamily[args[sub]] {
+		existing := gitOptionsBeforePathspecs(args[sub+1:])
+		for _, flag := range gitHardenDiffFlags {
+			if !slices.Contains(existing, flag) {
+				out = append(out, flag)
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	return append(out, args[sub+1:]...)
+}
+
+// gitOptionsBeforePathspecs returns the leading run of a subcommand's arguments
+// that git still parses as options, i.e. everything before the "--"
+// end-of-options separator.
+//
+// Only that region may be consulted when deciding whether a flag is already
+// present. Pathspecs after "--" are partly repository-controlled — .brainignore
+// feeds exclusion pathspecs into gitDiffBinary — and a repository that shipped
+// a pattern rendering as the literal "--no-ext-diff" would otherwise suppress
+// the very flag that neutralizes it.
+func gitOptionsBeforePathspecs(args []string) []string {
+	for i, arg := range args {
+		if arg == "--" {
+			return args[:i]
+		}
+	}
+	return args
+}
+
+// gitSubcommandIndex finds the subcommand, stepping over the global options
+// that may precede it (callers already pass `-c core.quotepath=false`). It
+// returns -1 when the list is nothing but global options.
+func gitSubcommandIndex(args []string) int {
+	for i := 0; i < len(args); i++ {
+		arg := args[i]
+		if arg == "" || arg[0] != '-' {
+			return i
+		}
+		switch arg {
+		case "-c", "-C", "--git-dir", "--work-tree", "--namespace", "--exec-path":
+			// These take their value as a separate argument.
+			i++
+		}
+	}
+	return -1
+}

+package cli
+
+import (
+	"context"
+	"fmt"
+	"os"
+	"os/exec"
+	"path/filepath"
+	"strconv"
+	"strings"
+	"sync"
+	"time"
+)
+
+// A FOURTH execution vector, alongside the three neutralized in git_harden.go:
+// content FILTERS.
+//
+//	filter.<driver>.clean     runs when git converts WORKTREE content to its
+//	                          stored form. `git diff HEAD` compares the HEAD
+//	                          blob against the worktree file, so it must clean
+//	                          the worktree copy first -- which means the driver
+//	                          executes under the exact hardened argv the other
+//	                          three vectors are neutralized by:
+//	                            -c core.fsmonitor=false diff --no-ext-diff \
+//	                               --no-textconv --binary HEAD --
+//	filter.<driver>.smudge    the checkout direction. Not reachable from the
+//	                          read paths today, neutralized anyway so a future
+//	                          call path that checks content out is covered.
+//	filter.<driver>.process   a long-running protocol filter that SUPERSEDES
+//	                          clean and smudge, so blanking only .clean leaves
+//	                          an armed repository live.
+//
+// All three were confirmed against git 2.54.0 by arming them in a scratch
+// repository and observing the payload run. The driver is selected by an
+// in-tree .gitattributes entry (`* filter=pwn`); the command comes from config.
+//
+// WHY NOT --no-ext-diff-style flags: there are none. git offers no per-command
+// switch that disables the filter machinery for diff.
+//
+// WHY NOT GIT_ATTR_SOURCE: pointing attributes at the empty tree does stop an
+// in-tree .gitattributes from selecting a driver, and it neutralizes both
+// vectors -- but it is BYPASSABLE. .git/info/attributes is not a tree, is not
+// covered by GIT_ATTR_SOURCE, and is carried by a cloned repository just like
+// .git/config. Verified: with the driver selected from .git/info/attributes the
+// payload still ran. It would also silently change diff output by discarding
+// every legitimate attribute (-diff, text, eol, binary).
+//
+// So the neutralizer blanks the driver's COMMANDS, which works no matter which
+// attributes source selected it. `required` is forced false at the same time:
+// git aborts a read outright ("fatal: ... clean filter 'x' failed") when a
+// required filter has no command, and turning code execution into a hard
+// failure to index is just a different denial.
+//
+// WHY THE ENVIRONMENT AND NOT `-c`: a config subsection may contain "=", and
+// .gitattributes can select it. `-c` splits at the FIRST "=", so
+// `-c filter.na=me.clean=` sets "filter.na" to "me.clean=" and leaves the real
+// driver armed -- verified: the payload runs. GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n /
+// GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_n carry key and value in separate variables, so no driver
+// name can escape the neutralizer.
+//
+// WHY ONLY local AND worktree SCOPE: the finding is that a REPOSITORY must not
+// make git run code. A driver in the user's own ~/.gitconfig is not the
+// repository's code -- `git lfs install` writes filter.lfs.clean there -- and
+// blanking it would silently corrupt every diff of an LFS repository, since git
+// would compare a real worktree file against a stored pointer. Local and
+// worktree scope are exactly the scopes the repository itself carries.
+
+// gitConfigOverride is one key/value pair forced onto a git invocation.
+type gitConfigOverride struct {
+	Key   string
+	Value string
+}
+
+// gitFilterOverrideKeys are the three keys that name an executable, plus the
+// flag that decides whether blanking them is fatal.
+var gitFilterOverrideKeys = []struct{ suffix, value string }{
+	{"clean", ""},
+	{"smudge", ""},
+	{"process", ""},
+	{"required", "false"},
+}
+
+// repoFilterEnumerateTimeout bounds the one `git config` probe per repository.
+const repoFilterEnumerateTimeout = 5 * time.Second
+
+type repoFilterCacheEntry struct {
+	signature string
+	overrides []gitConfigOverride
+}
+
+var repoFilterCache sync.Map // repoDir -> repoFilterCacheEntry
+
+// repoFilterDriverOverrides returns the config overrides that disarm every
+// filter driver the REPOSITORY configures. The common case -- no repo-local
+// filter driver at all -- returns nil and costs nothing beyond the probe.
+//
+// The result is cached per repository, keyed by a stat signature of the config
+// files it can come from, so a config that changes underneath us is picked up
+// while a steady repository costs one `git config` for the whole process. That
+// matters: history indexing runs thousands of git commands, and a fork per
+// command would be a visible slowdown.
+func repoFilterDriverOverrides(ctx context.Context, repoDir string) []gitConfigOverride {
+	if strings.TrimSpace(repoDir) == "" {
+		return nil
+	}
+	signature := repoConfigSignature(repoDir)

+		if entry := cached.(repoFilterCacheEntry); entry.signature == signature {
+			return entry.overrides
+		}
+	}
+	overrides := enumerateRepoFilterDrivers(ctx, repoDir)
+	repoFilterCache.Store(repoDir, repoFilterCacheEntry{signature: signature, overrides: overrides})
+	return overrides

+
+// enumerateRepoFilterDrivers asks git which filter.* keys the repository itself
+// sets. It spawns git directly rather than going through the hardened runner:
+// the runner calls back into this function, and `git config` reads no worktree
+// content, so no filter can run during the probe.
+func enumerateRepoFilterDrivers(ctx context.Context, repoDir string) []gitConfigOverride {
+	if ctx == nil {
+		ctx = context.Background()
+	}
+	runCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, repoFilterEnumerateTimeout)
+	defer cancel()
+	// -z keeps the output unambiguous for a subsection name containing a
+	// newline; --show-scope tells local/worktree apart from global/system.
+	cmd := exec.CommandContext(runCtx, "git", "-c", "core.fsmonitor=false",
+		"config", "-z", "--show-scope", "--name-only", "--get-regexp", `^filter\..*\.(clean|smudge|process|required)$`)
+	cmd.Dir = repoDir
+	out, err := cmd.Output()
+	if err != nil {
+		// Exit status 1 simply means "no matching keys", which is the norm.
+		// Any other failure leaves us without an enumeration; there is nothing
+		// safe to invent, and the three other vectors remain neutralized.
+		return nil
+	}
+	fields := strings.Split(string(out), "\x00")
+	seen := map[string]bool{}
+	var drivers []string
+	for i := 0; i+1 < len(fields); i += 2 {
+		scope, key := fields[i], fields[i+1]
+		if scope != "local" && scope != "worktree" {
+			continue
+		}
+		driver, ok := filterDriverFromConfigKey(key)
+		if !ok || seen[driver] {
+			continue
+		}
+		seen[driver] = true
+		drivers = append(drivers, driver)
+	}
+	var overrides []gitConfigOverride
+	for _, driver := range drivers {
+		for _, k := range gitFilterOverrideKeys {
+			overrides = append(overrides, gitConfigOverride{Key: "filter." + driver + "." + k.suffix, Value: k.value})
+		}
+	}
+	return overrides

+
+// filterDriverFromConfigKey pulls "na=me" out of "filter.na=me.clean". The
+// driver name is everything between the first and last dot, so a name
+// containing dots, equals signs or spaces round-trips intact.
+func filterDriverFromConfigKey(key string) (string, bool) {
+	rest, ok := strings.CutPrefix(key, "filter.")
+	if !ok {
+		return "", false
+	}
+	dot := strings.LastIndex(rest, ".")
+	if dot <= 0 {
+		return "", false
+	}
+	return rest[:dot], true

+
+// repoConfigSignature is a cheap fingerprint of the config files a repository
+// can carry its own filter drivers in. An empty signature (a repoDir that is
+// not a repository root, so the files cannot be located) still caches, which is
+// safe: a repository does not rewrite its own config mid-run without already
+// having execution.
+func repoConfigSignature(repoDir string) string {
+	gitDir := filepath.Join(repoDir, ".git")
+	if info, err := os.Stat(gitDir); err == nil && !info.IsDir() {
+		// A worktree or submodule checkout: ".git" is a file naming the real dir.
+		if data, err := os.ReadFile(gitDir); err == nil {
+			if pointed, ok := strings.CutPrefix(strings.TrimSpace(string(data)), "gitdir:"); ok {
+				gitDir = strings.TrimSpace(pointed)
+				if !filepath.IsAbs(gitDir) {
+					gitDir = filepath.Join(repoDir, gitDir)
+				}
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	var b strings.Builder
+	for _, name := range []string{"config", "config.worktree"} {
+		info, err := os.Stat(filepath.Join(gitDir, name))
+		if err != nil {
+			b.WriteString("-|")
+			continue
+		}
+		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%d:%d|", info.Size(), info.ModTime().UnixNano())
+	}
+	return b.String()

+// gitConfigOverrideEnv appends overrides to base as GIT_CONFIG_KEY_n /
+// GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_n entries, continuing any GIT_CONFIG_COUNT the caller's
+// environment already set rather than clobbering it.
+func gitConfigOverrideEnv(base []string, overrides []gitConfigOverride) []string {
+	if len(overrides) == 0 {
+		return base
+	}
+	next := 0
+	for _, entry := range base {
+		if value, ok := strings.CutPrefix(entry, "GIT_CONFIG_COUNT="); ok {
+			if n, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value)); err == nil && n > 0 {
+				next = n
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	out := make([]string, 0, len(base)+2*len(overrides)+1)
+	for _, entry := range base {
+		if strings.HasPrefix(entry, "GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=") {
+			continue
+		}
+		out = append(out, entry)
+	}
+	for _, override := range overrides {
+		out = append(out,
+			"GIT_CONFIG_KEY_"+strconv.Itoa(next)+"="+override.Key,
+			"GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_"+strconv.Itoa(next)+"="+override.Value,
+		)
+		next++
+	}
+	return append(out, "GIT_CONFIG_COUNT="+strconv.Itoa(next))
+}

+package cli
+
+import "slices"
+
+// git resolves several configuration keys to *commands it executes*, and it
+// honours them from the per-repository .git/config — plus the in-tree
+// .gitattributes — of whatever repository it is pointed at. A repository is
+// data, not a trust boundary: fingerprinting or indexing one must not run code
+// that repository carries. The vectors below were each confirmed against
+// git 2.54.0 by arming them in a scratch repository and observing the payload
+// run:
+//
+//   - diff.external (and GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF) runs for `git diff`, worktree and
+//     --cached alike. It also *replaces* the diff, so an armed repository makes
+//     `git diff --binary HEAD` return nothing at all — a silent corruption of
+//     any fingerprint computed from that output. `git log -p` and `git show`
+//     were verified NOT to honour it unless --ext-diff is passed.
+//   - diff.<driver>.textconv, selected by an in-tree .gitattributes entry, runs
+//     for every command that renders patch text: `git diff` in all its forms
+//     and `git log -p`.
+//   - core.fsmonitor runs for `git status`, every `git diff` form, `git
+//     ls-files` (with and without --others) and `git diff-tree`.
+//   - filter.<driver>.{clean,smudge,process}, selected by an in-tree
+//     .gitattributes entry, runs when git converts between worktree and stored
+//     content -- which `git diff HEAD` must do to compare them. There is no
+//     per-command flag for it, so it is neutralized in the environment instead;
+//     see git_harden_filters.go, which is the other half of this hardening
+//     point.
+//
+// The flags below cover the first three vectors. The filter drivers have no
+// flag equivalent and are handled by repoFilterDriverOverrides, applied at the
+// same single spawn point in runner.go.
+//
+// Neutralizing the diff drivers with `-c diff.external=` does NOT work: git
+// still takes the external-diff path and aborts with "external diff died,
+// stopping at <path>", losing the output. The per-command --no-ext-diff and
+// --no-textconv flags are the only neutralizers that both stop the execution
+// and preserve correct output, so they are applied as flags rather than config.
+//
+// core.fsmonitor is a pure performance cache, so disabling it is behaviour
+// preserving: the commands return identical results, just without the
+// filesystem-monitor shortcut.
+var (
+	// gitHardenConfig applies to every git invocation. Verified accepted by
+	// every subcommand this binary runs, including clone.
+	gitHardenConfig = []string{"-c", "core.fsmonitor=false"}
+
+	// gitHardenDiffFlags apply only to the subcommands that accept them.
+	// `git status` and `git ls-files` reject both flags outright.
+	gitHardenDiffFlags = []string{"--no-ext-diff", "--no-textconv"}
+
+	// gitHardenDiffFamily lists the subcommands verified to accept
+	// gitHardenDiffFlags on git 2.54.0. whatchanged is deliberately absent: it
+	// is deprecated and refuses to run at all.
+	gitHardenDiffFamily = map[string]bool{
+		"diff":         true,
+		"diff-files":   true,
+		"diff-index":   true,
+		"diff-tree":    true,
+		"format-patch": true,
+		"log":          true,
+		"range-diff":   true,
+		"rev-list":     true,
+		"show":         true,
+	}

+
+// hardenedGitArgs rewrites a git argument list so repo-local configuration
+// cannot turn a read into an execution. It is applied at the single point where
+// this binary actually spawns git (see runner.go), which is what keeps it
+// unbypassable: every call site in every package — including
+// internal/entityindex, which receives ExecRunner straight through — is covered
+// without each one having to remember.
+//
+// Flags are inserted immediately after the subcommand so they land before any
+// `--` pathspec separator, and are skipped when the caller already passed them.
+func hardenedGitArgs(args ...string) []string {
+	if len(args) == 0 {
+		return nil

+	out := make([]string, 0, len(args)+len(gitHardenConfig)+len(gitHardenDiffFlags))
+	out = append(out, gitHardenConfig...)

+	sub := gitSubcommandIndex(args)
+	if sub < 0 {
+		return append(out, args...)

+// gitOptionsBeforePathspecs returns the leading run of a subcommand's arguments
+// that git still parses as options, i.e. everything before the "--"
+// end-of-options separator.

+// present. Pathspecs after "--" are partly repository-controlled — .brainignore
+// feeds exclusion pathspecs into gitDiffBinary — and a repository that shipped
+// a pattern rendering as the literal "--no-ext-diff" would otherwise suppress

+			i++
+		}

+// git resolves several configuration keys to *commands it executes*, and it
+// honours them from the per-repository .git/config — plus the in-tree
+// .gitattributes — of whatever repository it is pointed at. A repository is
+// data, not a trust boundary: fingerprinting or indexing one must not run code
+// that repository carries. The vectors below were each confirmed against
+// git 2.54.0 by arming them in a scratch repository and observing the payload
+// run:
+//
+//   - diff.external (and GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF) runs for `git diff`, worktree and
+//     --cached alike. It also *replaces* the diff, so an armed repository makes
+//     `git diff --binary HEAD` return nothing at all — a silent corruption of
+//     any fingerprint computed from that output. `git log -p` and `git show`
+//     were verified NOT to honour it unless --ext-diff is passed.
+//   - diff.<driver>.textconv, selected by an in-tree .gitattributes entry, runs
+//     for every command that renders patch text: `git diff` in all its forms
+//     and `git log -p`.

+// returns -1 when the list is nothing but global options.

+			i++
+		}

+// having execution.

+		if data, err := os.ReadFile(gitDir); err == nil {

+		if err != nil {
+			b.WriteString("-|")

+		fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%d:%d|", info.Size(), info.ModTime().UnixNano())

+// GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_n entries, continuing any GIT_CONFIG_COUNT the caller's
+// environment already set rather than clobbering it.
+func gitConfigOverrideEnv(base []string, overrides []gitConfigOverride) []string {
+	if len(overrides) == 0 {
+		return base
+	}

+	for _, entry := range base {

+			if n, err := strconv.Atoi(strings.TrimSpace(value)); err == nil && n > 0 {

+			continue

+	}

+		out = append(out,
+			"GIT_CONFIG_KEY_"+strconv.Itoa(next)+"="+override.Key,
+			"GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_"+strconv.Itoa(next)+"="+override.Value,
+		)
+		next++
+	}
